item.title: Opus 5.5, in plain words.
item.description: Opus 5.5 in plain words: what changed, how it compares with Sonnet, Haiku and Fable, how to set effort, and a six-step self-check with prompts.
item.content:encoded:
There's a new Claude in your model menu.

It's called Opus 5.5.

You've seen the headlines and the benchmark charts.

But you have three simple questions. Should I use it? For what? And how do I get the best work out of it?

This issue answers all three, in plain words.

I teach people to use AI at work, and these are the questions I hear after every new model.

So every fact here comes from Anthropic's own announcement, help centre and documentation. No hype, and no made-up tests.

Inside:

  1. What changed, in six lines
  2. What Anthropic tested, and under which conditions
  3. The five models side by side
  4. Which Claude for which job
  5. How to switch, in three clicks
  6. How to set the effort
  7. A six-step loop that makes Claude check its own work
  8. When to stop checking
  9. The mistakes to avoid
  10. What stays the same
  11. The new words, in plain English

One practical guide at a time: the exact steps, the prompts to copy and the mistakes to skip.

What changed, in six lines

Anthropic announced Claude Opus 5.5 on September 22, 2026, the first model in the Claude 5.5 family.

Here's what Anthropic says is new, compared with Opus 5:

  • Smarter. It performs at the level of Claude Fable 5.1 on most work.
  • Cheaper. It costs 40% less to run than Opus 5 on typical workloads.
  • Faster. Its answers come more than 30% faster.
  • Easier to read. Main point first, less jargon, and it follows your writing rules.
  • More careful with facts. Anthropic's docs say it slips less often on figures and sources.
  • More room. At launch, Anthropic raised five-hour limits on Pro, Max, Team and seat-based Enterprise, and gave subscribers one limit reset.
Opus 5 Opus 5.5
API price per million tokens (in / out) $5 / $25 $4 / $20
Default effort on the API High Medium
Thinking (API) On by default, but could be switched off Always on, at every effort level
Knows the world up to May 2026 June 2026

The lower default isn't a downgrade. In Anthropic's tests, Opus 5.5 at Medium matches or beats Opus 5 at High on coding and knowledge work.

Clearer writing makes checking easier. Anthropic says it "has made Opus 5.5's work easier to follow and check". That idea runs through this issue.

Key point

If you only remember one thing: Anthropic's docs say that if you're unsure which model to use, start with Opus 5.5.

It follows writing rules closely, so give it yours at the start of a chat.

My writing rules
For everything you write in this chat, follow these rules:
- Put the main point in the first line.
- Short sentences. Plain words. No jargon.
- [Add your own: British spelling, no bullet points in emails, a word limit]
If a rule clashes with something I ask, tell me which rule you broke and why.

Use it when: you start a chat that will produce text other people read.

Read Anthropic's announcement

What Anthropic tested

These are Anthropic's own numbers, not independent tests.

The conditions

Unless noted, Anthropic ran these at max effort, with its production safety checks on, which it says likely reduce some scores. At Medium in the app, your results will differ.

Real-world work

GDPval-AA v2.1 tests real-world work across 44 occupations. Scores are Elo ratings: higher is better.

The full table

Test Area Opus 5.5 Compared with
GDPval-AA v2.1 Knowledge work, 44 occupations 1846 Elo Fable 5.1: 1735. Opus 5: 1708
Humanity's Last Exam, with tools Knowledge work 67.7%
Terminal-Bench 4.0, at Extra high Coding 66.4% Opus 5: 52.3%
CursorBench 4.0 Coding 57.8% 52.5% at Medium
OSWorld 2.1 (partial) Using a computer 81.8%
Chartography, with tools Reading charts 89.0%

At Medium, the default, Anthropic reports 54.6% on FrontierCode. It says that beats GPT-6 Astra's top score of 53.3%, for about a fifth of the cost per task.

Research without made-up numbers

Anthropic asked Opus 5.5, Fable 5.1 and Opus 5 to write a report on a company's quarterly results, using only what they could find on a copy of the web.

An automated grader checked every figure and every quote against the sources. One invented figure or quote meant a fail.

Across effort settings, 16 of 18 Opus 5.5 reports passed.

Neither Fable 5.1 nor Opus 5 passed in any attempt.

Note

Anthropic itself says benchmark margins have become a less reliable guide to real-world differences. In its own use, the gap between Opus 5.5 and Fable 5.1 is narrower than the scores suggest. Read the scores as direction, not as a promise for your work.

Send this to one colleague who keeps asking "which Claude should I use?"

The five models side by side

The current lineup, from Anthropic's own pages.

Opus 5 Opus 5.5 Sonnet 5.5 Haiku 5.5 Fable 5.2
What it's for The previous Opus Complex work that needs careful judgment Well-scoped everyday tasks, polished documents, slides and spreadsheets High-volume, quick tasks Demanding reasoning and long agentic work
Speed (Anthropic's label) Not rated. Opus 5.5 is 30%+ faster Moderate Fast Fastest Moderate
Knows the world up to May 2026 June 2026 June 2026 June 2026 June 2026
API price (in / out) $5 / $25 $4 / $20 $2 / $10 from $0.10 / $0.50 $8 / $40
On the Free plan? No No Sonnet: yes Haiku: yes No

Three notes:

  • API prices are what developers pay. In the app, you pay your plan price, and the model you pick changes how fast you use your limits.
  • Free plan: Anthropic's pricing table shows Sonnet and Haiku on Free. Opus is on Pro, Max and Ultra.
  • Fable 5.2 is on paid plans only. On Max and Ultra you can spend up to half your weekly limit on it. On Pro it runs on usage credits.

NewsletterRight tool, right job.Stop looking for one AI that does everything. Five everyday jobs, and where to start for each:

Which Claude for which job

Anthropic calls Opus 5.5 its "strongest daily driver".

Its advice: start most work with Opus 5.5. Move up to Fable when the job needs more. Move down to Sonnet 5.5 or Haiku 5.5 when it needs less.

Two questions get you to the right model.

"Careful judgment" means a recommendation, a risk, a trade-off, a long or messy file, or work going to someone who matters.

Not sure where your own work fits? Let Claude sort your week, using the same rules.

Sort my week by model
Here are the tasks on my list this week: [paste the list].

Sort them into four groups, using these rules:
- Opus 5.5: needs judgment, long files, or goes to someone important
- Sonnet 5.5: clear, well defined, and I want it quickly
- Haiku 5.5: small, quick and repeated
- Fable 5.2: the hardest reasoning, only if Opus already fell short

Give me a table: task, group, one-line reason. Flag any task you're unsure about.

Use it when: you plan your week, or you keep hitting your limits. Keep the table and reuse it.

Tip

Anthropic lists model choice and effort level among the things that use up your limits faster. Keep Opus 5.5 for the jobs that matter, and use Sonnet 5.5 or Haiku 5.5 for the rest.

How Claude usage limits work

Switch to Opus 5.5 in three clicks

The path, from Anthropic's help centre:

  1. Find the model name. On the web and the desktop app, it's next to the send button, below where you type. On mobile, it's at the top of the screen.
  2. Click it, then pick Opus 5.5. Click More models to see the rest.
  3. Click Effort and choose a level. Start with the one marked Default.

What you'll see: the model name changes to Opus 5.5. The change applies from Claude's next response, and you can change it again at any point.

Try it on one real task

Pick a task you did last week with another model. Run it again with Opus 5.5 at the default effort.

First test of Opus 5.5
I'm trying a new model on a task I do often.

Here's the task: [describe the task and paste the material].
Here's who will read the result: [your manager, a client, your team].
Here are my writing rules: short sentences, the main point first, no jargon.

Do the task. Then, in three lines, tell me what you were least sure about.

Use it when: you want to know if Opus 5.5 earns its place on a task you repeat.

What you'll get back: the task, plus three lines on its weakest points. Compare it with last week's answer yourself. That's the test that counts.

Set the effort for the job

Effort controls how much thinking Claude puts into a response. Higher is more thorough, but slower, and uses more of your limits.

The path: model name, then Effort, then a level. The recommended one is marked Default.

Level What Anthropic says Use it for
Low Works well for routine tasks and stretches your usage further Rewording, short replies, quick lookups in a file
Medium Opus 5.5's default Most everyday work: drafts, summaries, a first analysis
High The best overall balance of quality and speed A long document, a decision, a tricky analysis
Extra high For long-running coding and agentic tasks, with deeper reasoning than High Long coding or multi-step agent jobs
Max The most thorough option, for the deepest reasoning The hardest problem of your month, when you can wait

Three rules from Anthropic's docs:

  • Want a lighter answer? Lower the effort first. It cuts thinking, cost and waiting more reliably than typing "be quick".
  • Save Extra high and Max for work where you've seen them make a real difference.
  • Don't copy your old setting across. At the same level, Opus 5.5 tends to think more per turn than Opus 5, especially at Extra high and Max.

Plan high, write at the default

For big work, try two passes. Anthropic's Claude Code guide suggests a similar split: plan with Opus, then do the work with Sonnet.

Set effort to High and send this:

Plan it first
Before writing anything, plan this with me.
The task: [describe it]. The reader: [who]. The deadline: [when].
Give me the 3 to 5 sections you'd write, the facts each section needs, and anything you need from me.
Don't write the draft yet.

Use it when: the work is long, or a wrong start would waste an hour.

What you'll get back: a short outline with the gaps named. Then set effort back to Medium and ask for the draft, section by section.

Make Claude check its own work, in six steps

A smarter model still makes mistakes.

Anthropic's help centre says Claude can "hallucinate": give incorrect or misleading information, even about its own abilities, like claiming it sent an email. It says not to rely on Claude as your only source of truth.

Anthropic says Opus 5.5 slips less often on figures. Less often isn't never.

So here's a loop for anything with your name on it: six steps, one prompt each, in the same chat as the work.

Step 1: Set the finish line

Before Claude writes a word, decide what "done and right" means.

Anthropic's prompting guide says to treat Claude like a brilliant new employee who lacks context, and to be specific about the format and limits you want. A finish line does both, as tests.

Step 1: Set the finish line
Here's what I need: [the task].
It's for: [who reads it, and what they'll do with it].

Before you start, write the finish line: 3 to 7 tests this must pass to be done and right.
Make each test something I could check quickly, like a length, a position or a source.
Add any test you think I've missed. Then wait for my OK.

Use it when: someone else will read the result.

What you'll get back: a numbered list, such as "1. One page or less. 2. The recommendation comes first. 3. Every figure comes from the attached file." Edit it, then say OK.

Step 2: Allow "I don't know"

Now ask for the work, with one extra permission.

Anthropic says giving Claude explicit permission to say "I don't know" can drastically reduce false information.

Step 2: Do the work, flag the gaps
Do the task now, using only the material I've given you.
If something isn't in my material, or you're not sure, say "I don't know" or tag it [GUESS].
Don't fill gaps to make it read smoothly.
At the end, list the questions you'd want me to answer.

Use it when: the finish line is agreed. Attach your notes or files.

What you'll get back: a draft with a few [GUESS] tags and some questions. That's a good sign.

Step 3: Trace every claim

Next, make every fact show where it came from.

Step 3: Trace every claim
Before I use this, check your answer.
List every number, name, date and quote you used.
For each one, say where it came from: the file I gave you, a source you found, or your own knowledge.
Mark anything you can't trace to a source as "unverified".
Don't fix anything yet. Just show me the list.

Use it when: an answer has numbers, names or dates in it.

For long reports, contracts and threads, Anthropic suggests a stronger version: quotes first, answer second.

Step 3, for long files: Quotes first
Before you answer, find the word-for-word quotes in the document that matter for my question. Number them.
Then answer using only those quotes, citing them by number.
If a claim has no quote behind it, take it out and tell me you did.

For decks and spreadsheets, use what Anthropic says Opus 5.5 is now good at: catching details that are easy to miss in large files.

Step 3, for decks and sheets: Find the mismatches
Check this file for things that don't agree with each other.
For example: a chart that doesn't match the figures in the table, a total that doesn't add up, a date that falls on the wrong weekday, or a name spelled two ways.
List each mismatch with where you found it. Don't change anything yet.

Use it when: a deck or workbook is about to go to anyone else.

Step 4: Grade against the finish line

Now hold the draft up against the tests from Step 1.

Step 4: Grade against the finish line
Read the finish line we agreed again. Then read your draft.
Make a table with three columns: the test, the result (pass, partly or fail), and the line in the draft that proves it.
Be strict. If you can't point to a line, it's not a pass.
Don't fix anything yet.

Use it when: the draft is done, before you ask for any edits.

What you'll get back: rows like "Three risks: partly. Only two are named." The gaps are visible at a glance.

Step 5: Attack the weak spots

A draft can pass every test and still be wrong. So ask Claude to argue against itself, as your toughest reader would.

Step 5: Argue against yourself
Now take the other side, as [my reader: the client, our finance lead, a new starter] would.
Give me the three strongest reasons your draft could be wrong or fail with them, worst first.
For each one, quote the line it's about and say what I'd need to check to find out.
Then tell me if you'd still make the same recommendation, and why.

Use it when: the work recommends something, or someone senior will read it.

What you'll get back: three ranked objections, each tied to a line, and a clear "yes, still" or "no, change it".

Step 6: Fix, log and hand over

Only now does Claude fix anything. And it shows you what it changed.

Step 6: Fix, log and hand over
Fix only the tests that failed or were partly met, and the objections you agreed were fair.
Then give me:
1. The new version.
2. A change log: what you changed, and why, one line each.
3. A list of what I must still check myself, such as unverified claims, sources to open and figures to compare.

Use it when: Steps 4 and 5 are done, never before.

If Claude says it did something, one more check.

Step 6: Check the actions
List every action you said you took in this chat: files made, searches run, messages sent.
For each one, tell me whether you actually did it with a tool, or only described it.
Give me the file name or link for anything you made.

Use it when: Claude says it saved, sent, searched or created something.

The whole loop in one prompt

Use it when: the job is small, and six separate messages would be overkill.

The whole loop, in one go
Do the task below in six steps, and show each step under its own heading:
1. Write the finish line: 3 to 5 tests this must pass.
2. Do the task. Tag anything you're unsure of as [GUESS].
3. List every number, name and quote with its source, or mark it "unverified".
4. Grade the draft against the finish line: pass, partly or fail.
5. Give the two strongest reasons it could be wrong.
6. Fix what failed, and list what I must still check myself.

The task: [describe it and paste the material].

Watch out

A self-check makes Claude's work better. It doesn't replace yours. For anything with your name on it, open the sources and check the numbers yourself.

Newsletter Check a skill before you trust it. Mojeed Abisiga · mojeedabisiga.com
NewsletterCheck a skill before you trust it.A Claude skill can run code on your behalf. Here's what can go wrong, and the five-minute check to run first:

When to stop checking

Checking has a cost. Every round uses your limits and your time.

So decide your exits before you start.

Anthropic gives similar advice for long, unattended agent work: stop after two or three automatic nudges on the same task, so a stuck job ends and can be reviewed.

It also says to treat a "done" as a report, not as proof. Check the list.

Use this when: Claude stops, or says it's finished, with work still open.

Finish the open items
Your checklist still has open items: [list them].
Carry on with them now.
If one is blocked, tell me exactly what's blocking it and what you need from me.

The mistakes to avoid

The three that cost the most:

  • Asking "is this right?" A yes tells you nothing. Ask for a graded table with evidence (Step 4).
  • Max effort on everything. It's slower and uses more of your limits. Start at the default.
  • Staying on Sonnet 4.6. It leaves the model selector on Free, Pro, Max and Ultra on December 8, 2026. Anthropic recommends Sonnet 5.5 instead.

What stays the same

You don't need to relearn Claude. Here's what carries over, from Anthropic's docs:

  • The model menu. It's in the same place, next to the send button.
  • The effort levels. Low, Medium, High, Extra high and Max, with Medium as the default in the Claude apps.
  • Thinking stays on. As on Opus 5, Sonnet 5.5 and Haiku 5.5, you can't turn it off in the app. Lower the effort instead.
  • The amount of text it takes in. Up to 1M tokens in chat on paid plans, as with Opus 5. For scale, Anthropic says 200K tokens is about 500 pages.
  • Zero data retention. Like previous Opus models, Opus 5.5 is available with it.
  • Your prompts. A good brief is still a good brief.

Two things that might surprise you

Claude may switch models for some requests. Opus 5 and Opus 5.5 run safety checks on every request, and on what Claude reads, such as files and search results. Routine bug fixing is fine, but most cybersecurity tasks may be answered by Opus 4.8, and some biology requests by Opus 5. That's expected behaviour.

Research has its own model. Claude's Research feature runs on Opus 5.5, whatever model you picked for the chat.

For developers

The model ID is claude-opus-5-5, on the Claude API, Amazon Web Services, Google Cloud and Microsoft Azure. Fast mode runs it at up to 2.5x speed in Claude Code and on the Claude Platform, at $8 / $40. Requests that switch thinking off now return an error: set an effort level instead.

Brief Claude like a colleague

The new words, in plain English

Model launches come with their own vocabulary. Here's every term from this issue, in one line each.

If you learn one, make it effort: the setting you'll touch most.

NewsletterClaude is a toolkit.Six tools in one app, and how to set each one up:

What to do today

Open Claude.

Click the model name next to the send button and pick Opus 5.5.

Leave effort on the default.

Paste "My writing rules" at the top of a new chat.

Run one real task from your week.

Then run the six-step loop on it, starting with the finish line.

You'll learn more about your own work than any benchmark can tell you.

item.description: What Claude is, the plans, the apps, how to ask, what to trust and check, the features that matter, a ten-minute trial and eight ways professionals use it.
item.content:encoded:
Everyone seems to be talking about Claude.

You've never opened it.

Or you opened it once, typed a question, and weren't sure what to do next.

That's fine. This guide starts at zero and goes one step at a time.

I teach people to use AI at work, and my mission is to make data and AI easy for everyone. So: plain words, real steps, and a picture wherever you need to find something on screen.

By the end of this guide you'll have:

  • Claude on your phone and your computer, on the right plan
  • the few settings that matter, set once
  • a simple way to ask that gets good answers
  • a clear sense of what to trust and what to check
  • one real task done, and eight ideas borrowed from professionals

You need: a phone or a computer, an email address, and to be 18 or older.

How to read it: sections 1 to 4 get you set up. Sections 5 to 9 teach you to use it well. Sections 10 to 13 are practice.

Get the next one in your inbox

One practical guide at a time: the exact steps, the prompts to copy and the mistakes to skip.

Free. Delivered by Substack, one click to unsubscribe. Form not showing? Subscribe on Substack.

1. Meet Claude

Claude is an AI assistant made by a company called Anthropic.

Anthropic's help centre describes it as a large language model, trained to be helpful, honest and harmless, with a conversational tone.

In plain words: you write to it the way you'd write to a person, and it writes back.

It helps in two ways.

It answers. Ask a quick question, get a quick answer, then ask a follow-up.

It does the work. Describe the result you want, and Claude works through the steps: it searches the web, reads your files, runs code and hands back finished files. On paid plans, longer tasks keep running in the cloud if you close your laptop.

Anthropic calls itself a public benefit corporation. Its stated mission is the responsible development of advanced AI for the long-term benefit of humanity.

What it can make for you

Most beginners undersell this. Claude doesn't only write replies. It makes things you can use:

  • Files: Word, Excel, PowerPoint and PDF, to download or save to Google Drive. Spreadsheets come with working formulas.
  • Artifacts: a design, a deck, a document, a dashboard or a small interactive tool, opened beside the chat.
  • Diagrams and charts: drawn in the chat on the web and desktop when you say "draw this as a diagram".

Not sure where to start? Anthropic's own advice is to ask Claude what it can help with. Make it personal:

What can you do for me?
I work as [your job]. A normal week for me includes [three or four tasks, for example writing reports, answering customer emails, planning events]. List ten specific ways you could help me this week. For each one, give me the exact first message I should send you. Start with the ones that would save me the most time.

Use it in your first five minutes. You'll get ten jobs, each with a first message you can copy straight back in.

Key point

Treat Claude like a capable new colleague. Give it a proper brief, and check its work before anything goes out under your name.

2. See how it differs from ChatGPT

It's the first question most people ask.

Here's a fair answer, built only from what each company publishes about its own product.

Claude ChatGPT
Free plan Yes, with limited usage every 5 hours and every week Yes, advertised as unlimited text chats with GPT-6, within abuse guardrails
First paid plan Pro: $20 a month, or $17 a month paid yearly Plus: $20 a month
Bigger plans Max at $100 and Ultra at $200 a month Pro 100, Pro 200 and Pro 500, at $100, $200 and $500 a month
Ads None: Anthropic has committed to keeping Claude ad-free May appear on the Free and Go plans
Making pictures No photos or illustrations; it makes diagrams, charts and visuals Image generation on every plan (limited on Free)
Text it takes in at once Up to 1M tokens in chat on paid plans, with the newest models 27K to 128K tokens (GPT Instant) or 256K to 400K (GPT Reasoning), by plan

A token is a small piece of text. For scale, Anthropic says 200K tokens is about 500 pages.

What that means for you:

  • You want pictures made? ChatGPT makes images. Claude doesn't.
  • You work with long documents? Claude's paid plans take in more text at once.
  • You'd rather not see ads? Anthropic has promised no ads and no sponsored links in Claude. (Its announcement, and OpenAI's page on ads.)
  • Price? The first paid step costs the same: $20 a month.

Tip

Coming from ChatGPT? Your old chats can't move over, but its memory of you can. Go to Settings → Your Claude and select Start import. Claude shows you a prompt to use in your old assistant. Paste the answer back and click Add to memory. Anthropic calls this experimental. Its guide is here.

Newsletter Right tool, right job. Mojeed Abisiga · mojeedabisiga.com
NewsletterRight tool, right job.Stop looking for one AI that does everything. Five everyday jobs, and where to start for each:

3. Get Claude and pick a plan

Download and open it

One account, three places:

  • In a browser: go to claude.ai.
  • On your computer: Claude Desktop, from claude.com/download.
  • On your phone: search "Claude by Anthropic" in the App Store or the Play Store.

Your conversations, projects, memory and preferences sync between them.

Device Needs
Mac macOS 13 (Ventura) or newer
Windows Windows 10 or newer
Linux (beta) Ubuntu 22.04 or newer, or Debian 12 or newer
iPhone and iPad iOS or iPadOS 18.0 or newer
Android Android 8.0 (Oreo) or newer

You must be 18 or older and in a supported location. Nigeria, the United Kingdom and the United States are on Anthropic's list, with many others. Check yours here. A new account also needs a phone number from a supported location.

Sign in

There's no password. You get two ways in:

  1. Continue with Google: sign in with your Google account and click Next.
  2. Continue with email: type your email and click the button. Claude emails you a link titled "Secure link to log in to Claude.ai".

Opened that email on another device? The link gives you a code instead. Type it on the device where you started.

No email? Check your spam folder for a message from @mail.anthropic.com.

Pick a plan

Start on Free. It costs nothing and covers a lot.

These are US prices: Anthropic shows local currency where it supports it. Prices exclude tax and can change.

Plan Price What you get
Free $0 Chat on web, desktop and phone, web search, file creation, memory, connectors and artifacts
Pro $20 a month, or $17 a month billed yearly ($200 up front) More usage than Free, plus Cowork, Claude Code, Research, more models, and Claude in Chrome and Microsoft 365
Max $100 a month 5x Pro's usage, early access to features, priority at busy times
Ultra $200 a month 10x Pro's weekly usage, and no 5-hour limit for verified accounts
Team $20 a seat a month billed yearly, or $25 monthly (Premium seats: $100 or $125) Teams of 2 to 150, with admin controls
Enterprise $20 a seat a month billed yearly, plus usage at API rates Larger organisations, from 20 seats

See the full plan details.

  • Your first week: Free.
  • You keep hitting the limit, or want Cowork or Claude Code: Pro.
  • Pro's limits still stop you most days: Max or Ultra.

To upgrade: click your initials (bottom left), then Settings → Billing → Upgrade plan → Get Pro plan. Choose monthly or yearly and click Subscribe. Max and Ultra are monthly only.

How the limits work

There's no fixed number of messages. Instead:

  • Your limit runs on a five-hour window, starting with your first message.
  • Paid plans add a weekly limit, which resets at a fixed day and time.
  • On Free, how much you get also varies with demand.
  • Web, desktop, phone and Claude Code all draw from the same pool.

To see where you stand, open Settings → Usage. Current session shows how much of your five-hour limit you've used and when it resets. On paid plans, Weekly limits shows your weekly reset.

Paid plans also see Usage credits: a pay-as-you-go top-up, with a monthly cap you set. Leave it off in week one.

Watch out

Paying monthly? To stop, cancel in Settings → Billing at least 24 hours before your renewal date, or the next charge goes through. Your plan stays active until the end of the period you paid for.

How Claude's usage limits work

4. Find your way around

"Claude" can mean an app, a way of working or an add-in. Here's the map.

Chat, Cowork and Claude Code

Chat Cowork Claude Code
You Talk it through Hand over a task Build software
Plans All, including Free Paid Paid
A good first try A question or a draft A report from your files A small change to your code

Cowork brings Claude Code's way of working to everyday work, with no command line. Claude makes a plan, does the steps and hands back finished files. It runs in the cloud, so the work carries on if you close your laptop.

Claude Code reads a codebase, edits files and runs commands. Don't write code? Skip it.

Here's what a Cowork-sized request looks like:

A whole task (paid plans)
Research [five suppliers, tools or options] for [your situation and budget]. For each one, find the price, the main features and one weakness, and note your sources. Give me an Excel file with one row per option, and a one-page Word summary of which you'd pick and why. Ask me what you need to know before you start.

You'll get a plan first, then two files to download, with sources you can open.

Which do you have? Look at your message box.

  • It shows Chat and Cowork: select Cowork, bottom left, to hand over a task. Select Chat to go back.
  • It shows neither: you have the new Claude experience. Chat and Cowork are one conversation. Just describe what you need. It's rolling out to Pro, Max and Ultra, and once your account moves, it can't switch back.

Watch out

Cowork can take actions, like changing files. Anthropic warns that tools that change things carry more risk than tools that only read. For anything with real consequences, such as sending messages or changing important files, stay close and review what Claude does.

The message box and the + button

Everything starts in the message box. Type, then click send.

The + button, lower left, holds the extras:

  • Add files or photos: attach a document or an image, or drag it in.
  • Web search: answers with sources you can click.
  • Research (paid plans): many searches that build on each other.
  • Connectors: link the apps you use.

Type / to see more options and commands.

Note

Have the new Claude experience? There's no Web search switch: Claude searches when it helps. Research is still under +, or type /deep-research.

The model menu

The model name, next to the send button, shows which Claude you're talking to. On your phone, it's at the top of the screen. Click it to switch, or click More models.

Model Anthropic says it's for Speed Plans
Fable 5.2 Demanding reasoning and long, complex work Moderate Paid
Opus 5.5 Complex work that needs careful judgment Moderate Pro and up
Sonnet 5.5 Everyday tasks, documents, slides and spreadsheets Fast All, including Free
Haiku 5.5 Quick, high-volume jobs Fastest All, including Free

Not sure? Anthropic says start with Opus 5.5 (more on Opus 5.5). For everyday chat, it also suggests Sonnet or Haiku, which use less of your limit.

The same menu holds Effort: Low, Medium, High, Extra high and Max. Higher effort thinks longer and uses more of your limit. The recommended level is marked Default. For everyday tasks, leave it.

Two more things on screen. The ghost icon, top right when you start a new chat outside a project, opens an incognito chat: not saved to your history or memory, not used for training, though Anthropic keeps it for 30 days. Your initials, bottom left, open Settings.

5. Talk to it like a colleague

Anthropic's own advice: talk to Claude the way you'd talk to a coworker or a friend.

You don't need magic words. You need context. Give it three things:

  1. The outcome: what you want to end up with. "A one-page summary."
  2. The format: a Word document, a slide deck, a message you can paste.
  3. The inputs: paste the text, attach the file, or name the app.

See the difference:

Too thin
Write an email about the meeting.
A real brief
Write a short, friendly email to my team about Thursday's planning meeting.
Outcome: everyone knows the three decisions and who does what by Friday.
Format: under 150 words, one opening line, then bullet points.
Inputs: my notes are below.

[paste your notes]

Keep this fill-in template somewhere handy:

The brief template
I need [the outcome, for example a one-page summary or a table of options].
It's for [who will read or use it].
Work from [paste the text, attach the file, or name the source].
Give it to me as [the format: a Word document, bullet points, an email I can paste].
Keep it [length and tone].
Before you start, ask me anything you need to know.

Use it for any request that matters. You'll get a few questions first, then a draft that fits.

Not sure what Claude needs? Hand the questions over:

Let it ask first
I want to [the job]. Before you start, ask me the questions you need answered to do this well. One question at a time. When you have enough, tell me and start.

Five habits from Anthropic's own guides

  1. The colleague test. If a colleague with no background would be confused by your request, Claude will be too.
  2. Give the reason. "Under 100 words, because it'll be read on a phone" beats "under 100 words".
  3. Say what to do. "Write in flowing paragraphs" beats "don't use bullet points".
  4. Document first, question last. With a long document, put it first and your question at the end.
  5. Show one example. If the format matters, paste one you like.

The first answer is a draft. Refine it: "Shorter, and warmer." "Turn that into a table." "What's missing?"

Before a request that matters, let Claude check your brief:

Review my prompt
Here's a request I'm about to give you. Don't answer it yet. Tell me what's unclear or missing and what you would have to guess. Then rewrite it as a better brief I can approve.

[paste your request]

Tip

New topic? New chat. Long conversations use up your limit faster.

Guide Brief Claude like a new colleague. Mojeed Abisiga · mojeedabisiga.com
GuideBrief Claude like a new colleague.Short prompts get average answers. A two-minute brief gets the finished thing, first time:

6. Four jobs it does well

Four jobs where beginners get value fastest, each with a prompt.

Explaining anything at your level

Claude explains at whatever level you ask for, and it doesn't mind the fifth follow-up.

Explain it at my level
Explain how [a topic you've always half-understood] works. I'm a complete beginner. Use one everyday comparison and one short example, then ask me one question to check I've understood. If I get it wrong, explain it a different way.

You'll get a few short paragraphs, one comparison, one example and a question for you.

Writing and rewriting

Emails, posts, reports and hard messages, in the tone you ask for. Paste your own rough draft for the best results.

Rewrite my draft
Here's a message I need to send to [who]. Make it clear, polite and short. Keep my meaning and any facts exactly as they are. Give me two versions: one warmer, one more formal. Under each, tell me in one line what you changed.

[paste your draft]

You'll get two versions and a note on what changed, so you stay in control of the meaning.

Reading your files

Attach a file with + → Add files or photos, or drag it in.

Claude reads PDF, Word, Excel, CSV, text and several other document types, plus JPEG, PNG, GIF and WebP images. Up to 20 files per chat, and PDFs of up to 1,000 pages.

One catch: it looks at images and charts only in PDFs of 100 pages or fewer. In longer PDFs, it reads the text only.

Read a document
Read this document. Summarise it in five bullet points. Then list anything that needs a decision or an action from me, with the page or section where it appears. If something is unclear in the document, say so instead of guessing.

You'll get five bullets, then an action list with page numbers you can check.

Making real files

Ask for the file by name: "as an Excel file", "as a Word document", "as a PowerPoint deck", "as a PDF". Then download it or save it to Google Drive.

Won't make files? Check Settings → Capabilities → Create and edit files is on (Code execution and file creation in the older layout).

Get a spreadsheet back
Make me a monthly budget as an Excel file. Columns for income, fixed costs, spending and savings, one row per month for a year. Use formulas so the totals update when I change a number, and add a summary row at the bottom. Then tell me which cells I should fill in first.

You'll get a file to download, and a short note on where to type.

7. Know where it slips, and what to do instead

Here are the four ways Claude lets beginners down, and the fix for each.

It can be confidently wrong

Anthropic calls this hallucination: a confident answer that's wrong or misleading. Its advice: don't treat Claude as your only source of truth, scrutinise high-stakes advice, and check the sources it cites.

It can also claim things it didn't do, like sending an email. It can only use tools that are actually connected.

Check your own answer
Go back through your answer. List every fact, number, name and date you used, where each one came from, and how sure you are. Flag anything I should check myself. If you don't know something, say "I don't know" rather than guessing.

For long documents, Anthropic's guidance says asking for exact quotes first reduces made-up answers, though it doesn't remove them:

Quotes first
Before you answer, find the exact sentences in the document that relate to my question and quote them word for word. Then answer using only those quotes. If the document doesn't answer it, say so.

My question: [your question]

It doesn't know recent news

Claude's newest models were trained on data up to June 2026. They may not know what happened after that.

The fix: let it search. Web search brings in current pages, with citations, on every plan.

Get current facts
Search the web for the latest on [topic] in [your country or industry]. Give me the five most important points, each with its date and a link to the source. Tell me if sources disagree.

Anthropic suggests web search for questions that need one or two searches, and Research (paid plans) for ones that need five or more.

It won't make photos

Claude doesn't generate photos or illustrations. It makes diagrams, charts and interactive visuals with code, and it can read images you upload.

Draw it as a diagram
Draw this process as a simple diagram: [describe the steps, for example how a customer order moves from website to delivery]. Label each step in a few words and show who is responsible for each one.

To keep a diagram, use Copy as image, Download or Save as artifact. Need a real photo? Use an image tool for that part.

It runs out

Anthropic lists what uses your limit faster: long messages, big attachments, long conversations, Research and web search, bigger models, higher effort, artifacts and multi-step tasks.

Its fix: batch related questions into one message, with the background up front.

Batch it
I have four related questions about [topic]. Background: [two lines]. Answer each one in under 100 words, numbered, in one reply.
1. [question]
2. [question]
3. [question]
4. [question]

Watch out

Check every number, name, date, quote and link before you use it. Anthropic's own advice is to scrutinise high-stakes answers and check the sources Claude cites. Its note on wrong answers.

Guide Ask Claude about your data, and trust the answer. Mojeed Abisiga · mojeedabisiga.com
GuideAsk Claude about your data, and trust the answer.Claude will answer any question about your spreadsheet, confidently. Here's how to make sure the answer is right:

8. Meet the five features worth knowing

Five words make Claude far more useful. Learn these, skip the rest.

Projects

A workspace with its own chats, files and instructions. Use one per ongoing piece of work: a client, a course, a job search.

  1. Click Projects on the left, or go to claude.ai/projects.
  2. Click + New Project, upper right.
  3. Add a name and description. They're for you: Claude doesn't see them.
  4. On the right of the project page, click + to add files.
  5. Click Set project instructions, write them, then Save instructions.

Chats in a project don't share what's said in them. Only the project's files and instructions are shared, so put anything important there. The help centre says Free accounts can make up to five projects.

Project instructions
In this project I'm [the ongoing work, for example preparing for job interviews in marketing]. The files here are [what you uploaded]. Use them as your main source. Write in plain English, keep answers short, and end each answer with one suggested next step. If something isn't in the files, say so before using general knowledge.

Artifacts

Anything Claude makes that you'd put in front of someone: a design, a deck, a document, a dashboard or a small tool. It opens beside the chat. To share it, click Share and choose who can open it under Who has access.

Docs, Slides and Design templates are on every plan. Slides can be exported to PowerPoint or PDF.

Memory and Instructions

Memory is what Claude remembers about you between chats. It's on by default for Free, Pro, Max and Ultra, and each project keeps its own.

Instructions are standing rules for every conversation: your job, your tone, how long answers should be.

Both live in Settings → Your Claude. Select Manage next to Your memory to see and edit what Claude remembers.

Paste this into Instructions and make it yours:

Your Instructions
I work as [your job] in [your country]. Write in plain English, with [British or American] spelling. Keep answers short unless I ask for more. Use numbered steps for instructions. If my request is unclear, ask me one question before you start. If you're not sure about a fact, say so.

You can also add to memory any time:

Remember this
Remember this for future chats: [the fact, for example "I manage a team of six in customer support, and my reports go to the operations director every Friday"].

Connectors

Connectors link Claude to the apps you use, so it can find information and take actions there, with your own permissions. Find them with + → Connectors → Manage connectors, or in Customize → Connectors. Start with one app you use daily.

Skills

Folders of instructions and resources that teach Claude a specialised job, on every plan. You already use some: built-in skills make the Excel, Word, PowerPoint and PDF files. Later, you can add your own in Customize → Skills.

Note

Whether your chats help train Claude is a switch in Settings → Privacy. On Free, Pro, Max and Ultra you can opt out. On Team and Enterprise, content isn't used for training by default. Incognito chats are never used.

Guide Claude skills, from zero. Mojeed Abisiga · mojeedabisiga.com
GuideClaude skills, from zero.For anyone who pastes the same instructions into Claude every day: install your first skill safely and use it today.

9. Features to leave until later

You'll see these in announcements and on social media. None of them matters in your first week.

The two you'll meet first: tokens (Claude tells you if a message is too long) and effort (leave it on the default).

Claude in plain English

10. Ten small experiments for week one

One a day, or two if you have time.

Four of them already have prompts in section 6: learn something, fix a message, question a PDF, get a spreadsheet. Two are settings from section 8: your Instructions and a project. Here are the other four.

Plan something real
Help me plan [a trip, an event, a move or a project]. Ask me up to five questions first, one at a time. Then give me a simple plan as a table with dates, tasks and who does each one, followed by a checklist I can tick off.
Build an artifact
Make me a simple checklist for [my weekly shopping, my packing list or my Monday routine] that I can tick off as I go. Group the items into sections and add a button that clears all the ticks.

It opens beside the chat. Click into it and use it.

Search with sources
What changed this month in [your field or your city]? Search the web, give me the three most important updates with dates, and link the source for each one. Then open two of the links yourself.
Talk it through (voice mode)
I'm stuck on a decision: [describe it]. Ask me questions one at a time to help me think it through, then sum up the options and what you'd weigh most.

Voice mode is in beta on every plan. It works best on a phone, and it counts toward your usage limit.

11. Run one ten-minute trial

Now put it together on one real task from your week. Three steps.

Step 1: Give it a real brief

Open a new chat. Paste the prompt below and fill in the brackets.

Trial
I need [the thing you want, for example a one-page plan for next month]. It's for [who will read it]. Here's the background: [two or three lines]. Give it to me as [a table, a short document or bullet points]. Before you start, ask me up to three questions.

Step 2: Answer, then sharpen

Answer Claude's questions in one message. Read the draft. Then fix one thing: "Shorter", "More formal", "Add a timeline", "Put the costs in a table".

Step 3: Get the file, and check it

Ask for a file: "Now make this a Word document." Download it. Then ask what to verify:

What should I check?
What in this should I double-check before I use it? List each fact, number or assumption, and tell me where I can confirm it.

Last, open Settings → Usage and look at Current session. Now you know what a task like this costs you.

How you know it worked: you have a file you'd actually use, and a short list of things to verify before you do.

Write one good prompt

12. Watch eight professionals at work

Once the basics feel easy, borrow from people who use Claude for real work.

Eight roles, one job each, each built on a feature Anthropic documents. Swap in your own details.

The team lead: follow-ups in Outlook

Feature: Claude for Microsoft 365 (paid plans). Install Claude for Microsoft 365 from Microsoft AppSource with Get it now, then sign in with your Claude account. In Outlook, its drafts and invites open in the normal compose window and wait for you to click send.

Meeting follow-up
Here are my notes from today's meeting. Draft a follow-up email to everyone who attended: the decisions, each action with an owner and a date, and the open questions. Keep it under 200 words. Then draft an invite for a 30-minute follow-up meeting next week.

[paste your notes]

The analyst: answers from a workbook

Feature: Claude for Excel (paid plans). It answers questions with cell-level citations, changes assumptions while keeping formulas intact, and debugs errors.

Understand this workbook
Explain how this workbook works: what each sheet does and where the key numbers come from, with cell references. Then show me what happens to the final total if [the assumption] changes from [x] to [y]. Keep the existing formulas intact and tell me which cells you changed.

The researcher: a sourced briefing

Feature: Research (paid plans): many searches that build on each other. Turn it on with + → Research, or type /deep-research in the new Claude experience.

Research briefing
Research [the question, for example how small retailers in my country use online marketplaces]. I need a two-page briefing for [who]. Cover the main trends, three examples with sources, the key numbers with dates, and where sources disagree. Finish with three questions I should ask next.

The presenter: slides in your own template

Feature: Claude for PowerPoint (paid plans). It reads your slide master, fonts and colours, builds slides in your template, and turns bullets into editable diagrams and charts. On Free, ask in chat: "Convert this document into a PowerPoint presentation."

Deck from a document
Turn the attached document into an 8-slide deck for [audience]. One idea per slide, a short headline on each, no more than four bullets. Turn the numbers on page [x] into a chart. Use the layouts in this template. End with a slide of next steps.

The operations lead: a weekly report on a schedule

Feature: scheduled tasks (paid plans). Describe the task and how often, review Claude's proposal and click Schedule. Tasks run in the cloud, even when your computer is asleep.

Weekly digest
Every Monday morning, search the web for news about [your industry and region] from the past week. Give me the five items that matter most for [your role], each with one line on why it matters and a link to the source. Keep it to one screen.

Anthropic's advice: start simple, avoid sensitive data, review each run, and pause tasks you don't use.

The reviewer: long documents, with quotes

Feature: file uploads (every plan), plus the quotes-first habit from section 7.

Review against my questions
Read the attached [policy, contract or tender]. Answer each of my questions in a table with four columns: the question, the answer, the exact quote that supports it, and the page. If the document doesn't answer a question, write "Not covered". Don't use outside knowledge.

My questions:
1. [question]
2. [question]
3. [question]

Treat the table as a reading aid. Get professional advice where the stakes are high.

The trainer: a course project and a quiz

Feature: a project for the course materials, and an artifact for the quiz, which you can share.

Make a quiz
Using the session notes in this project, make a 10-question multiple-choice quiz as an interactive artifact. One correct answer per question, a one-line explanation after each answer, and a score at the end. Pitch it at [level].

The small-business owner: a whole task handed over

Feature: Cowork, or any conversation in the new Claude experience (paid plans).

Compare and recommend
I run [your business] in [your city]. Compare five [suppliers, tools or options] for [the need], with a budget of [amount] a month. Build an Excel file with one row each: price, key features, contract terms, one weakness and a source link, plus a formula that ranks them. Then make a three-slide PowerPoint summary with your recommendation. Ask me anything you need first.

Check prices at the source before you sign anything.

Tip

Pick the one role closest to yours and try it this week. One workflow you use every week beats eight you tried once.

13. Choose your first step

Here's the whole guide as a path, one stop at a time.

Before you finish

  • Claude is on my computer and my phone
  • I know which plan I'm on, and when I'd move up
  • My Instructions and my privacy choice are set
  • I know where Settings → Usage is
  • I've used the brief template at least once
  • I've asked Claude to check its own answer
  • I've tried at least three of the ten
  • I've done the ten-minute trial
  • I've picked one professional workflow to try

Questions

Does Claude cost anything?

The Free plan costs $0, with limited usage every five hours and every week.

Why did Claude stop answering?

You've most likely reached your usage limit. Claude tells you when you do. Settings → Usage shows when it resets.

Does Claude work in my language?

It's trained extensively in English and performs well in many other common languages.

Which model should I use?

On Free, Sonnet 5.5 for most things and Haiku 5.5 for quick jobs. On paid plans, Anthropic says start with Opus 5.5 if you're not sure.

What to do after week one

Hand over whole tasks. Cowork does the steps for you, from start to finished file.

Guide Cowork, from zero. Mojeed Abisiga · mojeedabisiga.com
GuideCowork, from zero.You don't code? Good. Here's how to hand Claude real work, step by step:

Build the daily habits that make Claude more useful every week.

Newsletter Claude, past the basics. Mojeed Abisiga · mojeedabisiga.com
NewsletterClaude, past the basics.Eighteen small habits that save time, usage and mistakes:

Take Anthropic's own course. Claude 101 in Claude Academy has 13 lessons and 1 quiz, takes about 2.5 hours and ends with a completion badge.

Open Claude today and give it one real job. That's day one done.

Mojeed

item.title: Right tool, right job.
item.description: One rule, then the AI to try first for writing, spreadsheets, search, other languages and slides, from what each company documents. Prompts included.
item.content:encoded:
You use one AI for everything.

Emails. Reports. Spreadsheets. Research. Slides.

Some days it's brilliant. Some days it's clumsy, and you can't tell why.

Often the problem is the match between the tool and the job.

Each tool is built around different strengths. The companies say so themselves, in their own help pages.

So stop hunting for the one AI that wins at everything.

Pick the right one for each job instead.

I teach people to use AI at work, and this is the question I hear most: "Which AI should I use?"

My honest answer: it depends on the job. Here's where to start for five of them.

Inside:

  1. One rule before any tool
  2. Deep work and writing
  3. Spreadsheets
  4. Search and research
  5. Work in other languages
  6. Presentations
  7. The whole map on one page
  8. How to test a tool on your own work

A quick promise: I didn't run a test or a ranking for this issue. Every choice below comes from what each company documents about its own product. Treat each one as where to start, then judge on your own work.

Get the next one in your inbox

One practical guide at a time: the exact steps, the prompts to copy and the mistakes to skip.

Free. Delivered by Substack, one click to unsubscribe. Form not showing? Subscribe on Substack.

One rule before any tool

Here it is:

Start with the tool built around the job, then keep it only if it works on your own material.

That's it. Three things follow from it.

  • Where your work lives matters. If your numbers live in Excel, an AI that works inside Excel beats copying and pasting.
  • The documented feature matters more than the hype. A tool that says it gives sources, keeps formulas or uses your template is telling you what it was built for.
  • Your own test beats anyone's ranking. Including mine.

You don't need five subscriptions for this. Several tools below have free plans, and the free version of this map shows where each free plan stops.

Key point

Whatever tool you pick, it can be wrong. Anthropic says plainly not to rely on Claude as a single source of truth, and to check cited sources on anything high-stakes. The same habit applies to every AI here.

Deep work and writing

Try first: Claude, on Opus 5.5.

This is the long, careful work. A report. A proposal. A difficult email. Making sense of a pile of documents.

Why Claude for this:

  • Anthropic's own advice is to start with Opus 5.5 if you're unsure, and it calls it the "strongest daily driver" for knowledge work.
  • It's built for clear writing. Anthropic says Opus 5.5 puts the most important information up front, uses less jargon, and follows the writing rules you give it.
  • It takes in a lot at once. On paid plans, Opus 5.5 has a 1M-token context window in chat. ChatGPT's published windows run from 27K to 400K, depending on plan and model.
  • Projects keep your material in one place, with their own chats and files. Free users can create up to five.

One thing to know: on the Free plan, Claude offers Sonnet and Haiku, not Opus. Opus 5.5 starts on Pro.

To pick it, click the model name next to the send button and choose Opus 5.5, or click More models.

Turn a pile of notes into a first draft
I've attached my notes, the client's brief and last quarter's report.

Write a first draft of a two-page proposal for [client].
Audience: their operations director, who is busy and sceptical.
Put the recommendation and the cost in the first paragraph.
Plain English, short paragraphs, no jargon.

Before you write, list anything in my notes that contradicts the brief, and ask me about it.

The last line matters. It makes Claude check before it writes, instead of guessing.

For quick, well-scoped jobs, Anthropic positions Sonnet 5.5 as strongest at everyday tasks and polished documents. Move down to it when Opus feels slow.

Guide Brief Claude like a new colleague. Mojeed Abisiga · mojeedabisiga.com
GuideBrief Claude like a new colleague.Short prompts get average answers. A two-minute brief gets the finished thing, first time:

Spreadsheets

Try first: whichever AI works inside the spreadsheet you already use.

This is the job where "where your work lives" matters most.

If you live in Excel: Claude for Excel

Claude for Excel is an add-in that works inside your workbook. Anthropic's docs say it:

  • answers questions about your workbook with cell-level citations, so you can see where a number came from
  • adjusts assumptions while keeping formulas intact
  • debugs errors and builds models

It runs on Excel on the web, Windows and Mac. Its docs list Pro, Max, Team and Enterprise plans.

To install it, find the Claude for Microsoft 365 listing on Microsoft AppSource, click Get it now, then sign in with your Claude account.

Inside Claude for Excel
Look at the Forecast sheet.
Explain in five plain sentences how next year's revenue figure is built, citing the cells you used.
Then change the growth assumption from 8% to 5% and tell me which totals move.
Don't overwrite any formula.

If you want charts from a file: ChatGPT data analysis

ChatGPT's data analysis takes spreadsheets (.xls, .xlsx, .csv) and PDFs, and for some tasks writes and runs Python.

It makes interactive bar, line, pie and scatter charts on Plus and Pro. To see the numbers behind a chart, open Chart options (•••) and choose View as table.

On Free, data analysis is limited.

If your team runs on Google Sheets: Gemini

Gemini with Google Workspace puts AI inside Gmail, Docs, Sheets and Slides. For businesses it starts at $14 a seat per month.

Tip

Whatever you use, ask for the working, not only the answer. A number with a cell reference or a table behind it is a number you can check.

Guide Ask Claude about your data, and trust the answer. Mojeed Abisiga · mojeedabisiga.com
GuideAsk Claude about your data, and trust the answer.Claude will answer any question about your spreadsheet, confidently. Here's how to make sure the answer is right:

Search and research

Try first: Perplexity for quick answers with sources. Claude Research or Gemini Deep Research for a full report.

Search has two jobs hiding inside it.

Quick, looked-up answers

Perplexity is built around search. On its Free plan you get practically unlimited basic searches and 3 Pro Searches a day. Pro adds advanced models and 10x as many citations per answer.

Claude can search too. Click + in the message box, then Web search, and the answers come back with citations. Free accounts can use it.

A proper report

When you need many searches that build on each other, use a research mode.

  • Claude Research (paid plans) runs multiple searches across the web and your connected tools. Turn it on with + → Research.
  • Gemini Deep Research is on Google's Free plan. Google says it can analyse hundreds of sources to write a research report.

Anthropic's own rule of thumb is useful for any tool: web search for a factual question that takes one or two lookups, Research for anything that needs five or more.

In words: click + in the message box, then Web search for a quick answer, or Research for a report. In the new Claude experience there's no Web search switch: Claude searches when it helps.

A research brief that's easy to check
Research [topic] for a one-page briefing to my manager.
Use only sources from the last 12 months, and say the date of each.
Give me: what's changed, the three numbers that matter, and what's still disputed.
Put a link next to every claim. If sources disagree, show both.

Watch out

Models don't know about events after their training cutoff. For anything recent, make sure search is actually on, and open at least the links you plan to repeat.

Work in other languages

Try first: Claude for writing and translating. Gemini when you need wide language coverage in the app itself, or text inside images.

Most AI advice assumes you work in English. Plenty of work happens in other languages too.

What Claude documents

Anthropic publishes a multilingual table that scores each language as a percentage of the same model's English score.

For Opus 5.5:

Language Score, as % of English
Spanish 99.3%
French 99.3%
Arabic 99.3%
Hindi 99.2%
Swahili 98.3%
Yoruba 96.3%

Read it the way Anthropic says to: it compares languages within one model, not one model against another.

Anthropic also says Claude works in many languages beyond the table, and that you should test with the ones you actually use.

What Gemini documents

Google says the Gemini web app is available in more than 70 languages, in over 230 countries and territories. The list includes Amharic, Arabic, French, Swahili and Zulu.

Gemini's image tool can also place clear text in images in many languages. Useful for a poster or a social card in your own language.

How to ask, in any tool

Anthropic's tips for multilingual work are simple:

  1. Name the input language and the output language.
  2. Paste text in its own script, not spelled out in Latin letters.
  3. Ask for natural, idiomatic wording, "as if written by a native speaker".
  4. Say who the reader is and where they live.
Translate for a real reader
Translate the message below from English to French for customers in Senegal.
Use natural, idiomatic French, as if written by a native speaker.
Keep it warm and short. Keep product names in English.
After the translation, list any phrase that might read differently there than in France.

[paste your message]

If you speak the language, read the result yourself. If you don't, ask someone who does before it goes out.

NewsletterWrite it plain.AI drafts that sound like everyone else's? Here's the fix, step by step:

Presentations

Try first: Claude for PowerPoint if your company has a template. Claude Slides or Gamma if you're starting from nothing.

When the deck must match your template

Claude for PowerPoint is an add-in. Anthropic's docs say it reads your deck's slide master, layouts, fonts and colour scheme, and uses them when it builds or edits slides.

The charts and diagrams it makes are editable, not flat pictures. It can also turn bullet points into diagrams and native PowerPoint charts.

Its docs list Pro, Max, Team and Enterprise plans. It's installed from the same Claude for Microsoft 365 listing as the Excel add-in.

In words: in PowerPoint, open Home → Add-ins on Windows or Tools → Add-ins on Mac, choose Claude, and sign in. To give it rules for every deck, open Settings in the add-in sidebar and fill in Instructions.

Inside Claude for PowerPoint, on a blank deck
Build a 10-slide deck for our quarterly review with the leadership team.
Use this deck's template, fonts and colours.
Slide 1: the one decision we need from them.
Slides 2 to 8: one idea per slide, a headline that states the point, at most three bullets.
Turn the revenue numbers I paste below into a native chart.
Last slide: next steps with owners and dates.

[paste your numbers and notes]

When you're starting from nothing

  • Claude Slides is one of the artifact templates on every Claude plan. You edit slide by slide, present inside Claude, and export to PowerPoint, PDF or straight to Google Slides.
  • Gamma builds a deck from one prompt. Its Free plan allows up to 10 slides per prompt, and free credits don't refresh. Paid plans remove the "Made with Gamma" badge.

GuideBetter slides, less effort.Three ways to build a deck with AI, and how your team can share one standard:

The whole map on one page

Here's everything above in one table. Save it.

The job Try first Why, in one line Also worth a look
Deep work and writing Claude, Opus 5.5 Clear writing, 1M-token context on paid plans Sonnet 5.5 for quick jobs
Spreadsheets in Excel Claude for Excel Cell-level citations, keeps formulas intact ChatGPT data analysis for charts
Spreadsheets in Google Gemini in Sheets Built into Google Workspace Claude or ChatGPT with an upload
Quick answers with sources Perplexity Search-first, free basic searches Claude web search
Research reports Claude Research or Gemini Deep Research Many searches that build on each other Perplexity Pro
Other languages Claude Published scores per language, clear tips Gemini, in 70+ languages
Slides on your template Claude for PowerPoint Uses your slide master and fonts Claude Slides
Slides from nothing Claude Slides or Gamma A deck from one prompt Claude for PowerPoint

One job is missing on purpose: pictures.

Anthropic says Claude doesn't generate photos or illustrations. It makes diagrams, charts and visuals instead. For images, ChatGPT lists image generation on every plan, and Gemini's Nano Banana 2 model is free in the Gemini app.

How to test a tool on your own work

A tool can look perfect on paper and still miss on your material.

So give it a fair, quick test on something real.

  1. Pick one real task you did last week. Not a toy example.
  2. Write one prompt with the goal, the reader and the format.
  3. Run the same prompt in your usual AI and in the one this issue suggests.
  4. Compare on three things: what you'd have to fix, whether you can check it, and how long it took.
  5. Keep the winner for that job. Only that job.
The same-prompt test
Here is a task I do every week: [describe it].
Here is the material: [attach or paste].
Do the task as if you were handing it to my manager.
Then tell me, honestly, which parts I should double-check and why.

The last line works in any tool. It tells you where the weak spots are before your manager finds them.

Note

Run the test on material you're allowed to share. Check your company's rules before you paste client or staff data into any AI.

Know a colleague who swears by one AI for everything? Send this to them.

What to do today

Pick the one job on this list you do most.

Try the tool named for it, with the prompt in that section.

Run the same-prompt test against what you use now.

Keep what wins. Leave the rest.

You don't need the best AI. You need the right one for the job in front of you.

item.title: Proof gets you hired.
item.description: What a certificate shows and what it can't, what employers and clients can actually check, and how to build one piece of visible proof with AI as your coach.
item.content:encoded:
You finished the course.

You passed the quiz.

You added the certificate to your profile.

Then nothing happened.

No calls. No clients. No change at work.

I want to be clear before anything else: that certificate was worth earning. I hold several myself.

But a certificate is where proof starts. It isn't the proof.

This issue is about the gap between the two, and how to close it.

Inside:

  1. What a certificate really shows
  2. Why it can't stand on its own any more
  3. What an employer or client can actually check
  4. How to build one piece of proof, with AI as your coach
  5. How to write it up and put it where people look
  6. The one line never to cross

Get the next one in your inbox

One practical guide at a time: the exact steps, the prompts to copy and the mistakes to skip.

Free. Delivered by Substack, one click to unsubscribe. Form not showing? Subscribe on Substack.

Certificates are a good start

I'm a data and AI leader and educator. My mission is to make data and AI easy for everyone.

I hold the Microsoft Professional Degree in Data Science. I'm a Celonis Analyst and Data Engineer. IBM gave me its Big Data Engineer Mastery Award.

I'm proud of every one of them.

Each one made me learn things I'd have skipped on my own. Each one gave me a structure, a deadline and a test.

That's what a good course does.

Some good AI courses are free, too. Anthropic's learning site, Claude Academy, costs nothing. A free Claude account saves your progress and earns completion badges.

Its "AI Fluency: Framework and foundations" course is 14 lessons, one quiz and about four hours.

Google AI Essentials takes under five hours and needs no experience. In the U.S. and Canada it costs $49 a month after a seven-day free trial.

So take the course. Learn the thing. Keep the certificate.

Key point

A certificate tells people you learned something. Proof tells them what you can do with it. You want both.

What a certificate actually shows

Read the small print on any certificate and it's honest about what it is.

Claude Academy says its badges record that you completed the course as it existed when you took it. The issue date sits on the verification page.

You earn the badge by passing the quizzes. Every lesson quiz, plus any final assessment.

Anyone can check it's genuine through a public link.

That's real. It's also narrow.

Here's what that same certificate can't show:

  • the problem you'd solve on day one
  • how you'd handle messy, real data or a vague brief
  • whether you check AI's work before you send it
  • how you explain a result to someone who isn't technical
  • your judgment

Claude Academy is careful here too. It says its completion badges are not certifications. Claude certification exams are a separate paid, proctored program, and only companies in Anthropic's partner program can get them.

Different credentials test different things. That's fine, as long as you know which one you hold.

Everyone has the certificate now

Here's the uncomfortable part.

Employers do want AI skills. The evidence is clear.

In Microsoft and LinkedIn's 2024 Work Trend Index, 66% of leaders said they wouldn't hire someone without AI skills. 71% said they'd rather hire a less experienced candidate with AI skills than a more experienced one without them.

The World Economic Forum's Future of Jobs Report 2025 puts AI and big data at the top of the fastest-growing skills. Two-thirds of employers plan to hire people with specific AI skills.

So people responded.

The same Work Trend Index reported a 142x increase in LinkedIn members adding AI skills like ChatGPT and Copilot to their profiles.

Think about what that means for you.

If everyone lists the skill, the list stops telling anyone apart.

LinkedIn's Skills on the Rise 2026 says employers increasingly prioritise skills over degrees, job titles or linear career paths.

Skills. Not the line on the profile.

And the most sought-after core skill in the WEF report isn't a tool at all. It's analytical thinking, essential for seven out of 10 companies.

You can't show analytical thinking with a badge. You show it with work.

What people can actually check

Put yourself in the hiring manager's seat. Or the client's.

They have a few minutes. What can they actually look at?

What you show What they can check What it tells them
A certificate or badge That it's genuine, and the date You finished a course and passed its quizzes
A line on your profile ("AI skills") Nothing That you typed it
A project they can open The thing itself: the sheet, the report, the tool What you can build
A short write-up Your reasoning, step by step How you think, and how you checked
A few pieces in one place A pattern over time That you keep doing it

The bottom three rows are the ones that start conversations.

They also give the interviewer something to ask about. "Walk me through this" is the easiest question in the world to answer when you did the work.

Microsoft built some of its own credentials this way. Microsoft Applied Skills are earned by completing interactive tasks that align to real work, in a lab-based assessment. Microsoft says they show employers you can hit the ground running.

Even the people who issue credentials want them to look more like real work.

You can go one step further and show the real work itself.

Build proof, with AI as your coach

Proof doesn't need to be big.

One small project, from a real problem, done well and explained clearly, beats ten certificates with nothing behind them.

Here's how to build one. AI helps at every step, but as a coach. You do the work. It asks the questions, spots the gaps and pushes you.

1. Pick a real problem

Start from your own work, or a cause or small business you care about.

Find my first proof project
I want to build one small project that proves I can use AI well at work.

About me:
- My job or the job I want: [role]
- Tools I use now: [e.g. Excel, Google Sheets, Claude, ChatGPT]
- A task at work that is slow, repetitive or messy: [describe it]

Suggest three project ideas I could finish in two weekends.
For each one: the problem it solves, what I would build, what "done" looks like, and what a hiring manager would learn about me from it.
Don't do the project. Ask me questions until we pick one.

2. Plan it in small steps

Plan the project with me
We picked this project: [paste it].

Break it into steps I can finish in one or two hours each.
For each step, tell me what I should be able to show at the end of it.
Point out where I'm most likely to get stuck, and what I should learn first if I don't know it yet.

3. Do the work, and get coached

This is the step that turns into proof. Do it yourself.

When you're stuck, ask for a hint, not the answer.

Coach me, don't do it for me
I'm working on this step: [step].
Here's what I've done so far: [paste or describe it].

Act as my coach.
Don't write the solution for me.
Ask me one question at a time that helps me find the next move.
If I'm going the wrong way, tell me plainly and explain why.

4. Check it like a reviewer would

Review my work like a tough manager
Here is my finished project: [paste it or describe it].

Review it like a manager who has to decide whether to trust it.
List:
1. What would make you trust it
2. What would make you doubt it
3. Any numbers or claims I should check again
4. One change that would make it clearly better

Be direct. I'd rather hear it from you than from an interviewer.

Tip

Keep notes as you go: what you tried, what failed, what you changed. Those notes become your write-up.

If your projects involve data, Ask Claude about your data walks through how to work with a spreadsheet step by step.

Learn to brief AI like a colleague

Write it up so people can follow

The project is the proof. The write-up is how people find it and understand it.

Keep it short. One page is plenty.

A simple shape:

  1. The problem, in two or three sentences
  2. What you did, step by step
  3. How you used AI, and how you checked its work
  4. The result, and what you'd do next
  5. What you learned

Say plainly how you used AI. LinkedIn recommends saying so when you relied heavily on it.

Turn my notes into a write-up
Here are my notes from a project: [paste your notes].

Help me turn them into a one-page write-up with these headings:
The problem, What I did, How I used AI and how I checked it, The result, What I learned.

Keep my words wherever you can. Don't add results, numbers or claims that aren't in my notes.
Mark anything that sounds vague, and ask me for the detail instead of making it up.

Then read every line yourself.

LinkedIn's guidance on AI-assisted content is worth knowing here. It says you're responsible for everything you post. It asks you to review, edit and approve anything AI helped with.

It also says it doesn't want "AI slop": content that sounds polished but has no clear point of view or substance. It judges whether a post adds value, not how it was made.

A real project, in your own words, is the opposite of slop.

Watch out

Never let AI add results you didn't get. A made-up number in a write-up costs you more trust than no number at all.

Get the next issue by email

One practical guide at a time: the exact steps, the prompts to copy and the mistakes to skip.

Free. Delivered by Substack, one click to unsubscribe. Form not showing? Subscribe on Substack.

Put it where people look

Proof only works if someone sees it.

Share the write-up on LinkedIn

A document post works well for a one-page write-up. People who can see the post can download it as a PDF.

On desktop, click Start a post, then More, then the Add a document icon. Click Choose file, add a title, and click Done. Add a description and click Post.

LinkedIn advises converting the file to PDF where possible. Document posts accept PDF, Word and PowerPoint files up to 100MB and 300 pages.

One thing to know: after you post, you can edit the description but not the document. Check it before you share.

Keep your badges next to your proof

Your certificates still belong on your profile. Put them next to the work.

If you have a Claude Academy badge, go to Your journey, open the badge, and choose Download PDF or Add to LinkedIn. Each badge also has a public verification link anyone can use to confirm it's genuine.

If you took courses on the old site, anthropic.skilljar.com, it closes in early December. Import your history into Claude Academy, using a Claude account with the same email, and save your certificate PDFs before then.

Build a small portfolio

After two or three projects, put them in one place: a simple page, or one post that links to each.

Each one gets a title, one line on the problem, and a link.

Plan my portfolio page
Here are my projects and write-ups: [paste titles and one line each].
Here's the job or client I want: [describe it].

Suggest the order to show them in, a one-line headline for each, and a short intro (three sentences, in plain words) about what I can do.
Tell me which project is weakest for this goal, and what I could build next to fill the gap.
Newsletter Bring the point. Mojeed Abisiga · mojeedabisiga.com
NewsletterBring the point.Using AI to write your LinkedIn posts? What it can't do for you, and what it can:

The line never to cross

Some people chase the certificate and skip the learning.

Don't.

When you take a course, take the quizzes yourself. A quiz is there to show you what you haven't learned yet. That's useful information.

Claude Academy lets you retake its quizzes as often as you need, unless you hit its daily limit on completion badges. Then the quiz opens again at midnight US Pacific time. So there's no reason to rush. Fail, learn, try again.

Use AI to explain a concept you're stuck on. Ask it for practice questions. Ask it to quiz you on yesterday's lesson.

Study with me before the quiz
I'm learning [topic] from a course. Here are my notes from this module: [paste them].

Explain the two ideas I seem least sure about, in plain words, with an everyday example.
Then ask me five practice questions of your own, one at a time.
Wait for my answer each time, tell me if I'm right, and explain why.

A certificate you earned is a small piece of proof by itself. One you didn't earn falls apart the first time someone asks you a question.

And they will ask.

What to do today

Keep your certificates. They show you were willing to learn.

Then pick one problem from your work this week.

Run the first prompt. Choose one project you can finish in two weekends.

Do the work yourself, with AI as your coach. Write one page about it. Share it.

That's your first piece of proof. The second one comes faster.

I teach people to use AI at work, and this is the advice I'd give anyone starting out.

Write one good prompt first
