item.title: Write it plain.
item.description: A plain-English style instruction for Claude, rules from official plain-language guides, a swap list of words to cut and a research-first prompt.
item.content:encoded:
You ask Claude to write an email.

It comes back fast, tidy and correct.

And you can tell from the first line that a machine wrote it.

Long words. Warm-up sentences. A summary at the end that repeats the start.

Nothing is wrong with it. It just sounds like nobody.

There's no magic phrase. What works is a small kit you set up once.

I teach people to use AI at work, and my mission is to make data and AI easy for everyone. Plain writing is the skill that makes every AI draft more useful.

What's inside:

  1. Why AI drafts come out bland
  2. What "plain" actually means, from official sources
  3. A short style instruction to add to every writing request
  4. A swap list of words and patterns to cut
  5. A research-first prompt to run before any piece of writing
  6. Ready-made versions for four everyday jobs
  7. A check you can run on any draft

Get the next one in your inbox

One practical guide at a time: the exact steps, the prompts to copy and the mistakes to skip.

Free. Delivered by Substack, one click to unsubscribe. Form not showing? Subscribe on Substack.

Why AI drafts come out bland

Anthropic's prompting guide gives a useful picture.

Treat Claude like a brilliant but new employee. Clever, but with no context on your norms or how your team works.

Ask that new hire to "write an email to the client" and you'll get the safe, average email.

The same guide says the more precisely you explain what you want, the better the result.

So when you don't describe a style, Claude picks a default one. And the default is polished, formal and wordy.

Three gaps cause most of it:

  • No reader. Claude doesn't know who will read the piece, so it writes for everyone.
  • No style. "Make it professional" is a mood, not an instruction.
  • No facts. When the facts are thin, the words get fat. Filler fills the space.

This issue closes all three gaps.

Key point

Plain writing is about the reader, not about hiding that you used AI. The goal is a draft people understand on the first read.

Brief Claude like a colleague

What "plain" actually means

"Write in plain English" sounds vague. It isn't.

Governments have written it down in detail, because their readers include everyone.

In the US, the Plain Writing Act of 2010 defines plain writing as writing that is clear, concise, well-organized and suited to the subject and audience.

In the UK, plain English is mandatory for all of GOV.UK. The Government Digital Service points to literacy data: 1 in 6 adults in England has very poor literacy skills.

And plain doesn't mean simple-minded.

Digital.gov, which now carries selected PlainLanguage.gov guidance, puts "write for your audience" first. It calls "dumbing down" a common myth. You match your readers' knowledge, expertise and interest.

So an expert reader can still get technical terms. A new customer gets everyday words.

The rules, side by side

Here's what three official sources say, in numbers you can hand to Claude.

Rule GOV.UK Digital.gov Simplified Technical English
Sentence length Try to split sentences over 25 words One idea per sentence 20 words for instructions, 25 for descriptions
Paragraphs No more than 5 sentences 3 to 8 sentences, under 150 words, never over 250 One topic per sentence
Voice Active: "You need an electronic travel authorisation" Everyday language Active, with commands for steps: "Install the component."
Words Short over formal: "buy" not "purchase" Cut filler like "very" and "really" About 900 approved words, one meaning each
Order Most important information first Write for your audience first Not stated

The third column needs a word of explanation.

Simplified Technical English (STE) is a controlled language first released in 1986 to help readers of English maintenance documentation. Its makers say it isn't meant for general writing. But they also say its principles, short sentences, one topic per sentence and the active voice, work well in other writing.

That makes it a good model for one job in particular: instructions people must follow.

Get the next issue by email

The style instruction

Here's the core of the kit.

One short instruction that you add to every writing request. Or better, save once (next section).

Two pieces of Anthropic's advice shape it.

First, give the reason behind a rule. Anthropic's guide shows a bare rule, "NEVER use ellipses", next to a better one that explains the reply will be read aloud. With the reason, Claude can apply the idea to cases the rule never named.

Second, say what to do, not only what to avoid. Ask for "flowing prose paragraphs" instead of "don't use markdown".

So every line below says what to do, and most say why.

Plain-English style instruction
Write in plain English for [who reads this: e.g. busy managers who read on their phones].

- Use short, everyday words: "buy" not "purchase", "help" not "assist", "use" not "utilise". Short words are faster to read.
- Keep sentences under 25 words, with one idea each. Long sentences lose readers.
- Put the most important point first. Most people scan and stop early.
- Use the active voice and talk to the reader as "you".
- Write short paragraphs of one to three sentences. Use a list only when order matters.
- Explain any technical term in plain words the first time you use it.
- Start with the answer and stop when you're done: no warm-up line, no closing summary.
- Keep every fact I give you. Add no facts, numbers or quotes of your own. If something is missing, tell me.

It's eight lines. That's deliberate.

Anthropic's article for Claude app users warns that longer, more complex prompts are not always better. A few clear rules beat a pasted style manual.

Fill in the first line for each job. The reader changes; the rules mostly don't.

Add one example

Words describe a style. An example shows it.

Anthropic calls examples one of the most reliable ways to steer tone and structure. Its article for app users says to start with one and add more only if the output still doesn't match.

It also warns that newer models pay very close attention to details in examples. So pick a clean one you'd be happy to see copied.

Add your own voice
Here is a short piece I wrote that sounds like me. Match its tone, sentence length and word choice. Don't copy its content.

[paste 100 to 200 words of your own writing]
Newsletter One good prompt. Mojeed Abisiga · mojeedabisiga.com
NewsletterOne good prompt.Getting bland, generic answers? Five rules and one template that fix them:

Save it once

Pasting the instruction into every chat works. Saving it is better.

You have two places to put it.

For everything you write: open Settings, then Your Claude, then Instructions, and paste it there. Anthropic's help centre says these account-wide instructions apply to all your conversations.

For writing only: make a project. Project instructions apply only inside that project, so your other chats stay as they are.

To make one:

  1. Go to claude.ai/projects and click + New Project. Call it something like "Plain writing".
  2. Click Set project instructions and paste your style instruction.
  3. Click + to add files, such as one example of your own writing.

Anthropic's project help page says projects are open to all users, and free accounts can create up to five. But its personalization page marks project instructions as paid-plans-only. If you don't see Set project instructions, use the account-wide instructions above instead.

Then start every writing job inside that project. The rules come with it.

Tip

Anthropic's help centre says skills customize how Claude formats and delivers responses. Once your instruction is settled, it can become a writing skill you use everywhere.

Make your first skill

The swap list

Most "AI-sounding" writing comes from a small set of words and habits.

A ban list helps. But remember Anthropic's advice: say what to do instead. So each item below comes with its swap.

Words to swap

The first six come straight from GOV.UK's guidance and its A to Z style guide, which keeps a "Words to avoid" list.

Instead of Write
purchase buy
assist help
approximately about
utilise use
collaborate work with
leverage use, or influence
in order to to
facilitate help, run, make easier
additionally, furthermore, moreover also, and, or nothing
crucial, vital, pivotal important, or say why it matters
comprehensive full, complete, or cut it
foster, empower help, let
showcase show
streamline simplify, speed up

Then cut the filler. Digital.gov names absolutely, actually, completely, really, quite, totally and very as usually unnecessary, and sometimes nonsensical.

Patterns to swap

Words are half of it. The other half is shape.

  • The warm-up. Praising the question or restating it. Swap: start with the answer.
  • The echo ending. "In conclusion" and a summary of what you just read. Swap: stop after the last useful point.
  • The trio. Three adjectives where one would do: "clear, concise and compelling". Swap: pick the one that's true.
  • The fake contrast. "Not just a tool, but a partner." Swap: say what it does.
  • The self-answered question. "The result? Faster reports." Swap: "Reports got faster."
  • Hedge stacks. "This may potentially help." Swap: one hedge, or none if you're sure.
  • Bold everywhere. Swap: bold the one phrase a scanner must see.
  • The offer at the end. "Let me know if you'd like me to..." Swap: nothing. You'll ask.
  • The passive. "A decision was made." Swap: say who: "We decided."
Swap list (add below your style instruction)
When you write for me, also apply these swaps:
- formal words → everyday words (purchase → buy, utilise → use, in order to → to, facilitate → help)
- linking words like additionally, furthermore, moreover → "also", "and", or a new sentence
- filler (very, really, actually, quite, totally) → cut it
- a question you answer yourself → a plain statement
- three adjectives in a row → the one that's true
- a closing summary or an offer to help further → end after the last useful point
- passive sentences → say who does what

Note

These swaps are a starting point, not a law. If a word is the right one for your reader, keep it. Digital.gov's rule still comes first: write for your audience.

Share this list with one colleague whose reports get skimmed.

Research first, then write

Here's the part most people skip.

Bland writing is often a facts problem.

When Claude has nothing specific to say, it fills the space with general words. Give it real facts and the writing tightens on its own.

So before any piece that matters, run a research step. And keep it separate from the writing.

Two Claude features help here.

Web search finds facts and gives answers with citations. Turn it on with +, then Web search. Anthropic's help page says the new Claude experience has no switch: Claude searches when it helps. Free accounts can use it.

Research runs several searches that build on each other, across the web and your connected tools. It's on paid plans. Turn it on with +, then Research.

Then use this prompt.

Research before writing
I'm going to write [what: e.g. a one-page update] for [who].
After reading it, they should [know / decide / do] [what].

Before you write anything, research:

1. Find the facts I'll need on [topic]. Use sources you can link to, and prefer official and primary ones.
2. List each fact as a short bullet with its source link and the exact words from the source in quotes.

3. Mark anything you couldn't confirm as "not confirmed". If you don't know, say "I don't know". Don't fill gaps with guesses.

4. Suggest an outline: the most important point first, one idea per section.

Stop there. Don't write the draft until I've checked the facts and the outline.

Each line has a reason.

Anthropic's guide to reducing hallucinations says that giving Claude permission to say "I don't know" can drastically reduce false information.

The same guide suggests pulling out word-for-word quotes first and basing the answer on them. Anthropic is clear that this reduces mistakes but doesn't remove them.

That's why the prompt stops before the draft. You check the facts while they're still a short list, not buried in polished paragraphs.

Once you've checked them:

Now write it
Good. Now write the [piece] using only the facts I approved above, following my plain-English style instruction.
Length: [about N words]. Format: [e.g. short paragraphs, no headings].
Where a fact was "not confirmed", leave it out.

Ask Claude about your data, the careful way

Four everyday versions

Your style instruction does most of the work. These add what each job needs on top.

An email people answer

Plain email
Write a reply to the email below. I want to [agree / say no / ask for more time].

Check every draft

Even with good rules, drafts drift.

So run a check before you edit by hand. It finds the problems; you decide the fixes.

Check the draft below against plain-English rules. Don't rewrite it yet.

1. Every sentence over 25 words
2. Every passive sentence, with an active version

4. Every filler word (very, really, actually, quite, totally)

That's the right rule for your inbox too.

  • Dumbing it down. Plain isn't childish. Match your reader's level.
  • Pasting a whole style manual. Eight clear rules beat eighty. Anthropic warns that longer prompts aren't always better.
  • Polishing thin facts. If the draft is vague, go back to the research step, not the style rules.
  • Trusting the first draft. Anthropic says the first prompt rarely works perfectly. Test and refine.
  • Skipping your own read. You sign it. You check it.

item.description: Why Claude's answers come back generic, five prompting rules from Anthropic's own guidance, one template to reuse and prompts to copy.
item.content:encoded:
You ask Claude for something.

It answers in seconds. Neat, polite, well organised.

And completely generic.

It could have been written for anyone.

Most of the time, the cause is the prompt. And the prompt is the part you control.

The good news: the fix is small, and Anthropic has written it down.

I teach people to use AI at work, and this is the lesson that pays off fastest. So I've boiled Anthropic's own prompting guidance down to what you need in a normal working day.

What's inside:

  1. Why answers come back generic
  2. Five rules that matter
  3. One template you can reuse for almost anything
  4. Ready-made versions for four everyday jobs
  5. The mistakes to stop making
  6. Where to save your rules so you never type them again

Get the next one in your inbox

One practical guide at a time: the exact steps, the prompts to copy and the mistakes to skip.

Free. Delivered by Substack, one click to unsubscribe. Form not showing? Subscribe on Substack.

Why answers come back generic

Picture a brilliant new hire on their first morning.

Sharp. Fast. Keen to help.

But they don't know your team, your customers, your standards or why the task matters.

Hand them a one-line request and they'll do the safest, most average version of it.

That's exactly how Anthropic tells you to think about Claude. Its prompting guide says to treat Claude like a brilliant but new employee who lacks context on your norms and workflows.

And it adds: the more precisely you explain what you want, the better the result.

So a generic answer is a signal. Claude filled the gaps with average guesses, because you left gaps.

Anthropic also gives a simple test you can run on any prompt:

Key point

Show your prompt to a colleague who knows little about the task. If they'd be confused about what to do, Claude will be too.

Here's the same request at three levels of detail:

Brief Claude like a colleague: the full guide

Five rules that matter

There are many prompting tricks. Most people need five.

Each one comes from Anthropic's own guidance.

1. Give the goal and the context

Say what you want, who it's for, and why.

The "why" matters more than it looks.

Anthropic's guide shows this with a rule: "NEVER use ellipses." On its own, it's a bare command. Add the reason (the reply will be read aloud by a text-to-speech engine) and Claude can apply the idea to cases the rule never mentioned.

So instead of a bare rule, give the reason behind it.

  • Weak: "Keep it short."
  • Strong: "Keep it under 100 words. My manager reads these on her phone between meetings."

2. Say what good looks like

Claude can't read your mind about format.

Anthropic's guide says to be specific about the output format and any limits. If order or completeness matters, ask for numbered or bulleted steps.

And if you want more than the minimum, say so out loud. Claude won't assume you want the extra effort.

One more detail from the same guide: tell Claude what to do, not what to avoid.

  • Weak: "Don't use bullet points."
  • Strong: "Write it as three short paragraphs of flowing prose."

It also helps to write your prompt in the style you want back. A prompt full of bullets tends to get bullets.

3. Show one example

Anthropic calls examples one of the most reliable ways to steer format, tone and structure.

Its developer guide recommends three to five varied examples. Its article for people using the Claude apps is gentler: start with one, and add more only if the output still doesn't match.

That article also warns that newer models pay very close attention to the details in examples.

So pick your example with care. If it has a typo or a strange heading, you may get those back too.

4. Let Claude say "I don't know"

Claude writes confidently even when it's wrong.

Anthropic's help centre says plainly that Claude can "hallucinate" incorrect or misleading information. It says not to rely on Claude as your only source of truth, and to check cited sources and high-stakes advice.

The simplest guard is one sentence. Anthropic's guide to reducing hallucinations says that explicitly giving Claude permission to say "I don't know" can drastically reduce false information.

For long documents, the same guide adds two more moves:

  • ask Claude to pull out word-for-word quotes first, then answer from those quotes
  • ask it to back each claim with a quote, or take the claim back

Anthropic is careful to say these reduce mistakes, but don't remove them. You still check.

5. Keep it short, and keep the rules few

More words don't mean a better prompt.

Anthropic's article for Claude app users warns against over-engineering: longer, more complex prompts are not always better.

The same article says the first prompt rarely works perfectly. You test, then refine.

It also says the heavy machinery is mostly optional now. XML tags and elaborate role-play are less necessary with modern models. Clear headings, white space and plain, explicit language work just as well for most jobs.

A short role still helps. Anthropic says even a single sentence makes a difference to Claude's tone and behaviour. Something like "You're an experienced HR adviser" is enough.

Three good rules beat fifteen vague ones.

Tip

Anthropic says Opus 5.5 follows the writing rules you give it. That's a reason to give a few clear ones, and to make each one count.

Before and after, side by side

Here are the five rules as quick swaps.

Instead of Try
"Write a project update." "Write a project update for the finance director. She needs to decide on extra budget by Friday."
"Make it professional." "Three short paragraphs, warm but direct, no jargon."
"Don't make it too long." "Under 150 words: it's read on a phone."
"Write it in our style." "Match the tone of this example: [paste one]."
"What are the facts?" "If you're not sure of something, say so. Don't fill gaps with guesses."
Fifteen rules in a row Three rules, each with a reason

Notice what the right-hand column has in common.

Every line answers a question a new colleague would ask you.

The one-good-prompt template

This is the template to keep.

It puts the five rules in order, with brackets to fill in. Delete any line you don't need.

The one-good-prompt template
You're [a role, in one sentence: e.g. an experienced editor for busy managers].

Goal: I need [the thing you want] so that [what it's for, and who will use it].

Context: [who the reader is, what they already know, what has happened so far, anything I've attached].

Good looks like: [length, format and tone]. Here's an example of the style I want:
[paste one short example]

Rules (only these):
- [rule], because [reason]
- [rule], because [reason]

If you're not sure about something, say so plainly and tell me what you'd need to know. Don't guess.

If something important is missing, ask me up to three questions before you start.

Fill it in once for a task you do every week.

Then save the filled-in version somewhere you can paste it from.

It looks long. Most of it is the context you'd give a new colleague anyway.

The last two lines do quiet, useful work. One gives Claude room to say "I don't know". The other stops it guessing when you forgot something.

Get the next issue by email

Four everyday versions

Here's the template already shaped for four common jobs.

Write an email that sounds like you

Email
Goal: Write a reply to the email below. I want to [agree / say no politely / ask for more time] and keep a good relationship with this person.

Context: [who they are, how well I know them, what's happened so far].

Good looks like: under 120 words, warm and direct, no corporate phrases. End with one clear next step.

Here's an email I wrote that sounds like me:
[paste one of your own emails]

If anything in their email is unclear, point it out instead of guessing what they meant.

Their email:
[paste it]

Summarise a long document

For long material, Anthropic's guide says to put the document near the top and your question at the end. Anthropic says putting the question at the end can improve answers by up to 30% in its tests on very long inputs.

Summary
[paste or attach the document first]

You're summarising this for [who], who needs to [decide / act on / understand] it.

First, pull out the word-for-word quotes that matter most for that purpose.

Then write a summary of no more than [five] bullet points, each one based on a quote.

If a point isn't supported by a quote, leave it out. If the document doesn't answer something important, say what's missing.

Think through a decision

Decision
Goal: Help me decide between [option A] and [option B].

Context: [the situation, the deadline, what matters most to me and why, what I've ruled out].

Good looks like: a short table of pros and cons for each option, then your recommendation in two sentences.

For every point, tell me how sure you are: high, medium or low. Where you're guessing, say so. If you'd need more information to answer well, ask me first.

Rewrite something in plain words

Plain words
Rewrite the text below for [who: e.g. customers with no technical background].

Goal: they should understand [the one thing] after one read.

Good looks like: short sentences, everyday words, the most important point first. Keep every fact. Don't add any.

If a term has no plain equivalent, keep it and explain it in brackets.

The text:
[paste it]

More on plain-English prompts

Mistakes to stop making

Most weak answers come from the same handful of habits.

  • The one-liner. "Write a LinkedIn post about AI." Claude can only give you the average post.
  • Hidden context. You know who the reader is. Claude doesn't, unless you say.
  • Only saying "don't". Anthropic's advice is to say what to do instead.
  • Rules without reasons. A reason lets Claude apply the rule sensibly. A bare rule gets followed to the letter, or not at all.
  • Rule pile-ups. Fifteen instructions compete. Three get followed.
  • Trusting the tone. Confident writing isn't proof. Check names, numbers and sources before anything goes out under your name.
  • Five messages instead of one. Anthropic's usage tips say to give background up front and combine related questions in one message. You get a better first answer and use less of your limits.
  • Stopping at the first draft. Anthropic itself says the first prompt rarely works perfectly. Refine it.

Watch out

Never paste a confident answer into a report, a contract or a client email without checking it. Anthropic's own help centre says Claude can be wrong and should not be your only source of truth.

Ask Claude about your data, the careful way

Three follow-ups worth keeping

The first answer is a draft. These three prompts turn it into a good one.

Find the gaps
What did you have to assume to write this? List each assumption, and tell me which ones I should confirm.
Check the claims
Go through your answer. For each fact or number, tell me where it came from: something I gave you, a source you can name, or your own general knowledge. Mark anything you're not sure about.
Make it better
Read your answer as [the reader]. What would they find unclear, missing or too long? Fix those things and show me the new version.

If an answer isn't working after two rounds, don't keep patching.

Go back and fix the prompt. Then start again.

Claude habits that save time and mistakes

Save your rules once

Some rules apply to everything you write.

Your audience. Your spelling. "No jargon." "Most important point first."

Don't type them into every chat. Put them in Instructions.

Here's where:

  1. Open Settings.
  2. Go to Your Claude.
  3. Open Instructions and add your standing rules, each with its reason.

Anthropic's help centre says these account-wide Instructions apply to all your conversations.

For rules that only belong to one piece of work, use project instructions instead. They apply only inside that project.

Instructions to adapt
I work as [your role] in [your field]. Most of what I write is read by [who].

When you write for me:
- Put the most important point first, because my readers are busy.
- Use plain, everyday words, because many readers aren't specialists.
- If you're not sure about a fact, say so instead of guessing, because I'll use your answers at work.

Keep it short. The same advice about few rules applies here too.

A note on effort

Sometimes the prompt is fine and the job is just hard.

In the Claude apps you can give Claude more room to think. Click the model name next to the send button, click Effort, and pick a level.

Anthropic says Low and Medium suit routine tasks and stretch your usage further. Higher effort uses more.

So keep routine work on a lower level. Save the higher levels for the hard problems.

Fill in the template for it. Every bracket.

Run the colleague test: would a smart newcomer know what to do?

item.title: Bring the point.
item.description: Why AI alone won't grow your LinkedIn: give first, break patterns, fix visuals, post steadily, pick your reader. Plus prompts that keep your voice.
item.content:encoded:
You asked AI for a LinkedIn post.

It gave you one in ten seconds.

Neat opening. Three tidy points. A question at the end.

You posted it. A few likes. Then nothing.

So you tried again. Same result.

Here's the honest reason: the post had no point that was yours.

AI can write. It can't decide what you know, what you believe, or who you're talking to.

That part is your job. And it's the part that makes people stop scrolling.

I teach people to use AI at work, and my mission is to make data and AI easy for everyone. This issue is the plain version of how to use AI on LinkedIn without sounding like everyone else.

Inside:

  1. What LinkedIn itself says about AI-written posts
  2. Give before you take
  3. Break your own patterns
  4. Fix your visuals
  5. Steady beats a burst
  6. Decide who you want reading
  7. Prompts that keep your voice

Get the next one in your inbox

One practical guide at a time: the exact steps, the prompts to copy and the mistakes to skip.

Free. Delivered by Substack, one click to unsubscribe. Form not showing? Subscribe on Substack.

What LinkedIn says about AI posts

Start with the rules of the room.

LinkedIn has a help page called Best practices for content created with the help of AI.

It says LinkedIn does not want "AI slop".

Its definition: low-effort, likely AI-generated content that sounds polished but lacks a clear point of view, unique perspective or substance.

Read that again. Sounds polished. That's exactly what a quick AI draft does well.

The same page says LinkedIn judges whether content adds value, not how it was made.

AI-assisted posts are welcome when they reflect a real person's perspective.

Generic or repetitive posts are less likely to be widely distributed.

And readers can now flag a post through its More menu with "Seems like AI slop". If a post gets enough of that feedback, its author sees a tip in Post analytics. LinkedIn says that's a tip, not a takedown.

LinkedIn also asks you to review, edit and approve anything AI helped with. You're responsible for everything you post. If you relied heavily on AI and it isn't obvious, it suggests saying so.

What a quick AI draft gives you What LinkedIn says it wants
Polished sentences A clear point of view
Safe, general advice A unique perspective
The same shape as every other post Substance, from a real person
Words nobody checked Content you reviewed, edited and approved

Key point

AI is allowed. Empty is the problem. Bring the point, and let AI help you say it well.

Nobody is waiting for your post

This one stings a little.

Nobody opens LinkedIn hoping to hear from you.

They open it for themselves: to learn something, solve something, or feel less alone with a problem at work.

LinkedIn's own words back this up. In its page on how the feed decides what to show, one of the content signals it lists is whether a post provides knowledge or advice.

Others include what the post is about, how recent it is, and how constructive the conversation under it is.

So the question for every post is simple.

What does the reader walk away with?

A method they can use tomorrow. A mistake they can now avoid. A number explained. A clear opinion they can argue with.

If the honest answer is "they learn that I'm busy", rewrite it.

Here's a prompt that makes AI ask you that question before it writes anything.

Find what you're giving
I want to write a LinkedIn post about this:
[paste your rough idea, a few lines is fine]

Don't write the post yet.

First, ask me five short questions, one at a time, to find out:
1. who exactly this is for
2. what they should be able to do or understand after reading
3. the one example or moment from my own work that proves it
4. what most people get wrong about this
5. what I actually believe that others might disagree with

When I've answered all five, tell me in one sentence what the reader gets from this post. If you can't, tell me the idea isn't ready.

The last line matters. A good assistant should be able to tell you "not yet".

Know someone whose posts read like a press release? Send them this issue.

Spot your own habits

Look at your last ten posts.

Same opening line style? Same length? Same three-point list? Same topic, every week?

Your readers notice before you do.

LinkedIn noticed too. When it announced changes to the feed in March 2026, it said it is showing less engagement bait and recycled content.

The examples it gave: "comment to agree" prompts, and videos that don't match the text.

And remember the AI page: generic or repetitive content is less likely to be widely distributed.

AI makes repetition worse, because it reaches for the same shapes every time. Ask it for "a LinkedIn post" and you get the average LinkedIn post.

So use AI the other way round: to spot your habits, not to repeat them.

Audit your last ten posts
Below are my last ten LinkedIn posts, separated by ---.

[paste them]

Act as a blunt editor. Tell me:
1. the openings I keep reusing
2. the structures I keep reusing (lists, questions at the end, and so on)
3. the topics I keep circling back to
4. phrases that sound like any other post on LinkedIn
5. the one post that sounds most like me, and why

Then suggest three different ways I could shape my next post. Don't write it.

Three ways to change a habit

  • Change the shape. If you always write lists, tell one short story. If you always tell stories, write a checklist.
  • Change the angle. Write about what went wrong, not what went right. Or argue with an idea everyone in your field repeats.
  • Change the format. If you always post text, try a document or a poll. More on that next.
Newsletter One good prompt. Mojeed Abisiga · mojeedabisiga.com
NewsletterOne good prompt.Getting bland, generic answers? Five rules and one template that fix them:

Your visuals need work

People see the image before they read a word.

A blurry photo, a crowded slide or a stock picture that has nothing to do with the text tells them to keep scrolling.

LinkedIn gives you more formats than most people use. From the composer you can add a photo or video, an event or a celebration. Under the Plus icon you can create a poll, add a document, share that you're hiring, or add Services.

Its posting help page lists these.

Document posts are worth a look. LinkedIn's documents page says they take PPT, PPTX, DOC, DOCX and PDF files, up to 100MB and 300 pages.

Two details to know before you upload:

  • after posting, you can edit the description but not the document itself
  • people who can see the post can download it as a PDF

LinkedIn advises converting files to PDF where possible.

And mind the match. LinkedIn named videos that don't match the text as one of the things it is showing less of. Your visual should say the same thing as your words, only faster.

AI is useful here, as a planner. Let it plan the pages; you check every word on them.

Plan a document post
I want to turn this idea into a short LinkedIn document post (a PDF of slides):
[paste your idea and the key points]

Plan it as 6 to 8 slides.
For each slide give me:
- a headline of at most 8 words
- one or two short lines under it
- what simple visual would help (a chart, an icon, a before/after), or "none"

Rules: one idea per slide. No slide may say anything I haven't told you. Flag any point where you need a fact or a number from me.

Tip

Before you post, look at your visual on your phone at arm's length. If you can't read the headline, nobody else will.

Want the full method for making the visual itself? The guides on infographics with AI and slides with AI walk through it.

Guide Infographics that stay sharp. Mojeed Abisiga · mojeedabisiga.com
GuideInfographics that stay sharp.Clear, editable one-page visuals with AI, and a template your team can reuse:

Steady beats a burst

Here's a pattern almost everyone falls into.

You get inspired. You post every day for a week. Then work gets busy and you vanish for a month.

AI makes the burst easier, because drafts cost nothing. That's the trap.

LinkedIn says it may limit the visibility of posts when it detects excessive posting that looks like inauthentic activity or an automation tool, and it may cap posts per time period.

It also says it takes action against comment automation, engagement pods and unauthorised third-party tools that create inauthentic engagement.

So a flood of AI drafts works against you.

What works for you is a rhythm you can keep: one you'd still manage in your busiest month.

LinkedIn has two simple tools for that.

Drafts. You can save a post as a draft and keep editing it later, even from another device.

Scheduling. On desktop, click Start a post, write or paste your edited draft, then click the Clock icon in the composer and pick a date and time. You manage scheduled posts from the post composer.

Burst Steady rhythm
How it feels Exciting for a week Boring, then normal
Quality Drops as you rush You have time to edit
Risk Looks like excessive posting A pace you choose
When work gets busy You disappear Scheduled posts keep going

Use AI to fill a short list of ideas, then write one post at a time, properly.

Build a month of ideas, not posts
Here's what I do at work and what I know well:
[a few lines about your role, your field and what people ask you about]

Give me 8 post ideas I could write over the next month.
For each one:
- the one thing the reader would take away
- which of my experiences it should draw on (ask me if you're not sure)
- a suggested format: text, story, document or poll

Mix the formats. Don't repeat an angle. Don't write the posts.

Know a colleague who posts in bursts and then goes quiet? This section is for them.

Decide who you want reading

"More followers" isn't an audience.

A small group of people in the exact role you want to reach can matter more than a crowd who'll never need you.

LinkedIn's feed thinks in these terms too. It says it looks at three main kinds of signals: Identity (profile details such as location, workplace and skills), Content, and Activity.

Its March 2026 update says ranking now uses signals you choose to share (industry, skills, experience, geography) alongside how you engage over time.

LinkedIn's engineering team adds that, for each post, its model reads the author's name, headline, company and industry along with the post text. It also says the new system surfaces posts from authors people don't follow.

In plain words: your profile, your words and the people you talk to all tell LinkedIn who your posts are for.

So decide it on purpose.

  • Your headline should name who you help, in words that person would use.
  • Your posts should talk about that person's problems, in their language.
  • Your comments on other people's posts count as activity too. Spend them where your audience already is.

LinkedIn also lets you choose Follow or Connect as the main button on your profile. Choose the one that fits what you want from people who find you.

Define the reader
Help me decide who my LinkedIn posts are for.

About me: [your role, field and what you're good at]
What I want from LinkedIn: [for example: clients, a new job, speaking invitations, peers to learn from]

Ask me questions until you can describe my ideal reader in five lines:
their job, their biggest work problem, what they already know, what they'd never read, and the words they use for their problem.

Then rewrite my current headline for that reader:
[paste your headline]
Give me three options of at most 20 words each.

Once you've chosen, check whether it's working. LinkedIn's help page says your post and audience analytics are in the Analytics section of your profile, or behind the Post impressions count on the left of your feed.

Newsletter Proof gets you hired. Mojeed Abisiga · mojeedabisiga.com
NewsletterProof gets you hired.Your AI certificates are a good start. Here's how to build the proof that comes next:

Prompts that keep your voice

This is where most AI posts go wrong.

People type "write me a LinkedIn post about X" and accept what comes back.

Do it the other way round. You write first, even badly. AI edits.

That keeps your ideas, your examples and your rhythm, and uses AI for what it's good at: questioning, sorting and tightening.

1. Capture your voice once

My voice notes
Below are 3 to 5 pieces of writing that sound like me: posts, emails or messages I'm happy with.

[paste them]

Describe my writing voice in a short list I can reuse:
- sentence length and rhythm
- words and phrases I use often
- words I never use
- how I open and how I close
- how formal or casual I am
- what I do with examples and numbers

Keep it under 150 words. Use only what you can see in the samples.

Save the result. Paste it at the top of every drafting chat. If you use Claude, you can put them in a project's instructions instead: those apply to every chat inside that project. This issue shows how to set one up.

2. Turn your rough notes into a draft

Edit, don't invent
Here are my voice notes:
[paste them]

Here's my rough draft of a LinkedIn post. It's messy on purpose:
[paste your notes or draft]

Edit it into a post of at most 1,300 characters.
Rules:
- keep my ideas, my examples and my opinions; add none of your own
- keep my words wherever they work
- short paragraphs, one or two lines each
- no hashtags, no emojis, no question at the end asking people to comment
- if something is unclear or unsupported, mark it with [?] and don't guess

The 1,300 is a choice, not a rule: LinkedIn allows up to 3,000 characters. Shorter usually forces you to pick one point. If you need more than 3,000, LinkedIn suggests writing an article instead.

3. Run the slop check

Slop check
Read this LinkedIn post as a tired professional scrolling on their phone:
[paste the post]

Tell me honestly:
1. Which lines could have been written by anyone? Quote them.
2. Where is the point of view? If there isn't a clear one, say so.
3. What does the reader walk away with, in one sentence?
4. Which line would make them stop scrolling, if any?
5. Any claim or number I should double-check before posting?

Don't rewrite the post. Just give me the notes.

Then fix it yourself. Read it out loud. If it doesn't sound like something you'd say to a colleague, it isn't done.

Watch out

Never use tools that post comments for you, or join groups that like each other's posts on cue. LinkedIn says it takes action against comment automation and engagement pods.

For a deeper look at writing prompts that work for any job, read one good prompt.

Get the next one in your inbox

One practical guide at a time: the exact steps, the prompts to copy and the mistakes to skip.

Free. Delivered by Substack, one click to unsubscribe. Form not showing? Subscribe on Substack.

What to do this week

Small steps. One post, done properly.

  • Read LinkedIn's AI best practices page. It takes five minutes.
  • Run the Audit your last ten posts prompt and note your top three habits.
  • Run My voice notes once and save the result.
  • Write your next post yourself, rough, then use Edit, don't invent and the Slop check.
  • Check every fact and every word before you post.
  • Pick a rhythm you can keep, and schedule your next post with the Clock icon.
  • Write down, in one sentence, who you want reading.

AI can make a good post better.

It can't make an empty post worth reading.

Bring the point. Let AI help with the rest.

If this helped, send it to one person who's been posting a lot and getting little back.

Brief AI like a colleague

item.title: Free, and enough.
item.description: The best free AI tool for chat, writing, research, slides, images, meeting notes and coding, with each free plan's limits from the vendor's own pages.
item.content:encoded:
You don't need to pay for AI to start using it at work.

You need to know which free plan does which job.

And where each one stops.

Most "best free AI tools" lists skip that last part. Then you hit a wall in the middle of a task.

I teach people to use AI at work. So this issue sticks to one rule:

Every limit below comes from the vendor's own pricing or help page. No guesses, no reviews, no rumours.

Pages were read on 27 November 2026, on US pages. Plans change often, and features vary by country, so check the link before you rely on a detail.

Inside, one free tool per job:

  1. Everyday chat: ChatGPT Free
  2. Writing and documents: Claude Free
  3. Research and search: Perplexity Free
  4. Slides: Gamma Free
  5. Images: Gemini
  6. Meeting notes: Otter Basic
  7. Coding: GitHub Copilot Free

Each one comes with a prompt to copy and the limit to watch.

Get the next one in your inbox

One practical guide at a time: the exact steps, the prompts to copy and the mistakes to skip.

Free. Delivered by Substack, one click to unsubscribe. Form not showing? Subscribe on Substack.

Think and write

Three jobs most people do every day: ask, write and look things up.

One free tool for each.

1. Everyday chat: ChatGPT Free

For quick questions, rewording an email, explaining a term: ChatGPT's free plan is the most generous on volume.

OpenAI's pricing page advertises unlimited text chats with GPT-6 on Free, subject to abuse guardrails.

What Free limits, in OpenAI's words: uploads, image creation, voice chats, deep research, and memory and context are all "limited".

Two more things to know:

  • Short memory per chat. The context window on Free is 27K tokens with GPT Instant. Plus has 54K. Long documents won't fit in one go.
  • Ads. OpenAI says ads may appear for Free and Go users. Paid plans from Plus up have none.
Everyday chat
Rewrite this email so it's shorter and friendlier, but keeps every date and number exactly as written. Then give me a subject line of six words or fewer.

[paste your email]

Prefer Microsoft? It also offers a limited free version of Copilot, subject to available capacity. When you hit a limit, you upgrade or come back later.

ChatGPT's plans · OpenAI on ads

2. Writing and documents: Claude Free

When you need a proper document, a report or a one-pager, use Claude's free plan.

Claude's pricing page lists a lot on Free: chat on web, desktop and mobile, web search, file creation and code, memory, connectors, Artifacts, and Claude Design, Slides and Docs.

It can hand you a real file. Claude creates Word, PowerPoint, Excel and PDF files in the conversation, and file creation is on by default for Free.

Anthropic has also committed that Claude will stay ad-free.

What Free limits:

  • Usage. Limited usage every 5 hours and every week. The number of messages varies with demand.
  • Models. Sonnet and Haiku only. Opus and Fable are on paid plans.
  • Apps. Chat works on Free. Claude Code and Cowork need a paid plan.
  • Projects. Up to five.
  • Sharing. Claude's help centre shows link sharing for new artifacts on paid plans, not Free.
Writing a document
Turn the notes below into a one-page Word document for my manager.

Structure: a two-line summary, then three sections (what happened, what it means, what I recommend), then a short list of next steps with owners.

Plain English. No jargon. Keep every number exactly as in my notes.

[paste your notes]

Claude's plans

3. Research and search: Perplexity Free

For questions where you want sources, start with Perplexity.

Its help centre says Free gives practically unlimited basic searches.

What Free limits:

  • 3 Pro Searches a day
  • 1 Research query a month
  • limited file uploads
  • no advanced AI models and no image generation

So save the one monthly Research query for the question that really matters.

Research with sources
What changed in [your topic] in the last 12 months? Give me five points, each with the source it comes from. Then tell me which two points the sources disagree on.

Need a longer report? Google's free Gemini plan includes Deep Research too. Google AI Plus gives twice the usage of Free, and AI Pro four times.

Tip

Google's free plan also includes Gemini Notebook, the name Google's plans page now uses for NotebookLM. It's listed as a "research and writing assistant". Paid plans add more notebooks and Audio Overviews.

Perplexity's plans

Guide Claude, from the first click. Mojeed Abisiga · mojeedabisiga.com
GuideClaude, from the first click.Never opened it? Everything you need for your first week, in plain words:

Make things

Two jobs that used to need a designer: a deck and a picture.

4. Slides: Gamma Free

Gamma turns a prompt into a presentation. Its free plan is a good way to get a first draft of a deck.

Gamma's help centre says Free includes AI creations, the AI Agent, basic image models, up to 10 slides per prompt and 50k input tokens.

The catch is credits:

  • Every AI action uses credits: presentations, images and AI-agent edits.
  • Free credits don't refresh. When they're gone, they're gone.
  • You earn 200 credits per referral and can hold up to 2,000.

Two more limits worth knowing. Removing the "Made with Gamma" badge from what you share or export is a Plus feature. So is going past 10 slides per prompt (Plus allows up to 100).

Slides draft
Make a 10-slide presentation for my team about [topic].

Audience: busy colleagues who haven't seen this before.
Slide 1: the one-sentence point. Slides 2 to 8: one idea each, a short headline and three bullets. Slide 9: the decision we need. Slide 10: next steps with owners.

Keep the words short. No more than 25 words per slide.

Since credits don't come back, write the prompt properly the first time. A clear outline costs the same credits as a vague one.

Already on Claude? Its free plan lists Slides too, and a deck made from a template exports to PowerPoint, PDF or Google Slides.

Gamma's plans

5. Images: Gemini

For pictures, use Google's Gemini app.

Google says the Nano Banana 2 image model is free in the Gemini app: it makes and edits images at 2K resolution. Its best image model, Nano Banana 2.1, needs a paid Google AI plan, which also gives higher image limits.

How to make one:

  1. Open the Gemini app and open the tools menu.
  2. Select Create images.
  3. Type your prompt, or upload an image you want to edit.

Good to know:

  • Every Gemini image carries a visible watermark and an invisible SynthID watermark.
  • It can put clear text inside an image, in many languages.
  • You can upload any image to Gemini and ask whether Google AI made it.
Image
A clean, flat illustration for a work presentation: a small team around a table looking at one big chart on a screen. Warm, friendly colours. Plenty of empty space at the top for a title. No text in the image.

Backups: ChatGPT Free also creates images, with a "limited" allowance. Claude doesn't make photos or illustrations, though it can draw diagrams and charts in a chat on the web and desktop.

Note

The visible watermark stays on free images. If you use one at work, say it was made with AI.

Gemini's free plan · Gemini images

Guide Infographics that stay sharp. Mojeed Abisiga · mojeedabisiga.com
GuideInfographics that stay sharp.Clear, editable one-page visuals with AI, and a template your team can reuse:

Capture and build

Two jobs that eat hours: writing up meetings and writing code.

6. Meeting notes: Otter Basic

Otter's Basic plan is free and built for meetings.

It works with Zoom, Microsoft Teams and Google Meet, transcribes live, tells speakers apart, and has AI Chat so you can ask questions about one meeting or across several. There are iOS and Android apps.

What Basic limits:

  • 300 transcription minutes a month. Unused minutes don't roll over.
  • 30 minutes per conversation. An hour-long meeting won't be covered in full.
  • 3 file imports, for life. Not per month.

For comparison, Otter Pro gives 1,200 minutes a month and up to 90 minutes per meeting.

Meeting follow-up (Otter AI Chat)
From this meeting, list every decision we made, every action item with its owner and deadline, and any question we left open. Then draft a five-line follow-up email I can send to everyone who attended.

Watch out

Tell people when a meeting is being recorded and transcribed, before you start.

Otter's plans

7. Coding: GitHub Copilot Free

If you write code, even small scripts, start with GitHub Copilot Free.

GitHub's docs say Copilot Free gives you limited access to a selection of features, "to try AI-powered coding assistance at no cost".

What you get:

  • code suggestions as you type, in your code editor
  • Copilot Chat in your editor, inline chat and slash commands
  • Copilot Chat in GitHub Mobile
  • an allowance of GitHub AI Credits

What Free limits:

  • 2,000 completions a month for code suggestions
  • No model choice. Models come through auto model selection only.
  • Individuals only. Not if you already have Copilot through an organization or enterprise.

Verified students can get Copilot Student for free. The first paid plan, Copilot Pro, is $10 a month.

Coding (Copilot Chat)
Explain what this script does, line by line, in plain English. Then point out anything that could break if the input file is empty, and suggest the smallest fix.

[paste your code]

What about Claude? Claude Code is on paid plans only. On Free, Claude's code execution and file creation is still on, so it can run code inside a chat to make files.

GitHub Copilot plans

Newsletter Right tool, right job. Mojeed Abisiga · mojeedabisiga.com
NewsletterRight tool, right job.Stop looking for one AI that does everything. Five everyday jobs, and where to start for each:

The whole stack on one page

Here's every pick side by side.

Job Free tool What Free gives you Where Free stops
Chat ChatGPT Free Unlimited text chats with GPT-6 27K context; limited uploads, voice, memory; ads may appear
Writing Claude Free Word, PDF and PowerPoint files; Docs and Slides; no ads Limits every 5 hours and every week; Sonnet and Haiku only
Research Perplexity Free Practically unlimited basic searches 3 Pro Searches a day; 1 Research query a month
Slides Gamma Free Up to 10 slides per prompt, AI Agent Credits don't refresh; badge removal is a paid feature
Images Gemini Nano Banana 2, 2K, generate and edit Visible watermark; best model is paid
Meeting notes Otter Basic 300 minutes a month, live, with AI Chat 30 minutes per conversation; 3 imports for life
Coding Copilot Free Suggestions and chat in your editor 2,000 completions a month; no model choice

Share this with one colleague who's about to pay for an AI tool they haven't tried free yet.

Make free plans go further

Free plans run out at the worst moment. A few habits help.

Give each tool one job

Don't ask your chat tool to make slides and your slides tool to research. Each free plan is strongest at its own job, and you spread the limits across several tools.

Save the scarce things

Some limits are tiny: one Perplexity Research query a month, three Otter imports for life, Gamma credits that never come back.

Use them for the work that matters. Do the warm-up thinking in a tool with room to spare.

Prepare before you spend

Paste clean notes, not a messy draft. Say who it's for and what format you want. One clear request uses less of your allowance than five corrections.

Tighten my request first
Here's what I'm about to ask another AI tool. Rewrite my request so it's clear, short and complete: say who it's for, the format, the length and what to avoid. Ask me up to three questions if something important is missing.

[paste your request]

Check your privacy settings

Claude's Free, Pro, Max and Ultra plans list model training as opt-out. Look for that setting in any tool before you paste work documents.

Key point

Free plans are for trying, learning and light work. When one tool hits its limit every week, that's the one worth paying for.

GuideStop running out of Claude.Hit the limit mid-task? How usage is counted, and twelve habits that make it last:

The three to start with

You don't need all seven this week.

Start with the three most people use every day:

  1. Claude Free for anything you'll send to someone: a document, a summary, a report.
  2. Perplexity Free when you need sources you can check.
  3. Otter Basic for your next short meeting, under 30 minutes.

Add Gamma, Gemini and Copilot when the job comes up.

Subscribe for the next issue

Pick one job you did by hand this week.

Find its row in the table. Sign up for that one free tool.

Copy the prompt from this issue and run it on real work.

Then note where the free plan stopped you, if it did. That tells you whether you'll ever need to pay.

item.title: Hand Claude the mouse.
item.description: Turn on computer use in Claude Desktop safely: what it needs, the switch, the approval mode, which apps to allow, five prompts and scheduling.
item.content:encoded:
Some jobs live inside an app.

No connector reaches them. No upload helps.

Someone has to open the app, click, type, copy, paste.

Until now, that someone was you.

Claude can now do it. It can see your screen, click, type and open apps on your computer.

Anthropic calls it computer use.

It's useful. It's also the most powerful thing you can switch on in Claude. So it deserves a careful set-up.

I teach people to use AI at work, and this is the set-up to get right first.

Inside:

  1. Check you have what it needs
  2. Switch it on
  3. Choose how much Claude asks first
  4. Allow apps one at a time
  5. Run a small first task
  6. Put a task on a schedule

Plus five everyday jobs with prompts you can copy.

Get the next one in your inbox

One practical guide at a time: the exact steps, the prompts to copy and the mistakes to skip.

Free. Delivered by Substack, one click to unsubscribe. Form not showing? Subscribe on Substack.

Why let Claude click for you

Claude always reaches for the most precise tool first.

If a connector can do the job, it uses the connector. If not, the browser. Only then does it work on your screen directly.

So computer use is the fallback for everything else: the desktop app with no connector, the old system nobody built a link to, the file that only opens in one program.

That's what it saves you. The clicking between apps.

Two honest limits before you start:

  • Working on the screen is slower than a connector.
  • Complex tasks sometimes need a second try.

Good to know before you judge it on day one.

New to Cowork? Start here

Step 1: Check you have what it needs

Computer use runs through Claude Desktop, the app you install on your computer.

Here's what the help pages say you need:

What you need
Plan Pro, Max or Ultra. On Team and Enterprise it's a beta that an owner must turn on first.
Computer A Mac (computer use needs macOS 14 or later) or a Windows PC (Windows 10 or higher).
Not supported Linux. Computer use isn't available there.
While it works Your computer awake, Claude Desktop open, and an internet connection.

Pro is $20 a month, or $17 a month if you pay yearly.

No Claude Desktop yet? Get it from claude.com/download.

On Team and Enterprise, there's one more catch. Computer use works only in the new Claude experience. It doesn't work in tasks started with the "Cowork" option, or in Claude Code.

How do you know you have the new experience? Your message box no longer shows "Chat" and "Cowork".

Note

Your Cowork tasks run on Anthropic's servers, in the cloud. But anything that touches your own screen, your local files or the browser needs Claude Desktop open on your computer.

Step 2: Switch it on

It's one switch.

  1. Open Claude Desktop.
  2. Go to Settings → Capabilities. (On some versions it's Settings → System, under "This computer".)
  3. Turn on Enable computer use.

That's it for the switch.

Nothing happens yet. Claude only asks for an app when you give it a task that needs one.

On a Mac

Claude also needs two macOS permissions: Accessibility and Screen & System Audio Recording.

If Claude can't see or click anything, check both are on.

Background or full control

On macOS 15 or later, Claude works in background windows by default. It doesn't take over your pointer, so you can keep working.

If you'd rather it drives the pointer, look for How Claude uses the apps you allow and choose Full control.

Start with the default.

Step 3: Choose how much Claude asks first

Every task has an approval mode. It decides how often Claude stops to check with you.

Mode What happens Use it when
Manually approve Claude pauses and you click Allow or Deny You're new to this, or the task touches anything sensitive
Automatically approve Claude keeps going, but each action is checked for safety and unsafe ones are blocked Routine work you've already watched it do
Skip all approvals Nothing checks Claude's actions Only when you fully trust every app, file and connector involved

The older names were "Ask before acting" and "Act without asking", in case you see those.

Anthropic is clear that the automatic check can miss risky actions.

For anything involving money, messages sent as you or important files, stay close or switch to Manually approve.

Watch out

Cowork normally asks before it permanently deletes a file. That protection does not cover computer use. Keep backups of anything that matters, and don't point Claude at files you can't afford to lose.

Step 4: Allow apps one at a time

Claude asks your permission before it touches each app.

Once you say yes, it can keep using that app for the rest of that session without asking again.

Not every app gets the same access:

Kind of app What Claude can do
Browsers, and many investment, trading and crypto apps Look only
Terminals and code editors Click and scroll, but not type
Most other apps Full access
Music, video streaming and e-book apps Nothing: they're off limits

You can also block apps yourself. Claude's requests for a blocked app are denied automatically.

What not to allow

Anthropic recommends you don't give computer use access to sensitive apps: banking, healthcare, government.

Treat that as a hard rule, not a suggestion.

Two things that surprise people

It can reach beyond your folders. In Cowork, Claude normally works only in the folders you connect. Computer use isn't limited that way.

Links can open other apps. If Claude clicks a link inside an app you approved, that can open another app, Chrome for example, even though you never approved Chrome.

Both are good reasons to start small.

Newsletter Check a skill before you trust it. Mojeed Abisiga · mojeedabisiga.com
NewsletterCheck a skill before you trust it.A Claude skill can run code on your behalf. Here's what can go wrong, and the five-minute check to run first:

Step 5: Run a small first task

Pick one app. One small job. Something you could check in a minute.

Use Manually approve, and watch.

If you have the "Cowork" option in your message box, select it first. If you have the new Claude experience, just type the task into any conversation.

First task: one app, one small job
Open [app name] on my computer.

Find [the item, e.g. last week's report] and tell me
[what you want to know, e.g. the total in the last row].

Rules:
- Only use [app name]. Ask me before opening anything else.
- Don't change, move, send or delete anything.
- If you get stuck, stop and tell me what you see.

Claude will ask to use the app. Allow it.

Then follow along. Read each step before you click Allow.

How to know it worked

You get the answer you asked for, and nothing else changed.

If it took a wrong turn, say so plainly and ask it to try again. A second try is normal for this kind of work.

What to watch for

You don't need to check every click.

Anthropic's advice is to watch for patterns you didn't expect: files or sites you never mentioned, a task quietly getting bigger.

If something feels off, stop the task.

Five everyday jobs to hand over

Once the small task goes well, try real work.

Each prompt below keeps Claude to one app and tells it where to stop. Swap the brackets for your own details.

1. Copy numbers out of an app with no connector

Pull figures into a spreadsheet
Open [app name] and go to [screen or report name].

Copy [the figures, e.g. this month's totals by region]
into a new Excel spreadsheet with clear column headings
and a total row that uses working formulas.

Save it in my [folder name] folder as [file name].
Don't change anything in [app name].

Cowork can make Excel files with working formulas, so the result is ready to use.

2. Fill in a form from a document

Fill a form, then stop
Open [document name] in my [folder name] folder.

Then open [app name] and fill in the [form name] form
using the details from that document.

Stop before you submit. Show me what you filled in
so I can check it and submit it myself.

The last line matters. You stay the one who presses send.

3. Turn notes from an app into a document

Notes into a clean summary
Open [notes app] and find my notes titled [title].

Turn them into a one-page summary document:
- three key points at the top
- decisions made
- actions, with who and by when

Save it to my [folder name] folder. Don't edit the notes.

4. Tidy a working folder (carefully)

Sort files without deleting any
Open my [folder name] folder.

Sort the files into subfolders by [type / month / client].
Make a list of every file you moved and where it went.

Never delete or rename a file. If you're unsure where
something belongs, leave it and add it to the list.

Remember: deletion protection doesn't cover computer use. The "never delete" rule in the prompt is your seat belt. A backup is your airbag.

5. Build slides from what's on screen

A short deck from an app's data
Open [app name] and look at [report or screen name].

Make a five-slide PowerPoint presentation for
[audience] that explains [what the numbers show].
One idea per slide, short titles, no more than
three bullets each.

Save it to my [folder name] folder.

Then check the numbers against the app yourself before it goes anywhere.

Tip

Each step of a multi-step task uses some of your usage, so these cost more than a quick question. Keep related work in one task, and check Settings → Usage if you're unsure how much you have left.

Understand Claude's usage limits

Step 6: Put a task on a schedule

Some jobs come round every week. Claude can run them for you.

Scheduled tasks are on every paid plan, in Cowork and in the new Claude experience.

The quick way

Type /schedule in any Cowork task.

Or, in the new Claude experience, describe the task and how often it should run in any conversation. Claude proposes a schedule. Review it, then click Schedule.

From the Scheduled page

  1. Click Scheduled in the left sidebar.
  2. Click New task.
  3. Pick Create with Claude. Claude asks you a few questions. Then click Schedule.

Prefer to fill it in yourself? Pick Set up manually. You'll give it:

  • a task name
  • the prompt
  • an approval mode
  • how often: hourly, daily, weekly, on weekdays, or manually
  • a model and a folder, if you want them

The catch with computer use

Scheduled tasks normally run remotely, even when your computer is asleep.

But computer use needs your computer awake and Claude Desktop open. The same goes for any task you give a folder: picking one switches on Require this computer.

So schedule screen-based jobs for a time your computer is on.

A weekly task to schedule
Every Monday at 9am:

Open [app name] and go to [report name].
Copy last week's figures into my [file name] spreadsheet
in the [folder name] folder, as a new row.

Then write me three lines: what went up, what went down,
and anything that looks unusual.

Don't send, delete or submit anything.

Keep scheduled tasks safe

Anthropic's advice for scheduled tasks:

  • Start simple.
  • Keep sensitive data and hard-to-undo actions out of them.
  • Review the output after each run.
  • Pause tasks you're not using.

From the Scheduled page you can see past and upcoming runs, edit the prompt, cadence or approval mode, pause, resume, delete, or run a task right now.

And remember: you stay responsible for what Claude does on your behalf. That includes scheduled runs and anything it does on your screen.

Guide Set up Cowork once. Mojeed Abisiga · mojeedabisiga.com
GuideSet up Cowork once.Already tried Cowork? Set it up properly in one sitting, and stop babysitting it:

If something looks different

Claude's menus are changing as the new Claude experience rolls out. If your screen doesn't match:

  • No "Enable computer use" under Capabilities? Try Settings → System, under "This computer".
  • No "Cowork" option in the message box? You have the new Claude experience. Type the task into any conversation.
  • On Team or Enterprise and it's not there? An owner has to turn computer use on first, and it works only in the new Claude experience.
  • On Linux? Computer use isn't available there.
  • Claude can't see or click on a Mac? Check it has the Accessibility and Screen & System Audio Recording permissions.
  • A task stopped halfway? Check your computer didn't sleep and Claude Desktop is still open.

The official help page has the latest: Let Claude use your computer. For safety, read Use Claude Cowork safely. For schedules, Schedule recurring tasks.

What to do today

Turn on Enable computer use.

Set your first task to Manually approve.

Pick one app you open every day. Not your bank.

Give Claude one small job in it, using the first prompt above. Watch every step.

When it's done right twice, schedule it.

Subscribe for the next one

Send this to one colleague who spends their morning copying numbers between apps.

Mojeed

That's one tool. Claude has at least six.

Set each one up once, and Claude stops being a tab you visit. It becomes the place you work.

I teach people to use AI at work. This is the set-up I'd want every one of them to have.

  5. Cowork, for tasks with several steps

  7. Where to double-check Claude
  8. A set-up you can finish in half an hour
