Pick the model, then the effort

The model menu next to the send button holds several Claude models.

Each one has a job:

Model Reach for it when Speed
Opus 5.5 Most of your work. Anthropic calls it the "strongest daily driver" Moderate
Fable 5.2 Hard reasoning, and long tasks with many steps Moderate
Sonnet 5.5 Everyday tasks, and polished documents, slides and spreadsheets Fast
Haiku 5.5 Lots of quick, simple jobs Fastest

On Free, you get Sonnet and Haiku. Opus is on Pro, Max and Ultra. Fable is on paid plans, though on Pro it runs on usage credits.

When to switch: start on Opus 5.5, as Anthropic's own docs advise when you're unsure. Move up or down only when the job asks for it.

Where to find it: click the model name next to the send button and pick a model, or click More models. On your phone, the model name sits at the top of the screen.

Then set the effort. Click the model name, click Effort and choose Low, Medium, High, Extra high or Max. The level Anthropic recommends for each model is marked Default.

A first prompt to copy: run one real task on two models, then compare.

Same task, two models
Here's an update I need to send my manager: [paste it]. Rewrite it so the decision we need comes first, then the three facts behind it. Keep it under ten lines.

Send it on Sonnet 5.5. Then switch to Opus 5.5 and send it again. The switch applies from Claude's next answer. On Free, compare Sonnet with Haiku.

What you get back: two versions of the same update. Keep the model whose answer you'd send without edits.

Still picking Sonnet 4.6? It leaves the model menu on Free, Pro, Max and Ultra on December 8, 2026. Anthropic recommends Sonnet 5.5 instead.

Tip

Leave effort on Default until you have a reason to change it. Higher effort takes longer and uses more of your limits, so save it for work that needs careful thinking.

Newsletter Opus 5.5, in plain words. Mojeed Abisiga · mojeedabisiga.com
NewsletterOpus 5.5, in plain words.What changed, which Claude and effort to pick, and a six-step way to make it check its own work:

Projects, for work that comes back

Some work isn't a one-off. A client. A course. The report you write every month.

A project gives that work its own space: its own chats, its own files and its own instructions. Claude keeps a separate memory for each project, too.

Projects are on every plan. Free accounts can make up to five.

When to use it: any piece of work you return to, with files you'd otherwise upload again and again.

Where to find it:

  1. Click Projects on the left, or go to claude.ai/projects.
  2. Click + New Project in the top right and name it. Claude doesn't see the name or description, so save instructions for step 4.
  3. In the project's knowledge, on the right, click + and add your files.
  4. Click Set project instructions, write how Claude should work here, then Save instructions.

A first prompt to copy, in a new chat inside the project:

Check what Claude knows
Using only the files and instructions in this project, tell me in five lines what this piece of work is about. Then list what's missing that you'd need to do it well, and ask me for it.

What you get back: a short summary, and a list of the gaps to fill before the real work starts.

Chats in a project don't share context with each other. If something matters to every chat, add it to the project's knowledge.

Tip

Keep the files you use again and again in the project, not in each chat. Project content is cached, so it counts less against your usage limits when you reuse it.

Skill, project or instructions? How to choose

Artifacts, for work you'll share

Some answers you read once. Others you send.

For the second kind, Claude makes an artifact: a document, deck, design, dashboard or small interactive tool that opens beside the chat. You can edit it, come back to it and share it.

Artifacts are on every plan, including the Docs, Slides and Design templates.

When to use it: whenever the result is something you'll send, present or reuse.

Where to find it: ask for one in any chat. Or select Output in the message box and choose a template. Everything you make is saved in the Artifacts tab in the sidebar.

Artifacts need Create and edit files switched on in Settings → Capabilities. It's on by default on Free, Pro, Max and Ultra.

A first prompt to copy:

Make it a doc
Turn the notes below into a one-page doc for my manager: the decision we need, three options with the cost and risk of each, and my recommendation. Plain English, no jargon.

[paste your notes]

What you get back: a doc beside the chat. Start it from the Docs template and you can type in it directly, then export it to Word, PDF, Markdown or Google Docs. Decks made with Slides export to PowerPoint or PDF.

Tip

Don't describe which paragraph to fix. Highlight it, click Edit with Claude and type the change. Claude edits right where you marked.

Get the next issue by email

One practical guide at a time: the exact steps, the prompts to copy and the mistakes to skip.

Free. Delivered by Substack, one click to unsubscribe. Form not showing? Subscribe on Substack.

Plugins and skills, for your role

Out of the box, Claude is a generalist. Plugins and skills fit it to your work.

Plugins bundle skills, connectors and sub-agents into one package, so you get a ready-made set-up for your role from the first conversation. The library covers sales, finance, legal, marketing, HR, engineering, design, operations, data analysis and more. Plugins are on paid plans.

Skills are folders of instructions, scripts and resources that Claude loads when a task needs them. They're on every plan. Claude already has built-in skills for Excel, Word, PowerPoint and PDF files, and uses them by itself.

Connectors let Claude reach your other apps and data, using your own permissions.

When to use them: a plugin when you want a set-up for your role without building it. A skill when you have one job you want done your way. A connector when the answer lives in another app.

Where to find them:

  1. Open Customize in the left sidebar. Your plugins, skills and connectors all live there.
  2. Open the Plugins tab, then Discover.
  3. Pick the plugin for your role and click Add.

To see the skills a plugin brought with it, type / in the message box or click +.

For a skill of your own, zip its folder. Then go to Customize → Skills, click +, then + Create skill → Upload a skill.

A first prompt to copy: see a built-in skill at work, on any plan.

Make a Word file
Turn the notes below into a two-page Word document: a title, three headings and a table of actions with an owner and a date for each. Leave a cell empty where the notes don't say.

[paste your notes]

What you get back: a Word file, made with Claude's built-in Word skill. Nothing to install.

Watch out

A plugin can include a local MCP server that runs on your computer with the same permissions as any program you run. Only add plugins from sources you trust.

Make your first skill

Cowork: hand over the whole task

A chat answers one message at a time.

Cowork takes on a whole task. You describe the result you want. Claude makes a plan, splits the work into steps and hands back finished work: formatted documents, organised files, research pulled together.

When to use it: for the jobs you'd hand a colleague with "go and do this". Several steps, several files, and a document, spreadsheet or deck at the end.

Where to find it: Cowork is on paid plans. In the message box, select Cowork, describe the task, then read Claude's plan and let it run. Select Chat to go back to a normal conversation.

No Chat or Cowork option in your message box? You already have the new Claude experience, where the two are one conversation. Just describe the task.

A first prompt to copy:

Hand over a task
Read the meeting notes in my Meetings folder. Make one Word document that lists every decision and every open action, grouped by project, with the owner and the date where the notes give them. Where they don't, write [missing]. Show me your plan before you start.

What you get back: a plan, then a Word document in your session that you can preview and download. If the plan looks wrong, jump in and correct it mid-task.

The work runs in the cloud, so it carries on if you close your laptop. Tasks that use files on your computer need the Claude Desktop app open.

Once a task works, you can save it as a scheduled task that runs on a schedule or whenever you ask.

Tip

Start with tasks that read your files and write new ones. Anthropic warns that tools that change things carry more risk than tools that only read. Claude asks before it permanently deletes files, but that check doesn't cover computer use.

New to Cowork? Start here

Excel: ask your workbook questions

If your work lives in spreadsheets, Claude can work there too.

Claude for Excel is an add-in. It answers questions about your workbook and cites the cells it used. Click a citation and you jump to that cell.

It can change an assumption and keep your formulas intact, track down an error, and build or fill in a model.

When to use it: a model someone else built that you need to understand, an error you can't trace, or a "what if" you'd otherwise rebuild by hand.

Where to find it: it's on Pro, Max, Team and Enterprise plans, in Excel on the web, Excel for Windows with Microsoft 365 (build 16.0.13127.20296 or later) and Excel for Mac (16.46 or later).

  1. Find the Claude for Microsoft 365 listing on Microsoft AppSource and select Get it now. Anthropic's Excel page links to it.
  2. Open Excel. On Windows, go to Home → Add-ins. On a Mac, go to Tools → Add-ins. Choose Claude.
  3. Sign in with your Claude account.

A first prompt to copy:

Explain a workbook
Explain how the final number on the Summary tab is worked out, from the raw inputs to the result. Point me to each cell along the way, and flag anything that looks wrong. Don't change anything yet.

What you get back: a step-by-step answer with cell citations you can click, and anything that looks wrong flagged for you.

Want the same number format or layout each time? Open Settings in the add-in's sidebar and fill in Instructions. They apply in Excel only.

Tip

Work on a copy. Anthropic's advice is to start from a trusted copy of the workbook, say exactly what you want changed and review every change. Claude also warns you before it overwrites existing data.

Guide Ask Claude about your data, and trust the answer. Mojeed Abisiga · mojeedabisiga.com
GuideAsk Claude about your data, and trust the answer.Claude will answer any question about your spreadsheet, confidently. Here's how to make sure the answer is right:

Where to double-check Claude

A good set-up includes knowing where to double-check.

Where it falls short What to do about it
It can be confidently wrong. Anthropic calls this hallucination. Don't use it as your only source. Check cited sources and anything high-stakes.
It can claim it did things it can't, like sending an email. It only has the tools you've connected. Check the result yourself.
The newest models' knowledge stops in June 2026. Use web search (+ → Web search). In the new Claude experience, it searches when that helps.
It doesn't make photos or illustrations. It builds diagrams and charts in code (HTML and SVG). Use an image tool for pictures.
It reads images and charts only in PDFs of 100 pages or fewer. Send the pages that hold the charts as a file of their own.
Usage limits: a rolling five-hour window, plus weekly limits on paid plans. Watch Settings → Usage. Long chats, big files, Research, higher effort and artifacts use it up faster.
Web pages and files can hide instructions (prompt injection). Point Cowork and Claude for Excel only at sources you trust.
Claude for Excel doesn't do data tables, macros or VBA. Keep a person reviewing final client work and audit-critical numbers.

Known issue: since the September and October 2026 Microsoft 365 updates on Windows, some people are missing chat history and uploaded skills in the Claude add-in.

Key point

Let Claude do the legwork. Keep the judgment, and the final sign-off, for yourself.

Guide Stop running out of Claude. Mojeed Abisiga · mojeedabisiga.com
GuideStop running out of Claude.Hit the limit mid-task? How usage is counted, and twelve habits that make it last:

A set-up you can finish in half an hour

The tools work together: instructions shape every chat, projects hold your files, plugins bring skills to chat and Cowork, and Claude for Excel can refine the spreadsheets Cowork builds.

Set them up once, in this order: six blocks of five minutes.

5 minutes: your settings

Open Settings → Capabilities and check that Create and edit files is on.

Then open Settings → Your Claude → Instructions and tell Claude how you work. Your instructions apply to every conversation.

Your instructions
I'm a [your role] at a [type of organisation]. Write in plain English, in short paragraphs. Put the answer first, then the reasons. If you're not sure of a fact, say so instead of guessing.

5 minutes: your model

Click the model name next to the send button. Pick Opus 5.5 if your plan has it, or Sonnet on Free. Leave effort on Default.

5 minutes: one project

Make a project for the work you do most. Add the files you always need, and set its instructions.

5 minutes: one artifact

In that project, turn real notes into a doc or a deck. Change one paragraph with Edit with Claude.

5 minutes: one plugin or skill

On a paid plan, open Customize → Plugins → Discover and add the plugin for your role. On Free, ask for a Word file and watch the built-in skill do the work.

5 minutes: one real task

On a paid plan, select Cowork and hand over the task from the Cowork prompt above. If you live in spreadsheets, install Claude for Excel and ask about one workbook instead.

That's the set-up. Thirty minutes, once.

After that, you open Claude knowing which of its tools fits the job in front of you.

New to Claude? Start from day one

Send this to one colleague who only ever uses the chat box.

Mojeed

item.title: Claude, past the basics.
item.description: Eighteen small Claude habits for memory, asking, checking answers, projects and usage limits, with prompts to copy and the exact clicks.
item.content:encoded:
Getting one good answer out of Claude is the easy part.

The rest of the week is where things slip.

The chat that runs so long it eats into your limits.

The number that went into a report without a check.

The file you upload again, and again.

The limit that arrives halfway through a task.

A better prompt won't fix any of those. Small habits will.

I teach people to use AI at work.

These are the habits I'd want every one of them to have.

Most take one click or one sentence.

Here are eighteen, in three groups:

  1. Before you ask: help Claude know you, and ask so the first answer lands.
  2. Before you trust the answer: five quick checks.
  3. Make it last: projects, fresh chats and the settings that stretch your usage.

New to Claude? Start with Claude, from day one, then come back.

Get the next one in your inbox

One practical guide at a time: the exact steps, the prompts to copy and the mistakes to skip.

Free. Delivered by Substack, one click to unsubscribe. Form not showing? Subscribe on Substack.

Before you ask

Six habits for the minute before you type.

1. Read what Claude remembers about you

Claude keeps a memory of you.

On the Free, Pro, Max and Ultra plans, it's on by default.

It saves what it learns as topics, while you chat. Mention that a deadline moved, and your next conversation already knows.

Useful, until something it remembers goes out of date.

So read it now and then:

  1. Click your initials, then Settings → Your Claude.
  2. Click Manage next to Your memory.
  3. Everything is listed under Topics. Open one, then use the edit icon to fix it, or Delete to remove it.

Fix a topic once, and every conversation from then on uses the fixed version.

You can also update it from any chat:

Update your memory
Please update your memory: I no longer [the old detail]. I now [the new detail]. Forget anything that says otherwise.

The change applies from your next conversation.

Note

On Team and Enterprise plans, the owner of your organisation decides whether memory is available.

2. Turn repeated corrections into Instructions

Caught yourself typing "shorter" or "no jargon" again?

A correction you make twice belongs in Instructions.

It's on the same page: Settings → Your Claude → Instructions.

Instructions apply to every conversation. Anthropic suggests four things to put there:

  • how you like to work
  • the terms you use
  • the situations you often face
  • how you want Claude to communicate
Instructions to adapt
I work as [your role] in [your field].
Write in plain English: short paragraphs, no jargon, no filler.
Start long answers with a three-line summary.
When I say "[a term you use]", I mean [what it means].
If something important is missing, ask me before you start.

Keep it general. Details for one task belong in that task's chat.

Pasting the same long brief for one kind of job? That's a skill. Make your first one.

3. Switch memory off before a one-off chat

Helping a friend with their CV?

Asking about something you don't want shaping later answers?

Turn memory off for that one chat. Do it before your first message: you can't change it later.

  1. Start a new chat.
  2. Click + in the message box.
  3. Click Memory to turn it off, then send your message.

A crossed-out memory icon then appears next to the chat title.

Want it kept out of your chat history too?

Open an incognito chat instead: the ghost icon in the upper right corner of a new chat, outside a project.

Memory off for one chat Incognito chat
Uses or adds to your memory No No
Stays in your chat history Yes No
Found when Claude searches past chats Yes No
How to start it + → Memory, before you send Ghost icon, upper right

Incognito chats aren't used for training.

They're kept for 30 days by default.

And in the new Claude experience, Claude can't make files or run code in them.

4. Send one full message, not five small ones

Anthropic's first tip for getting more from your plan: plan the chat before you begin.

  • Know what you need.
  • Group related questions into one message.
  • Give the background up front.
  • Paste the whole text you want edited, not one piece at a time.

Then read it once before you send.

A clear first message saves a round of follow-ups.

One message, everything in it
I'm preparing [the piece of work] for [who it's for].
Here's what I have: [paste it, or attach the file].
Please answer these together:
1. [first question]
2. [second question]
3. [third question]
Put each answer under its own heading. If you need anything else from me, ask before you start.

5. Ask Claude to find the old chat

On paid plans, Claude can search your past chats.

So you don't have to explain the background again. Just ask:

Pick up where you left off
Find our conversation about [topic]. Remind me what we decided, then let's continue from there.

You'll see the search in the chat as a tool call.

Inside a project, Claude searches only that project's chats.

6. Tell Claude whether to search the web

In the new Claude experience, there's no web search switch.

Claude searches when it decides a search helps.

You can still steer it, in plain words:

You need Do this Why
A quick, current fact Ask it to search the web One or two searches, with citations
A full report from many sources + → Research (paid plans) Five or more searches, over 1 to 3 minutes
Work on what you've given it Say "Don't search the web for this" Searches add to your usage

Brief Claude like a colleague: the guide

Before you trust the answer

Anthropic is clear about this.

Don't treat Claude as your only source of truth.

And look hard at any advice with high stakes.

Five checks turn that into a habit.

7. Open the sources behind your key claims

Answers that use web search come with citations.

Click the ones your point depends on.

The original page may hold context or detail that Claude's summary left out.

8. Ask where every number came from

Claude can write a quote that sounds authoritative and isn't grounded in fact.

Numbers, names and dates can slip the same way.

Before anything goes into a report, run this:

Trace every claim
Before I use this, list every number, name, date and quote in your answer. For each one, say where it came from: my file, a web source (with the link) or your general knowledge. Mark anything you're not sure of.

Then check everything marked "general knowledge" yourself.

9. Open the thinking on hard questions

On the newest models, like Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5, thinking can't be switched off.

A Thinking section sits above the reply.

Click it to read a summary of how Claude worked the problem.

Anthropic says this can help you check how Claude reached its conclusion.

If the reasoning rests on an assumption you'd never make, you've found the problem.

10. Check "sent" with your own eyes

Claude can claim it sent an email or made a document somewhere else.

It can also give you links that don't work.

But Claude can't use tools that aren't connected to it.

That includes your email and your word processor, unless you've connected them.

So when it says "sent", look in your sent folder.

When it gives you a link, click it before you forward it.

Watch out

A "done" from Claude is a claim. Check the outbox, the file or the page yourself.

11. Know what Claude can't see

Three blind spots to remember:

  • Recent events. The newest models learned from data up to June 2026. For anything later, ask Claude to search.
  • Charts in long PDFs. Claude reads charts and images only in PDFs of 100 pages or fewer. Beyond that, it reads the text only.
  • Charts in other files. From Word documents and other non-PDF files, Claude takes the text only.

If a chart matters, upload it on its own as an image, such as a PNG or JPEG.

Claude can read the images you upload.

Ask Claude about your data, the careful way

Make it last

Seven habits for work that runs for days, and for your plan's limits.

12. Give each ongoing piece of work a project

A project is a workspace with its own chats, files and instructions.

Every plan has projects. Free accounts can make up to five.

There's a usage reason too.

Files in a project are cached, so they count less against your limits each time you reuse them.

  1. Click Projects on the left, or go to claude.ai/projects.
  2. Click + New Project in the upper right corner.
  3. Click + in the project knowledge and add your core files.
  4. Click Set project instructions, write them, then Save instructions.

One detail worth knowing: Claude can't see your project's name or description.

Anything it needs goes in the instructions or the files.

Tip

The cache expires after a while without use. After a long break, your first message counts the project's files in full again.

13. Keep project instructions short and files current

Anthropic's advice: use project instructions for the big picture.

That means the context, the key guidelines and Claude's role.

Keep instructions for one task in that task's chat.

And clear out files you've stopped using.

Shorter instructions and fewer files help your context window and your usage.

14. Save decisions where the next chat can find them

Chats in the same project don't share context on their own.

Only what's in the project knowledge is there for every chat.

So when a chat settles something, save it:

Decision note
Write a short note on what we settled in this chat: the decisions, the reasons, the open questions and the next step. Plain text, no more than 10 lines, ready to add to the project knowledge.

Save the note as a text file. Then add it with + in the project knowledge.

Started the chat outside the project?

Click the dropdown arrow next to the chat name, then Add to project.

15. Match the effort to the job

Effort sets how much thinking Claude puts into each reply.

Higher effort is more thorough, but slower, and it uses more of your limits.

Click the model name next to the send button, click Effort, and choose:

  • Low or Medium for routine work. They stretch your usage furthest.
  • High for the best balance of quality and speed.
  • Max for the hardest problems, when you can wait for the answer.

Extra high is built for long coding and agent tasks.

You can change effort in the middle of a chat.

It applies from the next reply.

So raise it for the one hard question, then bring it back down.

Want the menu drawn out? It's in the model menu, step by step.

16. Start a fresh chat when a long one drags

When a long chat nears its limit, Claude can summarise the earlier messages to keep going.

You may see it "organizing its thoughts".

Handy, but those long chats use more of your limits.

Anthropic suggests a new chat when you're close to your limit in a long one.

Take the useful part with you:

Hand over to a new chat
Write a handover note for a fresh chat: the goal, what we've decided, the facts and files that matter, the open questions and the next step. Write it so I can paste it as the first message of a new chat.

17. Switch off what this chat doesn't need

Connected apps and tools use a lot of tokens.

Anthropic suggests turning off the apps a conversation doesn't need.

Click + in the message box and hover over Connectors.

Switch on only the apps this chat needs.

Lots of apps connected?

Under Connectors → Tool access, the default is Auto.

With 10 or more connectors active, Anthropic suggests On demand, to give your chats more room.

18. Check Settings → Usage before a big job

Your five-hour session starts with your first message.

It resets in full five hours later.

Paid plans add a weekly limit, which resets at a fixed day and time.

On paid plans, Settings → Usage shows three things:

  • how much of your current session you've used
  • how long that session has left
  • when your weekly limit resets

Look before you start something long, like a Research report.

If the bar is nearly full, plan around the reset.

Read the usage limits guide

Start with these three

Eighteen is a lot. You don't need them all this week.

Start with the three that pay off in your very next chat:

  1. Send one full message (habit 4). Fewer round trips, and a better first answer.
  2. Trace every claim (habit 8). Run it on anything you'll put your name to.
  3. Hand over to a fresh chat (habit 16). Long work keeps its thread, without a long chat's cost.

Then add one more habit each week.

Get the next issue by email

One practical guide at a time: the exact steps, the prompts to copy and the mistakes to skip.

Free. Delivered by Substack, one click to unsubscribe. Form not showing? Subscribe on Substack.

What to do today

Open Settings → Your Claude and read your memory topics.

Fix one thing that's out of date.

Then add one correction you keep making to your Instructions.

Two habits, done before your next chat.

Newsletter One good prompt. Mojeed Abisiga · mojeedabisiga.com
NewsletterOne good prompt.Getting bland, generic answers? Five rules and one template that fix them:

Send this to one colleague whose Claude chats run for days.

Mojeed

item.title: Better slides, less effort.
item.description: Build slides with Claude, with Gamma, or plan in Claude and build in Gamma. Then set up one shared deck standard for your whole team.
item.content:encoded:
You have a presentation due.

You have the content. Notes, a report, a few numbers.

What you don't have is three hours to push boxes around in PowerPoint.

AI can do most of that work now. But only if you use it the right way.

Ask for "a deck about Q3" and you get ten slides of generic bullets. Give it a real storyline and the right tool, and you get a draft worth editing.

I teach people to use AI at work, and my mission is to make data and AI easy for everyone. This guide is the method I'd show anyone who builds slides for a living, or just once a month.

By the end of this guide you'll have:

  1. a storyline prompt that makes every method work better
  2. method 1: a deck from Claude, as a file, a Slides artifact or inside PowerPoint
  3. method 2: a deck from Gamma's agent
  4. method 3: the words planned in Claude, the design built in Gamma
  5. one standard your whole team can reuse

You need: a Claude account (Free works for methods 1 and 3), a Gamma account (Free works to start), and the content for one real presentation.

Get the next one in your inbox

One practical guide at a time: the exact steps, the prompts to copy and the mistakes to skip.

Free. Delivered by Substack, one click to unsubscribe. Form not showing? Subscribe on Substack.

1. Get the story straight first

Most bad AI decks have the same cause.

The tool was asked to design and think at the same time.

So split the jobs. First decide what the deck says. Then let a tool make it look good.

A good storyline answers four questions:

  • Who is in the room? One kind of reader, not "everyone".
  • What should they do after? Approve, decide, learn, buy.
  • What's the one message? If they remember one line, which one?
  • What's the proof? The numbers and examples, each with its source.

You don't have to answer these alone. Ask Claude to interview you.

Storyline interview
I need to build a presentation. Before writing any slides, interview me.

Ask me one question at a time about:
- who the audience is and what they already know
- what I want them to do after the presentation
- the one message they should remember
- the evidence I have (I'll paste numbers and notes)
- how long I have to present

When you have enough, give me a storyline: a title, then one line per slide stating that slide's single message. Aim for 8 to 12 slides. Don't design anything yet.

Read the storyline out loud. If a slide's line doesn't push toward the one message, cut it.

Key point

One slide, one message. If you can't say what a slide is for in one sentence, no tool will make it clear.

2. Pick your method

There's no single best tool. There's the best tool for this deck.

Claude: deck file or Slides Claude for PowerPoint Gamma Claude, then Gamma
Best for A fast first draft from notes or a report Decks that must use your company template A designed look with little effort Strong words and a strong design
Where you work A Claude chat Inside PowerPoint Gamma, in your browser Claude for words, Gamma for design
What you get A .pptx file, or a Slides deck you can export Slides in your own master, fonts and colours A gamma you can present, share or export A Gamma deck with your exact wording
Plan you need Claude Free works A paid Claude plan Gamma Free to start Both free plans to start

A simple rule:

  • Your company has a PowerPoint template? Use Claude for PowerPoint.
  • You need it to look designed, and fast? Use Gamma.
  • The words matter most? Plan in Claude, build in Gamma.
  • You just need a quick .pptx? Ask Claude in a chat.

Not sure which AI suits a job? Read this

3. Method 1a: Ask Claude for a deck file

This is the quickest route, and it works on the Free plan.

Claude can make PowerPoint (.pptx), Word, Excel and PDF files right in a conversation. You download the file, or save it straight to Google Drive. (Anthropic's help page.)

Anthropic's built-in skills handle PowerPoint creation, and Claude uses them on its own when a request needs them.

Step 1: Check file creation is on

It's on by default for Free, Pro, Max and Ultra. Check once anyway.

Open Settings, then Capabilities. Make sure Code execution and file creation is switched on. In the newer layout, the help page says it's called Create and edit files.

Step 2: Give it your storyline and your content

Paste the storyline from section 1, then your notes, or attach your report. Files can be up to 30MB each.

Deck file from a storyline
Turn this storyline into a PowerPoint presentation (.pptx). Follow these rules.

- One message per slide. Use the storyline line as the slide title, written as a full sentence.
- No more than 30 words of body text per slide.
- Where I give numbers, make a simple chart instead of a bullet list.
- Use only the facts in my notes. If something is missing, leave a clear placeholder like [ADD FIGURE].
- Add speaker notes to each slide with what I should say.
- Use a clean, plain design: white background, one accent colour.

Storyline:
[paste the storyline]

Notes and numbers:
[paste or attach]

Step 3: Fix it in words

Open the file. Then tell Claude what to change, one thing at a time.

"Slide 4 has too much text. Split it into two slides." "Make the chart on slide 6 a bar chart."

Each change gives you a new file to download.

4. Method 1b: Use Claude's Slides template

Claude can also build a deck you work on right inside Claude.

It's called an artifact: something Claude makes that you'd put in front of someone. It opens beside your conversation. Slides is one of the templates, and it's on every plan, Free included. (Anthropic's page on artifacts.)

There are three ways to start one:

  1. Ask for a presentation in any chat.
  2. Select Output in the message box and choose the Slides template.
  3. Pick it in the Artifacts tab.

Slides are built from your notes, your reports or the work already in your chat. So the storyline you wrote in section 1 can become the deck in the same conversation.

Slides from this chat
Use the Slides template to turn the storyline above into a presentation.
Keep my slide titles exactly as written. Keep body text short.
Use the numbers I pasted earlier, and nothing else.

What you can do with it:

  • Edit slide by slide, by asking Claude or by typing on the slide yourself.
  • Present it without leaving Claude.
  • Export it: click Export to get PowerPoint or PDF, or send it straight to Google Slides as an editable file.

Tip

Talking about the deck with Claude first, then asking for Slides in the same chat, gives it all the context. You don't have to paste anything twice.

Learn to brief Claude properly

5. Method 1c: Build inside PowerPoint

If your company has a template, this is the method to learn.

Claude for PowerPoint is an add-in that works inside PowerPoint itself. It reads your deck's slide master, layouts, fonts and colour scheme, and uses them when it makes or edits slides. (Anthropic's docs.)

It can build slides in your templates, make pinpoint edits to one slide, and turn bullets into diagrams and native PowerPoint charts. Those charts stay editable. They aren't pictures.

Who can use it

You need a paid Claude plan. The PowerPoint docs name Pro, Max, Team and Enterprise. Pro costs $20 a month, or $17 a month paid yearly. (Claude's pricing.)

You also need a recent PowerPoint:

  • Windows: PowerPoint with a Microsoft 365 subscription, build 16.0.13127.20296 or later
  • Mac: PowerPoint version 16.46 or later

Step 1: Install it

  1. Find the Claude for Microsoft 365 listing on Microsoft AppSource and select Get it now.
  2. Open PowerPoint.
  3. Activate the add-in: Home → Add-ins on Windows, Tools → Add-ins on Mac.
  4. Sign in with your Claude account.

Step 2: Start from your template

Open a blank deck that uses your company template. Then describe your goal.

Claude builds a draft with a logical structure, in your template. You refine it from there.

First deck in your template
Build a presentation in this template from the storyline below.
Use the existing slide layouts. Don't change fonts or colours.
One message per slide, with the message as the slide title.
Turn any list of numbers into a native chart.

Storyline:
[paste the storyline]

Step 3: Make pinpoint edits

Select a slide and ask for one change.

One-slide fix
On this slide only: turn the bullets into a simple diagram that shows the three steps in order. Keep the title as it is.

Watch out

The add-in needs a paid Claude plan and a recent PowerPoint. Check both before you promise a team they can use it.

Get the next one in your inbox

Free. Delivered by Substack, one click to unsubscribe. Form not showing? Subscribe on Substack.

6. Method 2: Let Gamma build it

Gamma is a separate tool made for presentations, documents and webpages.

You start with a conversation with its agent. You describe what you want, it asks a few questions, shows you a plan, then builds the whole deck: writing, design and images. (Gamma's help page.)

Step 1: Describe the deck

From your Gamma dashboard, type what you want in the prompt bar. A sentence is enough, but more helps. You can paste notes, attach files or choose a template.

Gamma first prompt
A 10-slide presentation for our leadership team.
Goal: get approval to run a three-month pilot.
Audience: busy senior managers who want the cost, the risk and the decision.
Tone: plain and confident, no jargon.
Use my notes below for every fact and number. Don't add statistics of your own.

[paste notes]

Step 2: Choose a mode

Before you generate, pick a mode in the mode picker:

  • Plan (the default): the agent asks questions and waits for your go-ahead on its plan.
  • Express: it skips the questions and goes straight to a draft.
  • Research: it reads sources from the web first. It's on Pro and above, uses more credits, and only works with Plan.

Use Plan for anything that matters. Short on time? Choose Decide for me on any question.

Step 3: Check the plan

The plan covers the story, the style and the look. This is the best moment to fix things, before anything is built.

Compare it with your storyline. Move, add or cut slides here.

Step 4: Fix it in plain words

When the deck is built, tell the agent what feels wrong, in your own words:

  • "Slide 4 is too text-heavy. Make it more visual."
  • "Make the tone more formal."
  • "Tighten the summary slide."

Or edit by hand. Move, resize and rewrite directly.

Like the words but not the look? Ask for a new look. The agent offers a few style directions and restyles the deck in place. Your content stays.

Step 5: Export it

Click Share at the top right, then Export. Or use the three-dot menu, then Export. (Gamma's export page.)

You can export to PDF, PNG, PowerPoint or Google Slides. Choose All cards to export the whole deck. Tables arrive in PowerPoint as real, editable tables.

What it costs

Gamma's plans are Free, Plus, Pro, Ultra and Business. Every AI action uses credits: creating a deck, making images, asking the agent for edits. (Gamma's plans page.)

Plan What the help page lists
Free The AI agent, basic image models, up to 10 slides per prompt. Credits don't refresh (200 per referral, up to 2,000).
Plus 1,500 credits a month, up to 100 slides per prompt, no "Made with Gamma" badge
Pro 4,000 credits a month, password protection, headers and footers, viewer analytics
Ultra 20,000 credits a month

Unused credits roll over, up to double your plan's amount. Gamma bills per user.

Gamma's help page doesn't list prices, so check the current price on Gamma's own pricing page before you upgrade.

Watch out

On the Free plan, credits don't refresh. Use them on real decks, not on test prompts.

7. Method 3: Plan in Claude, build in Gamma

This is the method for decks where every word counts.

Claude does the thinking and the writing. Gamma does the design. You keep control of both.

Step 1: Write the slide text in Claude

Start from your storyline in section 1. Then ask Claude for the finished words, in a format Gamma understands.

Gamma treats three dashes (---) as the start of a new slide. So ask Claude to use them.

Slide text for Gamma
Write the final text for each slide of this storyline.

Format:
- Start each slide with its title as a full sentence.
- Then at most 3 short lines of body text, or one number with a one-line explanation.
- Put a line with three dashes (---) between slides.
- No slide over 30 words.
- Use only the facts in my notes. Mark anything missing as [ADD].

Storyline:
[paste the storyline]

Notes:
[paste notes]

Read every slide now. This is the cheapest moment to fix a fact or a weak line.

Step 2: Paste it into Gamma, word for word

Paste the text into Gamma's prompt bar. Then tell the agent to keep your words. (Gamma's page on creating.)

Keep my words
Keep my wording exactly as written and make one slide per section. Sections are separated by ---. Design each slide around its single message. Add images only where they help the message.

In Gamma's classic generator, the option is called Preserve this exact text. Want to add your own pictures later? Choose Image placeholders. Want none? Choose Don't add images.

Step 3: Restyle, then export

Now ask the agent for a new look until one fits. The words stay where they are.

Then export to PowerPoint, PDF or Google Slides, as in section 6.

Tip

Already have an old deck? Gamma can import .pptx, Word and PDF files. Click Import below the prompt box, then Add a file. (Gamma's import page.)

Newsletter One good prompt. Mojeed Abisiga · mojeedabisiga.com
NewsletterOne good prompt.Getting bland, generic answers? Five rules and one template that fix them:

8. Make it a team standard

One person with a good method makes good slides.

A team with a shared standard makes slides that all look like one company made them.

Here's how to set that up in each tool.

In Claude: a project for decks

A project is a workspace with its own chats, instructions and files. To make one, go to claude.ai/projects and click + New Project. Add files with + and rules with Set project instructions. (Anthropic's projects page.)

For a whole team, Claude's Team plan has Standard seats at $20 per seat a month paid yearly, or $25 monthly, for teams of 2 to 150.

Team deck project instructions
You help our team build presentations.

Always:
- Start by asking who the audience is and what decision we want.
- Write a storyline before any slides: one message per slide.
- Use slide titles that are full sentences.
- Keep body text under 30 words per slide.
- Use only facts from the files and notes we give you. Mark gaps as [ADD].
- Add speaker notes.

Brand:
- Colours: [your colours]
- Fonts: [your fonts]
- Tone: [e.g. plain, confident, no jargon]

Once the rules are stable, you can turn them into a skill: a folder of instructions Claude loads when a request needs it. Teammates upload the same zipped folder: Customize → Skills, then +, + Create skill and Upload a skill.

In Claude for PowerPoint: shared instructions

Each person opens Settings in the add-in sidebar and fills in the Instructions field. Those rules apply to every conversation in PowerPoint.

Paste the same short rules for everyone. Your template does the rest, because Claude reads the slide master.

In Gamma: a theme, templates and instructions

1. A workspace theme from your company deck. A theme is a saved look your whole workspace can use: colours, fonts, logo. (Gamma's themes page.)

In the left sidebar, go to Customize → Themes. Click + New Theme, then Import file, and upload your .pptx or Google Slides file. Check the colours, fonts and logo Gamma found, then click Save and finish.

2. Workspace templates for decks you make often. Any gamma can become a template, on every plan including Free. Open the Templates tab in the left sidebar, click + Add a gamma, choose one and click Save copy as template. Teammates hover over it and choose Use template. (Gamma's templates page.)

3. Instructions inside the template. On Pro and Ultra, you can add template instructions: rules for the AI that travel with the template, and locks on slides it must not change. They aren't available on Team or Business plans yet. (Gamma's page.)

On the Enterprise plan, admins can also set workspace custom instructions in Customize → Custom Instructions, and they apply to everyone's decks. (Gamma's page.)

Key point

A standard is three things: one storyline prompt, one template, one set of written rules. Put all three where the whole team can reach them.

9. Check before you present

AI makes drafts fast. You still own what goes on the screen.

Before any deck leaves your hands:

  • Every number matches its source
  • No [ADD] or [ADD FIGURE] placeholders are left
  • Each slide has one message, and its title says it
  • Fonts, colours and logo are your company's
  • Charts show the right numbers on the right axes
  • You've read it in present mode, not only in edit mode
  • Speaker notes say what you'll actually say

Gamma's exports match what you see in present mode. So check there before you export.

Questions

Which method is cheapest?

Method 1 in a chat, or with the Slides template, works on Claude's Free plan. Gamma's Free plan lets you start, but its credits don't refresh. Method 3 works on both free plans to begin with.

Which method keeps my company template?

Claude for PowerPoint. It reads your slide master, layouts, fonts and colours. In Gamma, import your deck as a workspace theme.

Can I edit the result in PowerPoint?

Yes. Claude makes .pptx files, and Slides exports to PowerPoint. Gamma exports to PowerPoint with editable tables. Claude for PowerPoint works inside PowerPoint already.

Which Claude model should I use for slides?

Anthropic describes Sonnet 5.5 as strongest at well-scoped everyday tasks and creating polished documents, slides and spreadsheets.

What to do today

Pick one presentation you need this month.

  1. Run the storyline interview in Claude.
  2. Build the deck with the method that fits it.
  3. Run the checklist before you present.

Then, if your team makes decks every week, set up the standard in section 8.

Make infographics that stay sharp

Make the story clear, and let the tools do the rest.

item.title: Cowork, from zero.
item.description: Claude Cowork for people who don't code: what it is, how to install it, why to let Claude interview you, plugins, everyday jobs and limits.
item.content:encoded:
You've used Claude to answer questions.

Maybe to rewrite an email. Maybe to explain something.

Then you hear that Claude can build a whole spreadsheet, or tidy a messy downloads folder, while you get on with something else.

That's Cowork.

And you don't need to write a single line of code to use it.

I teach people to use AI at work. So this guide is plain words and real steps. Nothing technical.

By the end of this guide you'll have:

  • a clear picture of what Cowork is, and when to use it instead of chat
  • the desktop app installed, with a safe folder set up for Claude
  • one real task done, from a two-line request
  • a better habit than long prompts: letting Claude interview you
  • one plugin or connector added for your kind of work
  • a short list of jobs to keep away from it

You need: a paid Claude plan (Pro or above) and a Mac, Windows or Linux computer.

Get the next one in your inbox

One practical guide at a time: the exact steps, the prompts to copy and the mistakes to skip.

Free. Delivered by Substack, one click to unsubscribe. Form not showing? Subscribe on Substack.

1. Know what Cowork is

Cowork is Claude doing a whole job for you, not just answering one message.

Anthropic describes it as bringing Claude Code's agentic abilities to knowledge work beyond coding.

"Agentic" just means it can take steps on its own.

Claude Code is the version for software engineers. Cowork uses the same approach for everyone else: research, analysis, documents. And it needs no terminal.

Here's what happens when you give it a task:

  1. Claude reads your request and makes a plan.
  2. It breaks the work into smaller steps.
  3. It works through them in a private, temporary workspace on Anthropic's servers.
  4. It hands back finished files you can preview and download.

You can watch what it's planning and doing the whole time. Step in when it matters. Or step away.

That's the idea in one line: describe the outcome, step away, come back to finished work.

What can "finished work" look like? Excel spreadsheets with working formulas. PowerPoint decks. Formatted documents. Organised folders. A research write-up.

It reads most of the files you already use: Word, PDF, Excel, PowerPoint, CSV, plain text and common images.

Key point

Chat is for questions. Cowork is for jobs. If you'd normally block out an hour for it, it's probably a Cowork task.

2. See how it differs from chat

Here's the difference, side by side.

Chat Cowork
You give it a question or a prompt an outcome you want
How it works one reply at a time plans, splits the job into steps, works through them
Your files you upload them on desktop, it reads and writes files in folders you connect
You get back an answer, sometimes a file finished files: spreadsheets, decks, documents, tidy folders
While it works you wait for the reply you can close your laptop and check back later
Plans every plan, including Free paid plans only
Usage less more, because each step uses some

One thing is changing.

Anthropic is rolling out what it calls the "new Claude experience". In it, chat and Cowork merge into one conversation. There's no mode to pick. Claude decides what the job needs, and a quick question still gets a quick answer.

How do you know if you have it? Look at the message box. If it no longer shows "Chat" and "Cowork" options, you have it.

Everything in this guide still works. You just skip the step where you pick Cowork.

New to Claude itself? Start here

3. Check your plan and install the app

Cowork is on paid plans only: Pro, Max, Ultra, Team and Enterprise.

The Free plan gets chat, but not Cowork.

The cheapest way in is Pro: $20 a month, or $17 a month if you pay for a year up front ($200). Prices exclude tax. (Claude's pricing page.)

Where you can use it:

Where Who gets Cowork
Claude Desktop (Mac, Windows, Linux in beta) all paid plans
Web and the Claude phone app Pro, Max, Ultra and Team (beta on Team); Enterprise if an owner turns it on
Claude in Chrome side panel all paid plans

Start with the desktop app. It's the only place Claude can reach the files on your computer.

To install it:

  1. Go to claude.com/download.
  2. Pick your version: macOS, Windows, Windows (arm 64) or the Microsoft Store. Linux links to setup docs instead.
  3. Install it and sign in with your Claude account.

Check your computer first. You need macOS 13 (Ventura) or later, or Windows 10 or later. On Linux, Cowork also needs about 25 GB of free disk space and at least 8 GB of memory. (Install Claude Desktop.)

4. Give Claude a folder of its own

On desktop, Claude can read and write your files directly. No uploading, no downloading.

But only in folders you connect.

Anthropic's own advice: make a dedicated working folder for Claude, rather than giving it broad access. And keep backups of anything important.

So do this before your first task:

  1. Make a new folder. Call it something like "Claude Work".
  2. Copy in the files for one real job. Copies, not originals.
  3. When Claude asks which folder to use, point it here.

There's a safety net too. Claude has to ask your permission, with an "Allow" prompt, before it permanently deletes any file.

Tip

Your files stay on your computer. When a task needs one, Claude fetches a copy of just that file, and those copies are deleted when you delete the session.

Set Cowork up properly, step by step

5. Run your first task

Here's how to start, in the desktop app:

  1. In the message box, select Cowork.
  2. Describe the task.
  3. Read Claude's plan, then let it run.

Before you send it, choose how much Claude checks with you. There's a setting for this in the message box, with three options:

Option What Claude does Use it when
Manually approve pauses and asks you to Allow or Deny actions your first tasks, and anything sensitive
Automatically approve keeps going, and screens each action for safety, blocking unsafe ones everyday work you've done before
Skip all approvals nothing checks its actions almost never: only when you fully trust every file, app and connector involved

"Automatically approve" is rolling out as the default on Pro, Max, Ultra and Team.

For your very first task, pick Manually approve. You'll see every step Claude wants to take. It's the fastest way to learn what it does.

Once the task is running, you don't have to sit and watch. Sessions keep going even if you close the app or your computer sleeps.

One exception: if the task uses files on your computer, keep the desktop app open so Claude can reach them.

6. Stop writing long prompts

Most people meet Cowork and do the same thing.

They spend twenty minutes writing a giant prompt. Every detail, every rule, every "make sure you".

Then they still forget the one thing that mattered.

There's a better way: write two lines, and let Claude interview you.

It suits how Cowork already works. Claude plans first, shows you its approach before it runs, and can stop to ask you questions during a task.

So you give it the outcome. It asks what it needs. You answer. It shows a plan. You say go.

You think about one question at a time, not everything at once. And Claude asks about the gaps you didn't know were there.

Here's the prompt. Replace the first line with your own task.

Interview me first
I want: [the finished thing, in one line].

Before you do anything, interview me.
Ask one question at a time and wait for my answer.
Ask about the goal, who it's for, which files to use, the format, and what "done" looks like.
Stop when you have enough, usually after five to eight questions.
Then sum up what you heard in five bullet points and show me your plan.
Don't start until I say go.

Three tips:

  • Answer in a few words. It's a conversation, not an exam.
  • Say "I don't know". Then ask Claude what it would suggest.
  • Correct the summary. That's your last cheap moment to fix a misunderstanding.

Want this every time, without pasting it? Save a standing instruction.

In the desktop app, go to Settings → Cowork, click Edit next to Global instructions, paste the text below and click Save. In the new Claude experience, it lives in Settings → Your Claude, under Instructions for Claude.

Standing instruction
For any task bigger than a quick question, ask me a few clarifying questions first, one at a time. Then show me your plan and wait for my go-ahead. For quick questions, just answer.

Note

Scheduled tasks already work this way. On the Scheduled tasks page, "New task" offers "Create with Claude": Claude asks you questions, and you click "Schedule" when it's right.

Guide Brief Claude like a new colleague. Mojeed Abisiga · mojeedabisiga.com
GuideBrief Claude like a new colleague.Short prompts get average answers. A two-minute brief gets the finished thing, first time:

7. Add plugins and connectors

Out of the box, Claude knows a lot. But it doesn't know your tools or how your kind of team works.

Two things fix that.

Connectors link Claude to your apps and data, so it can look things up and take actions there. A connector only sees what you can see: it uses your own permissions in that app.

Plugins are bundles made for a type of work. One plugin packs together skills (instructions for a job), connectors and helpers. Anthropic's first open-source plugins covered Productivity, Sales, Finance, Data, Legal, Marketing, Customer support and Product management, among others.

A plugin you add is saved to your account. So it works in chat too, not just Cowork.

Add a plugin

  1. Click Plugins in the left sidebar. (Older screens call it Customize, with a Plugins tab and a Discover section.)
  2. Browse the categories: topic, department, industry or everyday life.
  3. Open a plugin and read what it does. Then add it. (On older screens the button reads Add.)

Public plugins are labelled Verified or Community. Start with the ones that match your job.

To use it, type / or click + in the message box to see its skills.

Add a connector

In the message box, click +, then Connectors, then Manage connectors. Pick the app and sign in.

Watch out

Adding a plugin does not sign you in to its connectors. Open the plugin's Connectors tab: each one shows Connected, Not connected or Not added. Connect the ones you need yourself.

More on skills, the heart of every plugin

8. Hand it these jobs first

These are everyday jobs from Anthropic's own list of Cowork examples, written as prompts you can copy.

Each one is short on purpose. Add "Interview me first, one question at a time" to the end of any of them.

Tidy a messy folder

Tidy a folder
Organise the files in my Claude Work folder by type and date. Rename them in a YYYY-MM-DD pattern. Show me the new structure before you move anything, and don't delete anything.

Turn receipts into an expense report

Expense report
The receipts are in my Claude Work folder. Make an Excel expense report with date, supplier, amount and category for each one, a total, and working formulas. Flag any receipt you can't read.

Pull actions out of meeting notes

Meeting notes to actions
Read the meeting notes in my Claude Work folder. Make one Word document with three parts: decisions made, actions with an owner, and open questions. Quote the line each action came from.

Research while you're away

Research and compare
Research the main options for [what you're choosing] for a team like mine. Write a two-page comparison as a Word document, with a table and a list of the sources you used. I'll check back later.

Rough notes into slides

Notes to slides
Turn my notes in the Claude Work folder into a 10-slide PowerPoint deck I can present on Monday. One idea per slide, short bullet points, and speaker notes under each slide.

When it's done, open the file. Read it properly. Then ask for changes in the same conversation, the way you'd give feedback to a colleague.

If you find yourself running the same task every week, type /schedule in a Cowork task, or click Scheduled in the left sidebar, and let it run on a timetable.

9. Know where it falls short

Cowork does a lot. It also has limits. Here's what to expect.

  • It costs more of your usage. Multi-step tasks use more of your limit than a quick question, and every Claude app draws on the same allowance. Group related work into one task, start a new conversation for unrelated work, and check Settings → Usage.
  • Local work needs the desktop app open. Tasks that use files on your computer, the browser or your screen stop reaching them when the app is closed.
  • You can't share a session. You can share the files and artifacts it makes, but not the task itself.
  • It can be wrong. Claude can still get facts wrong. Anthropic says not to treat it as your only source of truth. Check numbers, names and anything with your name on it.
  • Some extras aren't everywhere. Computer use, where Claude clicks and types in your apps, works on Mac and Windows but not Linux. Cowork on Linux is still in beta.
  • It isn't on Free. You need a paid plan.

And one risk to understand: prompt injection.

That's hidden instructions inside a web page, file or email that try to steer Claude. It needs two things at once: Claude reading content you don't control, and Claude being able to act. Anthropic has safeguards, but says the chance of an attack is still not zero.

So watch for anything unexpected: files or sites you never mentioned, or a task that keeps growing. If something feels off, stop it.

Watch out

You stay responsible for everything Claude does on your behalf: messages sent, purchases, files changed. Switch to Manually approve for sensitive files, accounts or sites, for a new plugin, or when a mistake would be hard to undo. Keep it away from bank accounts and medical records. (Use Cowork safely.)

Newsletter Hand Claude the mouse. Mojeed Abisiga · mojeedabisiga.com
NewsletterHand Claude the mouse.Let Claude click, type and open apps for you, with the safety settings that matter, in six steps:

10. A half-hour plan

Here's the whole thing as one half-hour plan.

Minutes Do this
0 to 5 Install Claude Desktop from claude.com/download and sign in. Check you're on Pro or above.
5 to 10 Make a "Claude Work" folder. Copy in the files for one real, low-risk job.
10 to 15 Save the standing instruction from step 6.
15 to 25 Select Cowork, choose Manually approve, and send a two-line request with "Interview me first". Answer the questions, read the plan, say go.
25 to 30 Open the result and check it. Then add one plugin that fits your job.

Pick a job you'd happily do yourself if it went wrong. Receipts, meeting notes and a messy downloads folder are all good first tasks.

Save the client report for week two.

Get the next guide by email

Before you finish

  • I'm on a paid plan and Claude Desktop is installed
  • I've made a folder just for Claude, with copies of my files
  • I've run one task on Manually approve and read every step
  • I've saved the "ask me first" standing instruction
  • I've added one plugin, and connected its connectors myself
  • I know to check the output before it goes anywhere

Questions

Do I need to know how to code?

No. Cowork needs no terminal. You describe what you want in plain words.

Is Cowork the same as Claude Code?

Same engine, different job. Claude Code is built for software engineering. Cowork is built for everything else: research, analysis and documents.

Does my laptop need to stay on?

Not for most tasks. They run on Anthropic's servers and keep going if you close your laptop. Tasks that use files on your computer, the browser or your screen need the desktop app open.

Can I use it on my phone?

Yes, on Pro, Max, Ultra and Team (beta on Team), through the web and the Claude phone app. You can check progress, answer Claude's questions and redirect the work from there. For files on your computer, the desktop app still needs to be open.

I don't see a Cowork option. What's wrong?

Nothing. You probably have the new Claude experience, where chat and Cowork are one conversation. Just describe the task. (Anthropic's explainer.)

Ready for the next step? Keep your tasks organised by job:

Guide Give every job a home. Mojeed Abisiga · mojeedabisiga.com
GuideGive every job a home.Cowork projects, from your first one to three you'll use every week:
Guide Stop running out of Claude. Mojeed Abisiga · mojeedabisiga.com
GuideStop running out of Claude.Hit the limit mid-task? How usage is counted, and twelve habits that make it last:

Get the next one in your inbox

One practical guide at a time: the exact steps, the prompts to copy and the mistakes to skip.

item.title: Give every job a home.
item.description: Create your first Cowork project, set instructions, context and memory, and run three workflows: reporting, research and sales proposals.
item.content:encoded:
You use Cowork for real work now.

A report here. Some research there. A proposal on Friday.

And every time, you explain the same things again.

Who the client is. Which folder to use. How you like the numbers laid out.

Projects fix that.

A project is one home for one kind of work. It keeps the files, the rules and what Claude has learned, so the next task starts where the last one stopped.

I teach people to use AI at work. This guide gives you the set-up, the prompts and the limits, in plain words.

By the end of this guide you'll have:

  • a clear picture of what a Cowork project holds
  • your first project, created the right way
  • three ready workflows, with prompts, for reporting, research and sales proposals
  • a simple rule for when a classic chat project is still the better choice
  • a 15-minute set-up you can do today

You need:

  • a paid Claude plan (Pro, Max, Ultra, Team or Enterprise), because Cowork isn't on Free
  • the latest version of Claude Desktop, from claude.com/download
  • one piece of work you repeat every week or month

New to Cowork? Start with Cowork, from zero, then come back.

1. What goes inside a project

Cowork takes on multi-step work for you.

You describe the result, step away, and come back to finished work: a formatted document, organised files, a research summary.

A project wraps that work in a workspace.

Anthropic's help centre puts it simply: a project groups related tasks into a dedicated workspace with its own files, context, instructions and memory.

Each project has four parts:

Part What it does
Instructions Tone, formatting or rules that guide every task in the project
Context A local folder, a linked chat project, or a URL for Claude to reference
Memory What Claude learns from tasks here, applied to future tasks here
Scheduled tasks Recurring tasks that belong to this project only

New projects you create in Cowork are saved to your Claude account. So you can pick them up from your other devices.

The help centre also says projects work the same way in Cowork and in Claude.

Key point

One project per kind of work. Weekly reporting gets one. Each big client gets one. Mixing them is how Claude ends up using the wrong numbers.

2. Pick your way in

There are three ways to create a project. Pick by where your material already lives.

If... Choose What happens
The work is new Start from scratch You set up a new folder with instructions and files
You already have a classic chat project for it Import from project Its files and instructions move into a new Cowork project
The files already sit in a folder on your computer Use an existing folder That folder becomes the project's context

A few details worth knowing before you click:

  • Import from project shows a "Search projects in Chat..." field. Click into it to see recent projects, or search all of them.
  • You can import one chat project at a time. Bulk upload isn't supported.
  • With both import and an existing folder, you name the new project and choose where to save it on your computer.

Tip

Use an existing folder only if that folder holds just this one job. Anthropic advises giving Claude a dedicated working folder instead of broad access. If your folder is a messy mix, start from scratch and copy in what belongs.

3. Click through the set-up

Here's the click path, in words first.

  1. In Claude Desktop, find Projects in the left navigation panel.
  2. Click the + button.
  3. Choose Start from scratch, Import from project or Use an existing folder.
  4. Give the project a clear name, such as "Weekly sales report".
  5. Add instructions and attach any files you want it to start with.
  6. Click Create.

How to check it worked: the new project appears under Projects, and opening it shows its own page with Instructions, Context, Memory and Scheduled tasks.

If your message box no longer shows "Chat" and "Cowork" options, you have the new Claude experience. The help centre says some steps may look a little different there.

Not set up Cowork yet? Do that first

4. Write the instructions and add context

An empty project is just a folder with a name.

The instructions are what make it useful.

Write them like a note to a new colleague who will do this job every week. What's the job, who reads the result, what does good look like?

You don't have to write them alone. Let Claude interview you.

Draft the project instructions with me
I'm setting up a Cowork project for [the job, e.g. our monthly marketing report].

Interview me, one question at a time, until you understand:
- who reads the result and what they decide with it
- the files and sources I use
- the format, length and tone I want
- the mistakes I don't want repeated

Then write short project instructions, readable in one minute, that I can paste into this project's Instructions.

Then add Context. You have three options:

  • a local folder with the files this job uses
  • a linked chat project, if you keep reference material there
  • a URL, such as a public page Claude should always check

These instructions sit on top of your global instructions. Global ones apply to every Cowork session: your role, your usual tone. Set them at Settings → Cowork → Edit next to Global instructions. In the new Claude experience, they're part of Instructions for Claude in Settings → Your Claude.

So keep the global ones about you, and the project ones about the job.

Note

When you select a local folder on desktop, Claude can also keep folder instructions and update them itself during a session. Read them now and then, so you know what it's following.

5. Decide what it remembers

Memory is on for Cowork projects.

Claude remembers context from tasks you run in a project and applies it to later tasks in the same project.

What it learns in one project doesn't carry over to other projects.

But here's the part most people miss: a project also shares memory with your chats outside projects.

That's handy for a personal workflow. It's less handy for client work.

To keep a project fully separate:

  1. Open the project's page.
  2. Go to Memory.
  3. Turn off Use account memory.

A simple rule: client, HR or finance work gets Use account memory off. Your own recurring admin can leave it on.

6. Workflow one: the weekly report

Good for: analysts, managers, operations leads, anyone who sends the same update every week.

Set up the project once:

  • Instructions: who reads the report, the sections, the numbers that matter, the tone.
  • Context: one folder where the weekly export lands.
  • Example: last month's best report, so Claude can match it.

Cowork can produce Excel spreadsheets with working formulas, PowerPoint decks and formatted documents. So ask for the format your readers actually open.

Weekly report
Use the newest file in this project's folder.

1. Check the data first: list missing values, odd totals and anything that changed sharply since last week.
2. Then write this week's report in the format from my instructions: a three-line summary at the top, then one short section per metric.
3. Add an Excel file with the numbers behind each chart, using working formulas.
4. End with a list of anything you weren't sure about, so I can check it before it goes out.

Once it runs well by hand, put it on a timer.

Inside the project, open Scheduled tasks. Or type /schedule in a Cowork task, or click Scheduled in the left sidebar.

The manual form asks for a task name, the prompt, an approval mode, a frequency (hourly, daily, weekly, on weekdays, or manually), an optional model and an optional folder.

Watch out

If you pick a folder, the task gets Require this computer. It then runs only while your computer is awake and Claude Desktop is open. Without a folder, scheduled tasks run remotely, even when your computer is asleep. Choose on purpose.

Anthropic's advice for scheduled tasks: start simple, avoid sensitive data and hard-to-undo actions, review the output after each run, and pause tasks you aren't using.

7. Workflow two: a research project

Good for: consultants, strategists, students, product people, anyone answering one big question over several sessions.

Research is where memory earns its keep. Session one finds the sources. Session two builds on them, without you pasting everything back in.

  • Instructions: the question, who it's for, how sure you need to be.
  • Context: a folder of reports and notes, plus a URL or two you trust.

Start with a plan, not an answer.

Research kick-off
My question for this project is: [your question].

Before you research anything:
1. Restate the question in one sentence.
2. Split it into 3 to 5 smaller questions.
3. List which files in this project help with each one, and what's missing.

Wait for my OK before you start.

Then, in later sessions:

Research write-up
Using everything we've found in this project so far, write a two-page brief that answers my question.

- Lead with the answer in three sentences.
- Under each finding, name the source file or link it came from.
- Mark anything that rests on a single source.
- Finish with the open questions we still haven't answered.

Save it as a Word document in the project folder.

Watch out

Claude can get facts wrong. Anthropic says not to treat it as a single source of truth, and to check cited sources for high-stakes work. That's why the prompt asks it to name every source.

8. Workflow three: proposals for clients

Good for: account managers, founders, freelancers, agencies.

Make one project for your proposal process, or one per big client if each needs different rules.

  • Instructions: your offer, your pricing rules, your house style, what you never promise.
  • Context: a folder with two or three past proposals that won, your service sheet and your case studies.

Anthropic has also open-sourced a Sales plugin for Cowork, if you want more structure later.

New proposal from meeting notes
Here are my notes from today's call with [client]: [paste notes or name the file].

Draft a proposal in our house style from the instructions:
1. Their problem, in their words.
2. What we'll do, in three to five steps.
3. Timeline and what we need from them.
4. Price, using only the pricing rules in this project. If a rule doesn't cover something, flag it instead of guessing.

Then list three questions I should ask before I send it.

And when you want a sharper version:

Review as the buyer
Read the proposal draft as if you were the client's finance lead.
List the five places you'd push back or say no, in order of risk.
Then suggest one change for each. Don't rewrite the whole thing.

Note

On Team and Enterprise plans you can share a project with people in your organisation, as Can view or Can edit, and change or remove that access later. One shared proposal project keeps the whole team on the same rules.

9. When a classic chat project fits better

Classic projects, the ones at claude.ai/projects, haven't gone away.

They're self-contained workspaces with their own chat histories and a knowledge base. You create one with + New Project, add files with +, and add instructions with Set project instructions.

A simple way to choose:

You need... Better fit
A place to ask questions about a fixed set of documents Classic chat project
Claude to produce files: reports, spreadsheets, decks Cowork project
To work on the Free plan Classic chat project (Free users can create up to five)
Work that runs on a schedule Cowork project
Files from a folder on your computer Cowork project
A big knowledge base on a paid plan Classic chat project: near its limits, knowledge switches to retrieval, expanding capacity by up to 10x

One note on the classic kind: context isn't shared across chats in a project unless you add it to the project knowledge.

And you don't have to choose forever. You can link a chat project as Context in a Cowork project, or bring one over with Import from project.

10. Your 15-minute set-up

Pick one job you repeat. Then:

Minutes 0 to 3: the folder. Make one folder on your computer just for this job. Copy in only the files it needs. Back up anything important first.

Minutes 3 to 5: the project. Projects → + → Use an existing folder. Pick that folder, name the project, click Create.

Minutes 5 to 10: the instructions. Run the interview prompt from step 4. Paste the result into Instructions.

Minutes 10 to 12: memory. Decide on Use account memory. Client work: off.

Minutes 12 to 15: the first task. Give it one small, real piece of the job.

First task in a new project
Read the files and instructions in this project.
Tell me in five lines what you understand the job to be, what's missing, and three tasks you could do here.
Don't change any files yet.

If its summary is wrong, fix the instructions now. It's the cheapest moment to do it.

11. Know the honest limits

Projects are good. They're not magic. Here's what the official pages say.

  • Paid plans only. Cowork, and so Cowork projects, need Pro, Max, Ultra, Team or Enterprise.
  • Desktop app needed. Projects in Cowork require the latest version of Claude Desktop. Projects tied to a local folder support Cowork sessions on desktop only.
  • It won't save things into the project for you. Cowork won't change a project's contents, so add anything you want to keep to the project yourself.
  • Not in Claude Code yet. Projects are only in Cowork for now. Anthropic says Claude Code support is planned.
  • File size. The Cowork docs say Claude reads individual files up to 50 MB.
  • Archiving is light. Archiving removes the project from the app, but files and folders on your computer aren't touched.
  • Team and Enterprise without "Chat and Cowork unified": projects made from an existing folder stay on that computer and aren't saved to your account.
  • Usage. Multi-step tasks use more of your limit than a quick question. Group related work into one task, start a new conversation for unrelated work, and watch Settings → Usage.
  • The pages disagree. The help centre says Cowork projects are saved to your account and can be shared on Team and Enterprise. An older Cowork docs page says projects live only on your computer and can't be shared. If you see the second behaviour, that's probably why.

Watch out

You remain responsible for everything Claude does on your behalf. Switch the approval mode to Manually approve when a task touches sensitive files, accounts or sites, uses a new tool, or would be hard to undo.

Read the usage limits guide

What to do today

  • Claude Desktop is on the latest version
  • One dedicated folder holds only one job's files
  • My first project exists, with instructions written
  • I chose on purpose whether Use account memory stays on
  • I ran the first-task prompt and corrected the instructions
  • I picked which of the three workflows to set up next

Questions

Can my team use my project?

On Team and Enterprise plans, yes: share it with Can view or Can edit access. The help centre lists project sharing for those two plans.

What happens to my old folder-based projects?

Claude Desktop moves projects you made from a folder into your Claude account. Their names, descriptions and instructions move, plus a copy of the memory if memory is on. The folders and files stay on your computer. Nothing is uploaded or deleted.

Can I start a chat inside a project?

Yes. The help centre says projects are on every surface, and from a project you can start a chat or a Cowork session. Claude uses the project's knowledge as context either way.

Where's the official page?

Anthropic's projects in Cowork help article, plus the pages on scheduled tasks, using Cowork safely and classic projects.
