item.title: Skill, project, instructions or connector?
item.description: Custom instructions, projects, connectors and skills: what each gives Claude, when it applies, and the two questions that pick the right one.
item.content:encoded:
You've told Claude how you like things done.

Then you told it again, in a new chat.

And again the next day.

The problem usually isn't Claude. It's that you put the instruction in the wrong place.

Claude gives you four ways to shape how it works. Each one applies at a different moment. Pick the right one and you explain things once.

By the end of this guide you'll know:

  • what each of the four gives Claude
  • when each one applies, and when it doesn't
  • the two questions that pick the right one in ten seconds

1. The four, side by side

Feature What it gives Claude When it applies
Custom instructions Your general preferences Every conversation
Projects Background documents and knowledge Chats inside that project
Connectors (MCP) Access to other apps and data, such as your drive or calendar When Claude needs that app
Skills A way of doing one particular job Only when a request needs it, in any chat

The last column is the one that matters. It tells you when Claude will remember what you taught it.

2. Custom instructions: how you like things, everywhere

Custom instructions hold your general preferences.

They apply to every conversation, whatever you're working on.

Put here: the things that are true in every chat. How plain you want the language. How long answers should be. The words you never want to see.

Don't put here: the steps of one particular job. Those would follow you into every chat, even the ones that have nothing to do with that job.

An example of custom instructions
Write in plain English. Keep answers short. Ask me before you assume anything about my work.

3. Projects: the background for one piece of work

A project holds background documents and knowledge.

It applies only to the chats inside that project.

Put here: the files Claude should read for one client, one course or one big piece of work. Open a chat inside the project, and Claude has the background.

Don't put here: a way of doing a job you repeat everywhere. The project's chats would know it, and every other chat wouldn't.

Ask inside a project
Using the files here, summarise what changed this month.

4. Connectors: reach into your other apps

Connectors give Claude access to other apps and data, such as your drive or calendar.

They apply when Claude needs that app.

Use them for: anything where the answer lives somewhere else. The latest version of a document. The meetings on your calendar. The tickets in your project tracker.

A connector gives Claude access. It doesn't teach Claude how you want a job done. That's the next one.

5. Skills: one job, done your way, in any chat

A skill is a way of doing one particular job.

It applies only when a request needs it, in any chat.

It's a small folder of instructions, and sometimes scripts and templates. Its first lines hold a name and a description. Claude reads the description to decide when to use it.

Use them for: the jobs you repeat. The weekly report. The meeting summary. The email in your team's format.

Key point

Skills load in layers. Claude always sees just the name and description of each skill you've switched on, a line or two each. It reads the instructions only when a request matches. So you can install many without slowing Claude down.

My rule: once you've explained the same thing to Claude three times, make it a skill.

Make your first skill, step by step

6. Use them together

They aren't rivals. They work best together.

A connector lets Claude reach your project tracker.

A skill teaches it how your team writes tickets.

Your custom instructions keep the tone plain. A project holds the background for the work you're tracking.

Tip

When something keeps going wrong, ask where the fix belongs. A preference for every chat goes in instructions. Background for one piece of work goes in a project. A job you repeat goes in a skill.

7. The two questions

Not sure? Ask these, in order.

Question 1: Is it a way of doing one particular job?

  • No, and it should apply to every conversation? Custom instructions.
  • No, and it's background for one piece of work? A project.

Question 2: Have you explained it to Claude three times?

  • Not yet? Just ask in the chat. Save the prompt you liked.
  • Yes? Make it a skill.

Need Claude to reach another app along the way? Add a connector.

Before you finish

  • My general preferences are in custom instructions, and nothing job-specific is in there
  • Each big piece of work has its own project with its files
  • The apps Claude needs are connected
  • The job I've explained three times is on my list for a skill

Questions

Can I use all four at once?

Yes. They apply at different moments, so they work together: preferences everywhere, background inside a project, other apps when needed, and a skill when a request needs that job.

Will lots of skills slow Claude down?

No. Claude sees just a line or two per skill until a request needs one.

Where do I start with skills?

item.title: Ten skills worth writing.
item.description: Ten Claude skill ideas for learning, research, your career, everyday work and data, each with what makes it work and a request to try.
item.content:encoded:
People ask me the same question every week.

"I get what a skill is. But what should I actually make one for?"

So here's my answer, in full.

These are the ten skills I wrote for the people I teach.

Each one does one job, the way I'd want it done.

I'll show you what each does, the rules that make it work, and a request to try.

Steal the ideas. Then write your own versions, for the way you work.

What's inside:

  1. Two skills for learning
  2. Two for research
  3. Two for your career
  4. Two for everyday work
  5. One for data
  6. One that writes the others
  7. How to choose your first

Get the next one in your inbox

One practical guide at a time: the exact steps, the prompts to copy and the mistakes to skip.

Free. Delivered by Substack, one click to unsubscribe. Form not showing? Subscribe on Substack.

The ten, on one page

Every skill below follows the same pattern.

A clear job. A few firm rules. One thing it never does.

That last part matters most. A good skill isn't only what Claude does. It's what Claude refuses to do.

Learn and remember

learn-anything

A patient tutor for any topic.

It doesn't start explaining right away. First it asks what you already know.

Then it makes a short plan, and explains one idea at a time, each with an analogy and a small example. Before moving on, it checks you understood.

Why it works: most explanations start in the wrong place. Too basic, and you're bored. Too advanced, and you're lost. Asking first fixes both.

Try
Teach me how neural networks learn. I know basic algebra.

Tip

Always say what you already know. "I know basic algebra" changes the whole explanation.

quiz-me

Turns your notes, a document or a topic into practice questions.

It asks them one at a time. It explains every answer, keeps track of what you miss, and comes back to it.

Why it works: reading notes feels like learning. Answering questions is learning. And coming back to the ones you missed is where it sticks.

Try
Quiz me on these lecture notes. Ten questions, mixed.

Make your own version: the five steps

Research and explain

research-brief

Answers a question with a one-page, sourced brief.

It separates what's known from what's only claimed. It gives each finding a confidence level. And it never invents a source.

Why it works: the danger with AI research isn't a wrong answer. It's a wrong answer that sounds certain. Confidence levels and real sources make the uncertainty visible.

news-explainer

Turns AI and tech news into a plain explainer, in four parts:

  1. What happened
  2. Why it matters
  3. Who it affects
  4. What's still unknown

Every claim is attributed. No hype.

Why it works: the fourth part. Most news coverage skips what isn't known yet. Naming it keeps you honest with your readers.

Try
Explain this announcement for my newsletter readers.

Paste the link or the text under it.

Grow your career

linkedin-post

Writes LinkedIn posts in your own voice, from an idea, a lesson or a piece of work.

You get an opening worth reading and one clear point.

What you don't get: invented stories or engagement bait.

Why it works: it learns your voice from your own old posts. So the post sounds like you on a good day, not like a template.

Try
Turn this project I finished into a post. Here are two of my old posts.

job-application

Tailors your CV and cover letter to one specific job ad.

It matches your real experience to what the employer asks for. And it tells you honestly where the gaps are.

Why it works: honesty. A tailored CV that invents experience falls apart in the interview. One that tells you where you're weak gives you time to prepare.

Try
Here's my CV and the job ad. Tailor both.

Get the next issue by email

One practical guide at a time: the exact steps, the prompts to copy and the mistakes to skip.

Free. Delivered by Substack, one click to unsubscribe. Form not showing? Subscribe on Substack.

Get work done

meeting-to-actions

Turns meeting notes or a transcript into:

  • the decisions
  • the actions, with owners and deadlines
  • the open questions
  • a follow-up email, ready to send

It never invents an owner or a date.

Why it works: a summary nobody acts on is wasted. Owners and deadlines turn a meeting into work that gets done. And refusing to invent them means you find the gaps before they cost you.

Try
Here's the transcript of today's team call.

presentation-planner

Plans a talk before you open slide software:

  • the story
  • one message per slide
  • titles that state the point
  • the visuals
  • the speaker notes

Why it works: most bad decks are a planning problem, not a design problem. Fix the story first, and the slides almost write themselves.

Try
Plan a ten-minute talk on our quarterly results for the board.

Work with data

check-the-numbers

Answers questions about spreadsheets, CSV files and SQL results, and proves the answer first.

A script profiles each file before Claude answers:

  • missing values
  • numbers stored as text
  • repeated rows and keys
  • gaps in the dates

Every join is checked for multiplied rows. And the answer comes with its caveats.

Why it works: this is the skill where a script earns its place. Checking data must come out the same every time, and code does that better than words.

Try
Which products drove last quarter's revenue? Here's the export.

Key point

When a step must be exact (a calculation, a format check, a conversion), put it in a script, not in the instructions.

Make your own

skill-maker

The one that writes the others.

It interviews you about a task you repeat. Then it writes the SKILL.md, checks it against the rules, and packages the folder as a zip, ready to upload.

Why it works: the hardest part of a skill is describing your own job. Being interviewed is much easier than starting from a blank page.

Try
Help me turn the way I write our weekly report into a skill.

The full walkthrough: make your first skill

What a good skill looks like inside

Every skill above is the same shape inside: a name, a description, and short, firm instructions.

Here's how learn-anything could look, so you can see the pattern:

---
name: learn-anything
description: Teaches any topic step by step, starting from what the learner already knows. Use when someone asks to learn, understand or be taught a topic.
---

## Steps
1. Ask what I already know about the topic, and why I want to learn it.
2. Make a short plan: three to five ideas, in order.
3. Explain one idea at a time, with an analogy and a small example.
4. Ask one question to check I understood before moving on.

## Mistakes to avoid
- Don't explain everything in one long answer.
- Don't move on if my answer shows I'm confused.

## Example
(one short exchange you liked)

Notice three things.

The description says what and when. That's how Claude knows to reach for it.

The steps are numbered and short. Claude follows them in order.

The mistakes come from real failures. Every line there is something that went wrong before the skill existed.

Make them yours

These ten are starting points, not finished products.

The best skills capture the tasks you repeat every week, the way your organisation does them.

So before you write your version, ask:

For learning skills

What do you study most? A new tool, a field, a language? Put your level and your goal into the instructions.

For research skills

Which sources do you trust? Which ones should never be cited? Write that down.

For career skills

Paste two of your best posts, or the CV you're proudest of, as the example. That's what teaches Claude your voice.

For work skills

What does your team's format look like? Headings, order, length, tone. The more exact, the better.

For data skills

What goes wrong with your data most often? Missing dates, duplicate rows, text where numbers should be? Make the skill check for exactly that.

Tip

Open a skill, change its steps to match how you work, and upload your version. That's how a generic skill becomes yours.

How to choose your first

Don't write ten.

Look at your last week of chats with Claude. Find the job you explained more than once.

That's your first skill.

Then ask three questions before you start:

  • Is it one job, not three?
  • Have I explained it to Claude three times already?
  • Can I describe when Claude should use it, in one line?

Three ticks? Start writing.

Watch out

Found a ready-made skill online instead? Read every file before you switch it on. A skill can contain code that runs when Claude uses it.

Notice what you had to explain, and what Claude got wrong.

That list is the first draft of your skill.

item.title: Make your first skill.
item.description: Pick the right task, write a SKILL.md Claude can choose from, zip it the right way, and test it with five requests.
item.content:encoded:
Every morning, the same ritual.

You open Claude.

You paste the same long block of instructions.

You explain the format again. The tone. The headings. The thing it got wrong yesterday.

Then you correct the same mistakes.

There's a better way, and it takes about an hour, once.

You teach Claude the job one time, in a skill. From then on, Claude picks it up by itself whenever a request needs it.

No pasting. No re-explaining. Your way, every time.

Here's everything you need to make your first one:

  1. Know when a task deserves a skill
  2. Pick the right first task
  3. Understand what's inside a skill
  4. Write the SKILL.md, and the line that matters most
  5. Write the instructions
  6. Add templates and scripts (only if you need them)
  7. Zip it the right way
  8. Upload it and test it with five requests
  9. Fix it when Claude doesn't use it

Get the next one in your inbox

One practical guide at a time: the exact steps, the prompts to copy and the mistakes to skip.

Free. Delivered by Substack, one click to unsubscribe. Form not showing? Subscribe on Substack.

Know when a task deserves a skill

Not everything should be a skill.

Claude already gives you three other ways to shape how it works. Each one fits a different need:

  • Custom instructions hold your general preferences. They apply to every conversation.
  • Projects hold background documents and knowledge. They apply to the chats inside that project.
  • Connectors give Claude access to other apps and data, such as your drive or calendar, when it needs them.
  • A skill is a way of doing one particular job. It applies only when a request needs it, in any chat.

My rule is simple.

Once you've explained the same thing to Claude three times, make it a skill.

Once is a one-off. Twice is a coincidence. Three times is a job, and jobs deserve skills.

Tip

Skills and connectors work well together. A connector lets Claude reach your project tracker; a skill teaches it how your team writes tickets.

Not sure what a skill is? Start with the guide

Pick the right first task

Your first skill should be boring.

That's a compliment. Boring jobs are the ones you repeat, and the ones you repeat are where a skill pays off fastest.

Good first tasks

  • The weekly report your manager expects in a fixed format.
  • The summary you write after every client meeting.
  • The email you send in your team's tone, again and again.
  • The checklist you run before you send anything important.

Tasks to leave for later

  • A job you do once a quarter. You won't remember to use it.
  • A job that is really three jobs. Split it, or the skill will do all three badly.
  • A job you can't describe yet. If you can't explain it to a colleague, you can't explain it to Claude.

One skill, one job. If you need two jobs, make two skills.

Throughout this issue, I'll use one example: a weekly report.

Understand what's inside a skill

A skill is just a folder.

It has one required file, SKILL.md, and a few optional ones:

weekly-report/
├── SKILL.md        required: name, description and instructions
├── reference.md    optional: detail Claude reads only when it needs it
├── templates/      optional: files to fill in
└── scripts/        optional: code for steps that must be exact

That's the whole thing. No app to build. No code to write, unless you want to.

Why you can have many skills

Skills load in layers.

  1. Always: Claude sees just the name and description of every skill you've switched on. A line or two each.
  2. When a request matches: Claude reads that skill's instructions.
  3. Only if needed: it opens the extra files. Scripts run, and only their results come back.

So ten skills don't slow Claude down. Each one costs a line or two until the moment it's needed.

Key point

This is also why the description matters so much. Most of the time, it's the only part of your skill Claude sees.

Write the SKILL.md

Make a folder named after your skill: weekly-report.

Inside it, make a file called SKILL.md. It starts with a name and a description, between two lines of dashes:

---
name: weekly-report
description: Turns the week's notes and numbers into our team's weekly report format. Use when someone asks for the weekly report or pastes weekly updates.
---

The name

  • Lowercase letters, numbers and hyphens only.
  • 64 characters at most.
  • The same as the folder's name.
  • It can't contain "claude" or "anthropic".

The name is also the command you can type, like /weekly-report.

The description: the line that matters most

Claude decides when to use your skill from the description alone.

Write it badly, and your skill sits there unused. Write it well, and Claude reaches for it at the right moment, every time.

A strong description does two things:

  1. Says what the skill does.
  2. Says when to use it.

Write it in the third person ("Turns the week's notes...", not "I help you..."). Keep it to 200 characters in the Claude apps (the API allows 1,024). No tags in angle brackets.

Compare these two:

Weak
Helps with reports.
Strong
Turns the week's notes and numbers into our team's weekly report format. Use when someone asks for the weekly report or pastes weekly updates.

The first one could mean anything. The second one tells Claude exactly when to step in.

Get the next guide by email

One practical guide at a time: the exact steps, the prompts to copy and the mistakes to skip.

Free. Delivered by Substack, one click to unsubscribe. Form not showing? Subscribe on Substack.

Write the instructions

Below the dashes comes the job itself.

Write it the way you'd brief a sharp new colleague on their first day. Keep it under 500 lines, and include four things:

  1. Numbered steps. What to do, in order.
  2. The mistakes to avoid. The ones Claude made last time.
  3. One short example. A good finished result.
  4. A checklist, if the job is long.

Here's how the weekly report skill could start:

## Steps
1. Read the notes and numbers I paste.
2. Group them under: Wins, Numbers, Risks, Next week.
3. Keep each point to one line.
4. Put the three numbers that changed most at the top of Numbers.

## Mistakes to avoid
- Don't invent numbers. If one is missing, write [missing].
- Don't add a greeting or a sign-off.

## Example
(paste one report you were happy with)

Tip

Your best example is a real one. Paste a report you were proud of, with anything private removed.

Let Claude draft it with you

Don't want to start from a blank page? Ask Claude to interview you first:

Draft it with Claude
Help me turn the way I write our weekly report into a skill. Ask me questions first, then write the SKILL.md.

Answer its questions honestly. Then read what it writes, and change anything that isn't how you work.

Add templates and scripts, only if you need them

Most first skills are a single file. That's fine.

Add more only when the job needs it:

  • reference.md for detail Claude should read only sometimes, like a style guide.
  • templates/ for files to fill in, like a report layout.
  • scripts/ for steps that must come out the same every time: calculations, format checks, conversions.

Link each extra file from SKILL.md, and say when to read it. For example: "For the client list, read reference.md."

Watch out

Never put passwords, API keys or personal data in a skill, in any file.

Zip it the right way

This is where most first uploads fail.

Zip the folder, not the files inside it.

The zip must contain weekly-report/SKILL.md. If the files sit at the top of the zip without their folder, the upload won't work.

  • On a Mac: right-click the folder, then Compress.
  • On Windows: right-click the folder, then Send to → Compressed (zipped) folder.

Right-click the folder, not the files inside it. Then upload the zip as it is. Don't unzip it.

Upload it and test it

Turn skills on

In Claude, open Settings → Capabilities and turn on Create and edit files. In the older layout, it's called Code execution and file creation.

On Team plans, skills are on by default. On Enterprise plans, an owner turns them on first.

Upload

  1. Open Customize → Skills.
  2. Click +, then Create skill → Upload a skill.
  3. Choose your zip.
  4. Check that the skill's switch is on.

Test it with five requests

This is the step everyone skips. Don't.

  1. Write three requests that should use the skill.
  2. Write two that shouldn't.
  3. Try all five.
Your test plan
Should use it:
1. Here are this week's notes. Write the weekly report.
2. Turn these updates into the report for Friday.
3. Weekly report please: [paste notes]

Shouldn't use it:
4. Summarise this article for me.
5. Write a thank-you email to a client.

All five behaved? You're done.

Save this checklist: the skills guide

Fix it when Claude doesn't use it

Claude ignored your skill? Or used it when it shouldn't have?

Fix it in this order:

  1. Check the switch in Customize → Skills. It's off more often than you'd think.
  2. Name it in your request: "Use my weekly-report skill on these notes."
  3. Rewrite the description. It's what Claude uses to choose. Make the "when" more specific.

Then run your five requests again.

Note

In Claude Code, you can also type / and pick a skill from the list. In Claude Code, skills live in folders: ~/.claude/skills/ for every project, or a project's .claude/skills/ folder to share it with your team.

One more shortcut

On a Mac, Cowork can record you doing a task and propose a skill from it, on Pro, Max and Team plans.

What to do today

Open the last chat where you pasted your usual instructions.

Copy them into a SKILL.md.

Give it a name and a description that says what and when.

Zip the folder. Upload it. Run the five requests.

That's your first skill. The second one will be faster.

Newsletter Ten skills worth writing. Mojeed Abisiga · mojeedabisiga.com
NewsletterTen skills worth writing.The ten Claude skills I wrote for the people I teach: what each one does, why it works, and a request to try:

Send this to one colleague who still pastes the same prompt every morning.

item.description: What a Claude skill is, where skills work, how to install one in four steps, how to use it and how to stay safe.
item.content:encoded:
You paste the same long instructions into Claude.

You explain the same format again.

You correct the same mistakes.

A skill ends that. You teach Claude a job once, and it does it your way from then on.

By the end of this guide you'll have:

  • one skill installed and switched on
  • a clear idea of when Claude uses it
  • a short safety check you can run on any skill

You need: a Claude account and ten minutes.

Get the next one in your inbox

One practical guide at a time: the exact steps, the prompts to copy and the mistakes to skip.

Free. Delivered by Substack, one click to unsubscribe. Form not showing? Subscribe on Substack.

1. Know what a skill is

A skill is a small folder of instructions. Sometimes it also holds scripts and templates.

Every skill has one required file: SKILL.md.

Its first lines hold two things:

  • a name, which is also the command you can type, such as /learn-anything
  • a description of what the skill does and when to use it

Below that come the instructions: steps, rules, examples and checklists.

Key point

Claude decides when to use a skill from its description alone. A clear description is the difference between a skill that works and one that sits there.

2. See how skills differ

You already have other ways to shape Claude. Here's where a skill fits:

Feature What it gives Claude When it applies
Custom instructions Your general preferences Every conversation
Projects Background documents and knowledge Chats inside that project
Connectors (MCP) Access to other apps and data When Claude needs that app
Skills A way of doing one job Only when a request needs it, in any chat

They work well together.

A connector lets Claude reach your project tracker. A skill teaches it how your team writes tickets.

3. Check where skills work

Skills work in more places than most people think:

  • Claude on the web and in the desktop app, on every plan from Free to Enterprise, once code execution is on.
  • Claude Code, from folders on your computer.
  • Claude for Excel, PowerPoint, Word and Outlook.
  • Cowork, which uses the skills switched on for your account.
  • The Claude API, in beta, where skills run in a sandbox with no internet access.

Skills also follow an open standard, the Agent Skills specification. A skill you write isn't locked to one product.

4. Turn skills on

Open Settings → Capabilities.

Turn on Create and edit files. In the older Settings layout, it's called Code execution and file creation.

Note

On Team plans, skills are on by default. On Enterprise plans, an owner turns them on first, in Organization settings → Plugins & skills, on the Policy tab.

5. Install a skill

There are two ways to get one.

Ready-made: open Customize → Skills, click +, then Browse skills. You'll find skills from partners such as Notion, Figma and Atlassian, built to work with their connectors.

From a zip (one you made, or one from a source you trust):

  1. Get the skill's zip file. Don't unzip it.
  2. Open Customize → Skills, click +, then Create skill → Upload a skill.
  3. Choose the zip.
  4. Check that the skill's switch is on.

That's it. Ask for something the skill covers.

Make your own skill

6. Use it

You rarely need to do anything special.

Claude reads the descriptions of your skills and uses one by itself when your request matches.

To be sure, name it:

Name the skill
Use my weekly-report skill on these notes.

In Claude Code and in the Microsoft 365 add-ins, you can also type / and pick a skill from the list.

Tip

Claude didn't use the skill you expected? Check that its switch is on, name it in your request, or make its description clearer about when it applies.

7. Add skills to Claude Code

Claude Code reads skills from folders on your computer.

  • For every project: unzip the skill into ~/.claude/skills/, so you end up with ~/.claude/skills/learn-anything/SKILL.md.
  • For one project (and everyone who works on it): unzip it into the project's .claude/skills/ folder and commit it.

Run a skill by typing a slash and its name, or just ask. /skills lists what's installed.

Skills you switch on in your Claude account also sync to Claude Code when you sign in with the same account.

Find skills worth installing

There are three good places to start.

1. Claude's own directory. In Customize → Skills, click +, then Browse skills. You'll find skills from partners such as Notion, Figma and Atlassian, built to work with their connectors.

2. Anthropic's examples. At github.com/anthropics/skills. Good to learn from, and to adapt to the way you work.

3. Your own. The best skills capture the tasks you repeat every week, the way your organisation does them. Nobody else can write those for you.

Make your own

Once you've explained the same thing to Claude three times, it's worth a skill.

The short version:

  1. Make a folder named after the job, like weekly-report.
  2. Write SKILL.md: a name and a description between two lines of dashes, then numbered steps, the mistakes to avoid and one short example.
  3. Zip the folder, not the files inside it.
  4. Upload it in Customize → Skills, and switch it on.
  5. Test it with three requests that should use it and two that shouldn't.

8. Stay safe

A skill can contain code that runs when Claude uses it.

So treat an unknown skill like an unknown app.

Watch out

Never put passwords, API keys or personal data in a skill.

The two main risks:

  • Prompt injection: hidden instructions that steer Claude into something you didn't ask for.
  • Data leaks: a script that sends your information somewhere.

The fix is the same for both: check before you trust. On Enterprise plans, owners can also turn on skill scanning, which checks uploaded skills for malicious content.

Before you finish

  • Create and edit files is on
  • One skill is installed and its switch is on
  • I read every file of that skill before switching it on
  • I asked for something it covers, and Claude used it

Questions

Do many skills slow Claude down?

No. Skills load in layers. Claude always sees just the name and description of each skill you've switched on, a line or two each. It reads the instructions only when a request matches, and extra files only if needed.

When is a skill worth making?

Once you've explained the same thing to Claude three times.
